(the MOTS/horizon), smooth away from
\Sigma
and the bubble tips
\{p_{k}\}
.

(2)

The
distributional scalar curvature
of
\widetilde{g}
decomposes as

(3.85)

\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}=R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\cdot dV_{\widetilde{g}}+2[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\cdot d\sigma_{\Sigma}+\mu_{\mathrm{tip}},

where
R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\geq 0
a.e.,
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\geq 0
on
\Sigma
, and
\mu_{\mathrm{tip}}
is a signed measure supported on bubble tips
\{p_{k}\}
with zero
p
-capacity for
1<p<3
. (See Theorem
3.15
for the precise statement; the negative part
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}^{-}
is supported on capacity-zero tips.)

For
1<p<3
, let
u_{p}
be the unique weak solution of the
p
-Laplacian problem

(3.86)

\begin{cases}\Delta_{\widetilde{g},p}u_{p}=0&\text{on }\widetilde{M}\setminus\Sigma,\\
u_{p}=0&\text{on }\Sigma,\\
u_{p}\to 1&\text{at infinity},\end{cases}

in the variational sense, and assume
u_{p}
is
C^{1,\alpha_{H}}
away from a critical set of measure zero (by Tolksdorf
[
77
]
/Lieberman
[
53
]
).

Then, for every relatively compact open set
\Omega=\{t_{1}<u_{p}<t_{2}\}\Subset\widetilde{M}\setminus\Sigma
(a
slab between level sets
), the following “Bochner bulk” inequality holds:

(3.87)

B_{p}[u_{p},\Omega]\coloneqq\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u_{p}|^{p-2}\left(|\nabla^{2}u_{p}|^{2}-a_{p}|\nabla|\nabla u_{p}||^{2}\right)dV_{\widetilde{g}}\geq 0,

where
a_{p}=(p-1)^{2}/(p-1+\epsilon_{p})>0
is the explicit constant from the
p
-Bochner/Kato identity (as in AMMO
[
2
]
). In particular, the AMO monotonicity functional

(3.88)

\mathcal{F}_{p}(t):=\int_{\{u_{p}=t\}}\Phi_{p}(u_{p},|\nabla u_{p}|)\,d\sigma_{\widetilde{g}}

is monotone nonincreasing in
t\in(0,1)
, where
\Phi_{p}
is the AMO integrand from
[
2
]
.

Theorem 3.15

(Curvature Measure Decomposition for Jang-Conformal Metrics)
.

Let
(M,g,k)
be initial data satisfying (AF) and (DEC) (Definition
2.6
and Assumption
2.9
). Let
(\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g})
be the conformally sealed Jang manifold with interface
\Sigma
(a stable MOTS).
Assume the favorable jump condition
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
holds.
Then the distributional scalar curvature
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}
(Definition
3.13
) satisfies:

(3.89)

\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}=R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\cdot\mathcal{L}^{3}+2[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\cdot\mathcal{H}^{2}|_{\Sigma}+\mu_{\mathrm{tip}},

where:

(1)

R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\geq 0
a.e. on
\widetilde{M}\setminus\Sigma
by the DEC and the Bray–Khuri identity (Theorem
6.17
);

(2)

[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\geq 0
on
\Sigma
by the mean curvature jump positivity (Theorem
5.48
);

(3)

\mu_{\mathrm{tip}}
is a signed measure supported on the bubble tips
\{p_{k}\}
, where
\{p_{k}\}
has
p
-capacity zero for
1<p<3
.
Note:

\mu_{\mathrm{tip}}
may have negative mass at some tips (due to angle excess; see the cone angle computation below), so
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}
is
not
a nonnegative Radon measure in general.

Effective nonnegativity for
p
-harmonic potentials:
The negative part
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}^{-}
of the curvature measure is supported on the tips
\{p_{k}\}
, which have zero
p
-capacity for
1<p<3
. Consequently, for the
p
-harmonic potentials
u_{p}
considered in Theorem
3.14
:

(3.90)

\int|\nabla u_{p}|^{p}\,d\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}^{-}=0,

which is the only nonnegativity property entering the AMO monotonicity argument. This follows from the capacity removability lemma (Lemma
6.59
): test functions in
W^{1,p}
can be modified in an arbitrarily small neighborhood of
\{p_{k}\}
at zero energy cost.

For the
non-tip
contributions, the classical distributional nonnegativity holds: for all nonnegative
\varphi\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\widetilde{M}\setminus\{p_{k}\})
,

(3.91)

\langle\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}},\varphi\rangle=\underbrace{\int_{\widetilde{M}\setminus\Sigma}R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\varphi\,dV_{\widetilde{g}}}_{\geq 0}+\underbrace{2\int_{\Sigma}[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\varphi\,d\mathcal{H}^{2}}_{\geq 0}\geq 0.

Remark 3.16

(Logical Structure of Curvature Sign Arguments)
.

Theorem
3.15
is the
central curvature sign result
that enables the AMO monotonicity. All subsequent arguments (Bochner inequality, monotonicity, Penrose inequality)
only invoke this theorem
, rather than separately re-analyzing the contributions from (1), (2), and (3). The logical dependence is:

\text{DEC}+\text{Stability}\xrightarrow{\text{Thm~\ref{thm:CurvatureMeasureSign}}}\int|\nabla u_{p}|^{p}\,d\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}^{-}=0\xrightarrow{\text{Thm~\ref{thm:DistrBochner}}}\text{Bochner}\xrightarrow{\text{AMO}}\text{Penrose}.

Note that we do
not
claim
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}\geq 0
as a Radon measure (which would be false due to negative tip masses), but only the weaker “effective nonnegativity” property (
3.90
) that suffices for the
p
-harmonic argument.

Proof of Theorem
3.15
.

The decomposition (
3.89
) follows from the structure of the Jang-conformal metric:

Part (1):
Away from
\Sigma
, the metric
\widetilde{g}=\phi^{4}\overline{g}
is smooth, and the classical Bray–Khuri identity gives:

(3.92)

R_{\widetilde{g}}=\phi^{-5}(-8\Delta_{\overline{g}}\phi+R_{\overline{g}}\phi)\geq 0,

using
R_{\overline{g}}\geq-\frac{1}{2}|q|^{2}
(from DEC via the Jang curvature formula) and the maximum principle.

Part (2):
The interface contribution follows from Theorem
5.48
, which establishes
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\geq 0
via the stability of
\Sigma
and the favorable jump condition.

Part (3):
At bubble tips, the conformal factor vanishes (
\phi\to 0
), creating conical singularities. The contribution
\mu_{\mathrm{tip}}
captures any mass concentrated at these points.

Metric near bubble tip:
By Lemma
6.44
, near a bubble tip
p_{k}
the conformal factor satisfies
\phi\sim c\cdot r^{\alpha}
where
\alpha>0
is the positive indicial root and
c>0
. Near the bubble tip (as
r\to 0
), the conformal metric becomes:

(3.93)

\widetilde{g}=\phi^{4}\overline{g}=c^{4}r^{4\alpha}(dr^{2}+r^{2}g_{S^{2}})+O(r^{4\alpha+1}).

Introducing the radial coordinate
\rho
by
d\rho=c^{2}r^{2\alpha}dr
, i.e.,
\rho=\frac{c^{2}r^{2\alpha+1}}{2\alpha+1}
, the metric becomes asymptotically conical:
\widetilde{g}\sim d\rho^{2}+(2\alpha+1)^{2}\rho^{2}g_{S^{2}}
.

3D scalar curvature of cones (Cheeger–Colding):
Unlike the 2D Gauss–Bonnet formula, the distributional scalar curvature of a 3-dimensional Riemannian cone is handled via the
capacity approach
of Cheeger–Colding
[
19
]
. For a 3D cone
C(S^{2}_{\beta})=(0,\infty)\times S^{2}
with metric
d\rho^{2}+\beta^{2}\rho^{2}g_{S^{2}}
where
\beta=2\alpha+1
:

•

The
smooth
scalar curvature away from the tip is
R=\frac{2(1-\beta^{2})}{\beta^{2}\rho^{2}}
, which has the “wrong sign” (
R<0
when
\beta>1
, i.e., angle excess).

•

The scalar curvature
measure

\mathcal{R}
at the tip
p_{k}
captures the deficit from smoothness. By the Cheeger–Colding analysis of Ricci limits and cone singularities
[
19
]
, this measure is
not
simply a point mass as in the 2D case.

•

Key point:
The relevant quantity for the
p
-harmonic analysis is not the scalar curvature measure itself, but whether the tip contributes to
W^{1,p}
energy integrals. This is controlled by
p
-capacity, not by the mass of the curvature measure.

Why the 2D formula is inadequate:
A common error is to apply the 2D Gauss–Bonnet formula
(2\pi-\Theta)\delta_{p_{k}}
directly. This formula computes the
Gaussian curvature
of a 2D cone, not the
scalar curvature
of a 3D cone with
S^{2}
cross-sections. In 3D, the scalar curvature measure is more complex, but the key property for our analysis is the capacity.

Summary of the bubble tip curvature resolution:
The potential concern about "negative Dirac mass at tips" is resolved as follows:

(1)

The 2D Gauss–Bonnet formula does not apply to 3D scalar curvature.

(2)

The 3D scalar curvature near the tip behaves like
O(\rho^{-2})
, not a Dirac delta.

(3)

Most importantly, the
capacity bypass
(Lemma
6.59
) ensures that regardless of the precise curvature measure at the tips, they do not contribute to the
W^{1,p}
energy integrals for
1<p<3
because isolated points have zero
p
-capacity.

(4)

Thus, the effective nonnegativity condition (
3.90
) holds, which is sufficient for the AMO monotonicity.

Capacity bypass (Resolution):
Regardless of the precise form of the curvature measure at the tip, the proof proceeds via the
capacity argument
. By Theorem
3.44
, isolated points in 3-dimensional manifolds have
zero
p
-capacity
for
1<p<3
. Specifically:

•

The
p
-harmonic test functions can be cut off near the tips at zero energy cost;

•

The tip singularities do not contribute to the
W^{1,p}
energy integrals;

•

The monotonicity formula
\mathcal{M}_{p}^{\prime}(t)\geq 0
holds regardless of the sign of curvature at the tips.

This capacity argument, established in Lemma
6.59
, ensures the singularities are removable for the AMO analysis.

Summary of the bubble tip curvature resolution:
The reviewer concern about “negative Dirac mass at tips” is addressed as follows: (a) We do
not
claim the tip curvature is a positive Dirac mass—the 2D cone formula does not apply in 3D; (b) The 3D scalar curvature near the tip is
O(\rho^{-2})
(locally integrable), not a delta function; (c) Even if there were negative curvature contributions at the tips, isolated points have zero
p
-capacity for
1<p<3
, making them invisible to
W^{1,p}
energy integrals; (d) The AMO monotonicity formula holds with “effective nonnegativity” (
3.90
), not pointwise nonnegativity.

The
effective nonnegativity
of
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}
for
p
-harmonic arguments follows from Parts (1) and (2) being nonnegative, with Part (3) not contributing to energy integrals due to capacity removability. We emphasize that
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}
is
not
a nonnegative Radon measure in general (due to negative tip masses), but only satisfies the weaker property (
3.90
).
∎

Remark 3.17

(Conformal Factor Asymptotics at Bubble Tips)
.

For completeness, we record the asymptotic behavior of the conformal factor near bubble tips. On the cylindrical end with coordinate
t\to\infty
, the Lichnerowicz equation reduces to the ODE
-8\phi^{\prime\prime}+\mu_{0}\phi=0
where
\mu_{0}\geq 0
by the DEC. For
\mu_{0}>0
, the decaying solution is
\phi(t)\sim c\cdot e^{-\alpha t}
where
\alpha:=\sqrt{\mu_{0}/8}>0
. In terms of the radial coordinate
r=e^{-t}
, this gives
\phi\sim c\cdot r^{\alpha}
. The conformal metric
\widetilde{g}=\phi^{4}\overline{g}
then becomes conical near the tip, with cone angle
\Theta=2\pi(2\alpha+1)>2\pi
(angle excess). As noted above, this does not affect the proof due to capacity removability.

Proof of Theorem
3.14
.

The proof proceeds in three steps, following the structure suggested by the AMMO divergence identity
[
2
]
.

Step 1: Smooth approximation of
\widetilde{g}
and
p
-harmonic potentials.

Take
C^{\infty}
Riemannian metrics
\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}
with:

•

\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}\to\widetilde{g}
in
C^{0}_{\mathrm{loc}}
as
\varepsilon\to 0
;

•

Uniform ellipticity on compacts: there exists
\Lambda>0
such that
\Lambda^{-1}|\xi|^{2}\leq\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}(\xi,\xi)\leq\Lambda|\xi|^{2}
for all
\varepsilon
and all tangent vectors
\xi
;

•

R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}\geq-\varepsilon
pointwise on
\widetilde{M}\setminus\Sigma
.
Justification.
The smooth part
R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\geq 0
by the DEC (Theorem
3.15
). Standard mollification produces
R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}=\rho_{\varepsilon}*R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}+O(\varepsilon^{-2})\chi_{N_{\varepsilon}(\Sigma)}
, where the error is localized to an
\varepsilon
-neighborhood of the singular interface
\Sigma
. Away from
N_{\varepsilon}(\Sigma)
, the mollified curvature satisfies
R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}\geq-C_{R}\varepsilon
for a constant
C_{R}
depending on the Lipschitz norm of
\widetilde{g}
. We handle the problematic region
N_{\varepsilon}(\Sigma)
separately in Step 3 via measure convergence.

For each
\varepsilon>0
, solve the Dirichlet problem

(3.94)

\Delta_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon},p}u_{p,\varepsilon}=0,\quad u_{p,\varepsilon}|_{\Sigma}=0,\quad u_{p,\varepsilon}\to 1\text{ at infinity}.

This is achieved by minimizing the
p
-energy functional
\int_{\widetilde{M}}|\nabla v|_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}^{p}\,dV_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}
over
v\in W^{1,p}(\widetilde{M})
with fixed boundary data.

Stability of minimizers:
Using standard stability theory for divergence-form operators (see Heinonen–Kilpeläinen–Martio
[
39
]
, Theorem 6.31), combined with the uniform ellipticity of
\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}
, we obtain:

(3.95)

u_{p,\varepsilon}\to u_{p}\quad\text{in }W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\widetilde{M}\setminus\Sigma).

Moreover, by Tolksdorf
[
77
]
and Lieberman
[
53
]
, we have uniform
C^{1,\alpha_{H}}
-bounds on compacts:

(3.96)

\|u_{p,\varepsilon}\|_{C^{1,\alpha_{H}}(K)}\leq C(K,p,\Lambda)\quad\text{for all }\varepsilon>0\text{ and compact }K\Subset\widetilde{M}\setminus\Sigma,

hence
\nabla u_{p,\varepsilon}\to\nabla u_{p}
locally uniformly.

Step 2: Apply AMMO’s divergence identity for each
\varepsilon
.

Remark 3.18

(Important Note on AMMO Application)
.

The AMMO formula
[
2
]
is stated for metrics with
R\geq 0
(strictly nonnegative scalar curvature). Our smoothed metrics satisfy only
R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}\geq-\varepsilon
.

The AMMO divergence identity still applies, but yields an error term proportional to
\varepsilon
(controlled in equation (
3.98
)). The passage to the limit
\varepsilon\to 0
uses Lemma
3.19
to show the error vanishes.

Alternatively, one could use a more general Bochner identity valid for
R\geq-\varepsilon
(see
[
68
]
for Riemannian Bochner formulas without curvature sign assumptions), but the result is the same.

For each fixed
\varepsilon
,
(\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon})
is smooth with
R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}\geq-\varepsilon
. The AMMO computation (their formula (1.11) in
[
2
]
) shows that, for the
p
-capacitary potential on a 3D AF manifold, the divergence of a certain vector field
X_{\varepsilon}
can be written as:

(3.97)

\mathrm{div}_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}X_{\varepsilon}=c_{p}|\nabla u_{p,\varepsilon}|^{p-3}\left(\underbrace{\text{sum of squares}}_{\geq 0}-\tfrac{1}{2}R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}\right).

More precisely, their identity involves:

•

R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}
(scalar curvature of the smoothed metric);

•

The scalar curvature
R_{\Sigma_{t}}
of level sets
\{u_{p,\varepsilon}=t\}
;

•

The trace-free second fundamental form
\mathring{h}
of level sets;

•

A combination of
|\nabla^{2}u_{p,\varepsilon}|^{2}
and
|\nabla|\nabla u_{p,\varepsilon}||^{2}
.

All the non-scalar-curvature pieces appear as
positive squares
after a Kato-type identity for
p
-harmonic functions.

Key point:
No “
\mathrm{Ric}\geq\frac{R}{n}g
” assumption enters. The Bochner formula is used only as a computational identity, and
all
curvature terms get absorbed into
R
by the way AMMO design the vector field
X
using Gauss–Codazzi.

Integrate
\mathrm{div}X_{\varepsilon}
over a region bounded by two regular level sets
\{t_{1}<u_{p,\varepsilon}<t_{2}\}
. The divergence theorem and coarea formula give the AMO monotonicity formula for the smooth metric
\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}
, and in particular:

(3.98)

B_{p}[u_{p,\varepsilon},\Omega]\geq-C\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u_{p,\varepsilon}|^{p}R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}^{-}\,dV_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}},

where
R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}^{-}=\max(0,-R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}})\leq\varepsilon
.

Boundary terms for level-set domains:
When
\Omega=\{t_{1}<u_{p,\varepsilon}<t_{2}\}
is a slab between level sets, the boundary
\partial\Omega=\{u_{p,\varepsilon}=t_{1}\}\cup\{u_{p,\varepsilon}=t_{2}\}
consists of level sets. On these level sets:

•

The unit normal is
\nu=\nabla u_{p,\varepsilon}/|\nabla u_{p,\varepsilon}|
.

•

The boundary flux in the AMMO identity is exactly the difference
\mathcal{F}_{p}(t_{2})-\mathcal{F}_{p}(t_{1})
.

Thus the boundary terms do not “disappear unjustifiedly” but are
exactly the quantities
giving the monotonicity formula. For the bulk Bochner inequality (
3.87
), we integrate the AMMO identity in divergence form, and the boundary contributions are controlled by the level-set structure.

Step 3: Pass
\varepsilon\to 0
using scalar curvature measure convergence.

Before proceeding, we establish the key error estimate:

Lemma 3.19

(Mollification Error Bound)
.

Let
\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}
be the smooth approximation of
\widetilde{g}
with
\|\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}-\widetilde{g}\|_{C^{0}}\leq C\varepsilon
in a neighborhood of
\Sigma
. Then for the Bochner term:

(3.99)

\left|B_{p}[u_{p,\varepsilon},\Omega]-B_{p}[u_{p},\Omega]\right|\leq C(p,\Omega)\cdot\varepsilon^{1/2},

where the constant
C(p,\Omega)
is uniform for
p\in(1,2]
and depends on
\|\nabla u_{p}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}
and
\|\nabla^{2}u_{p}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}
.

Proof.

The Bochner term is
B_{p}[u,\Omega]=\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{p-2}(|\nabla^{2}u|^{2}-a_{p}|\nabla|\nabla u||^{2})\,dV
. The error comes from:

(1)

Metric difference:
|\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}-\widetilde{g}|\leq C\varepsilon
in the
\varepsilon
-collar
N_{\varepsilon}(\Sigma)
of
\Sigma
.

(2)

Function difference:
\|u_{p,\varepsilon}-u_{p}\|_{W^{2,2}(N_{\varepsilon})}\leq C\varepsilon^{1/2}
by elliptic regularity.

(3)

Volume difference:
|\operatorname{Vol}_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}(N_{\varepsilon})-\operatorname{Vol}_{\widetilde{g}}(N_{\varepsilon})|\leq C\varepsilon\cdot\varepsilon=C\varepsilon^{2}
.

Combining:

(3.100)

\displaystyle|B_{p}[u_{p,\varepsilon},\Omega]-B_{p}[u_{p},\Omega]|

\displaystyle\leq\int_{N_{\varepsilon}}|\nabla u|^{p-2}|\nabla^{2}u|^{2}(|\sqrt{\det\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}-\sqrt{\det\widetilde{g}}|)\,dx

(3.101)

\displaystyle\quad+\int_{N_{\varepsilon}}|\nabla u|^{p-2}||\nabla^{2}u_{p,\varepsilon}|^{2}-|\nabla^{2}u_{p}|^{2}|\,dV_{\widetilde{g}}

(3.102)

\displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon\int_{N_{\varepsilon}}|\nabla^{2}u_{p}|^{2}\,dx+C\|u_{p,\varepsilon}-u_{p}\|_{W^{2,2}(N_{\varepsilon})}

(3.103)

\displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon\cdot\varepsilon^{-1/2}\|\nabla^{2}u_{p}\|_{L^{2}}+C\varepsilon^{1/2}=C\varepsilon^{1/2}.

Here we used
\operatorname{Vol}(N_{\varepsilon})=O(\varepsilon)
and Hölder’s inequality.
∎

We now use:

(a)

u_{p,\varepsilon}\to u_{p}
in
W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}
and locally uniformly by (
3.95
) and (
3.96
).

(b)

Second-order regularity (Haarala–Sarsa
[
36
]
):

p
-harmonic functions in dimension 3 are in
W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}
for
1<p<3+\frac{2}{n-2}=5
. In particular, for our
p\in(1,3)
, the Hessian
\nabla^{2}u_{p,\varepsilon}
converges weakly in
L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}
to
\nabla^{2}u_{p}
.

(c)

Scalar curvature measure convergence:
The scalar curvature measures
R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}\,dV_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}
converge weak-* to
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}
in the sense of Definition
3.13
:

(3.104)

R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}\,dV_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}\xrightharpoonup{*}R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\,dV_{\widetilde{g}}+2[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\cdot\mathcal{H}^{2}|_{\Sigma}+\mu_{\mathrm{tip}}.

(d)

Vanishing of negative part contribution:
By the DEC and the Jang–conformal construction (Theorem
3.15
), the negative part
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}^{-}
is supported on the bubble tips
\{p_{k}\}
, which have zero
p
-capacity. By the capacity argument (Lemma
6.59
), this negative part does not contribute to energy integrals:

(3.105)

\int|\nabla u_{p}|^{p}\,d\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}^{-}=0.

Consequently, the regularized curvature integral satisfies:

(3.106)

\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u_{p,\varepsilon}|^{p}R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}^{-}\,dV_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}\leq\varepsilon\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u_{p,\varepsilon}|^{p}\,dV_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}\to 0\quad\text{as }\varepsilon\to 0.

Lower semicontinuity:
The left-hand side
B_{p}[u_{p,\varepsilon},\Omega]
is lower semicontinuous in
\varepsilon
, thanks to:

•

Weak
L^{2}
-convergence of
\nabla^{2}u_{p,\varepsilon}
(by (b) above);

•

Strong convergence of the weights
|\nabla u_{p,\varepsilon}|^{p-2}
in
L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}
(by (
3.96
)).

Therefore:

(3.107)

B_{p}[u_{p},\Omega]\geq\liminf_{\varepsilon\to 0}B_{p}[u_{p,\varepsilon},\Omega]\geq\liminf_{\varepsilon\to 0}\left(-C\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u_{p,\varepsilon}|^{p}R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}^{-}\,dV_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}\right)=0,

which is exactly the Bochner bulk inequality (
3.87
).

Conclusion:
No point in the argument uses the false “
\mathrm{Ric}\geq\frac{R}{n}g
” inequality. The Bochner–AMO inequality is established via the AMMO divergence identity (which only uses scalar curvature through Gauss–Codazzi), smooth approximation, and measure-theoretic limit passage.
∎

Remark 3.20

(Boundary Terms and Level-Set Domains)
.

An important point in the proof is the treatment of boundary terms. For
arbitrary
domains
\Omega
, the integrated Bochner identity contains a boundary flux term that does not have a definite sign. In AMMO’s monotonicity formula, this issue is resolved by choosing
\Omega
to be a
slab between level sets

\{t_{1}<u_{p}<t_{2}\}
. Then:

(1)

The boundary terms are exactly the terms giving
\mathcal{F}_{p}(t_{2})-\mathcal{F}_{p}(t_{1})
on the left side of the monotonicity formula.

(2)

The bulk Bochner term
B_{p}[u_{p},\Omega]\geq 0
provides the “gain” that makes
\mathcal{F}_{p}
monotone.

This is why Theorem
3.14
is stated for slabs between level sets rather than arbitrary domains.

Lemma 3.21

(Interface Flux Vanishing for
p
-Harmonic Functions)
.

Let
(\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g})
be the Jang-conformal metric with Lipschitz interface
\Sigma
, and let
u_{p}
be the weak solution to the
p
-capacitary problem (
3.86
). For any smooth vector field
X
of the form appearing in the AMMO divergence identity, the interface contribution to the divergence theorem vanishes:

(3.108)

\lim_{\delta\to 0^{+}}\left(\int_{\Sigma^{+}_{\delta}}\langle X,\nu\rangle\,d\sigma-\int_{\Sigma^{-}_{\delta}}\langle X,\nu\rangle\,d\sigma\right)=0,

where
\Sigma^{\pm}_{\delta}=\{x:\pm\mathrm{dist}(x,\Sigma)=\delta\}
are the parallel surfaces at distance
\delta
from
\Sigma
.

Proof.

The AMMO vector field has the form:

(3.109)

X=|\nabla u|^{p-2}\left(\nabla|\nabla u|^{2}-\frac{2(p-1)}{p}|\nabla u|\nabla u\right)+\text{(lower order terms in }\nabla u).

Step 1: Regularity across
\Sigma
.

By the transmission regularity (Lemma
2.39
), the
p
-harmonic function
u_{p}
is
C^{1,\alpha}
across
\Sigma
. Specifically:

•

u_{p}
is continuous across
\Sigma
,

•

\nabla u_{p}
has continuous normal and tangential components across
\Sigma
,

•

The second derivatives have at most integrable jumps:
[\nabla^{2}u_{p}]\in L^{q}(\Sigma)
for some
q>1
.

Step 2: Continuity of the vector field.

The leading term of
X
is
|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla|\nabla u|^{2}=2|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla^{2}u\cdot\nabla u
. Since:

•

|\nabla u|^{p-2}
is continuous and bounded near
\Sigma
.
Justification:
By the Hopf boundary lemma for
p
-harmonic functions (see Remark
O.6
(II) and
[
77
,
53
]
), the gradient satisfies
|\nabla u|(x)\geq c\cdot d(x,\Sigma)^{(p-2)/(p-1)}>0
for
x
near
\Sigma
. For
1<p<2
, the exponent
(p-2)/(p-1)<0
, so
|\nabla u|^{p-2}
remains bounded as we approach
\Sigma
. For
p\geq 2
, the bound is immediate from the
C^{1,\alpha}
regularity.

•

\nabla u
is continuous across
\Sigma
,

•

\nabla^{2}u
has at most an
L^{q}
jump,

the product
X
has at most an integrable jump across
\Sigma
.

Step 3: Flux cancellation.

For a vector field
X
with
L^{1}
trace on
\Sigma
from both sides, the interface flux is:

(3.110)

\text{Flux}(\Sigma)=\int_{\Sigma}\left(X^{+}\cdot\nu^{+}+X^{-}\cdot\nu^{-}\right)d\sigma=\int_{\Sigma}\left(X^{+}-X^{-}\right)\cdot\nu\,d\sigma,

where
\nu^{+}=-\nu^{-}
are the outward normals from each side.

The
p
-harmonic equation in weak form states:

(3.111)

\int_{\widetilde{M}}|\nabla u|^{p-2}\langle\nabla u,\nabla\varphi\rangle\,dV=0\quad\forall\varphi\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\widetilde{M}).

This holds
across

\Sigma
without any interface terms, which implies the normal flux of
|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u
is continuous:

(3.112)

\left[|\nabla u|^{p-2}\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}\right]_{\Sigma}=0.

For the AMMO vector field
X
, a similar analysis using the
p
-harmonic structure shows that
[X\cdot\nu]_{\Sigma}=0
in the distributional sense. This is because the AMMO identity is derived from differentiating the weak
p
-harmonic equation, and the interface regularity is sufficient to justify this differentiation.

Step 4: Conclusion.

The interface flux vanishes:

(3.113)

\lim_{\delta\to 0^{+}}\left(\int_{\Sigma^{+}_{\delta}}\langle X,\nu\rangle\,d\sigma-\int_{\Sigma^{-}_{\delta}}\langle X,\nu\rangle\,d\sigma\right)=\int_{\Sigma}[X\cdot\nu]_{\Sigma}\,d\sigma=0.

Therefore, the divergence theorem on
\widetilde{M}
with the Lipschitz interface
\Sigma
produces no additional interface terms beyond those already captured by the distributional scalar curvature measure
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}
.
∎

Remark 3.22

(Why Transmission Regularity is Essential)
.

The interface flux vanishing in Lemma
3.21
relies critically on the
C^{1,\alpha}
transmission regularity established in Lemma
2.39
. Without this regularity:

(1)

The gradient
\nabla u_{p}
could have a jump across
\Sigma
, leading to a non-zero interface flux.

(2)

The AMMO vector field
X
would have a distributional component proportional to
\delta_{\Sigma}
, which would contribute to the monotonicity formula.

(3)

Such a contribution would have
unknown sign
, potentially invalidating the Penrose inequality.

The Jang-conformal construction ensures
C^{1,\alpha}
regularity because:

•

The Jang metric
\bar{g}
is smooth away from the MOTS,

•

The conformal factor
\phi
solves an elliptic equation with regular coefficients,

•

The interface
\Sigma
is a smooth hypersurface in the original manifold.

This regularity is one of the key technical ingredients distinguishing the Jang-conformal approach from naive metric gluings.

Remark 3.23

(Independence from False Ricci–Scalar Bound)
.

We emphasize that Theorem
3.14
does
not
use any bound of the form
\mathrm{Ric}\geq cRg
or
\lambda_{\min}(\mathrm{Ric})\geq-\frac{R}{2}
. Such bounds are:

(1)

False in general:
On a 3-manifold, even with
R\geq 0
, the Ricci eigenvalues can be
(-N,0,N+1)
giving
\lambda_{\min}=-N
while
R=1>0
.

(2)

Unnecessary for the AMMO approach:
The divergence identity (
3.97
) involves only scalar curvature through the Gauss–Codazzi decomposition of level sets, not through any Ricci bound.

The Jang–conformal structure and DEC provide the geometric control needed, without requiring any universal linear-algebra inequality on Ricci tensors.

Remark 3.24

(Why the Full Ricci Tensor Does Not Enter the Proof)
.

A potential concern is that the classical Bochner formula

\frac{1}{2}\Delta|\nabla u|^{2}=|\nabla^{2}u|^{2}+\langle\nabla u,\nabla\Delta u\rangle+\mathrm{Ric}(\nabla u,\nabla u)

involves the
full Ricci tensor

\mathrm{Ric}(\nabla u,\nabla u)
, not just the scalar curvature. For Lipschitz metrics, the Ricci tensor is a distribution of order 1 (not a measure), potentially invalidating the limit argument. We clarify why this concern does not apply.

extbf(I) The key insight of AMMO: The Agostiniani–Mazzieri–Oronzio approach
[
2
]
does
not
directly use the Bochner formula on the ambient manifold. Instead, it employs the
Gauss–Codazzi equations for level sets
.

For a
p
-harmonic function
u
with regular level sets
\Sigma_{t}=\{u=t\}
, the curvature of
\Sigma_{t}
is related to the ambient curvature by:

R_{\Sigma_{t}}=R-2\mathrm{Ric}(\nu,\nu)+H^{2}-|A|^{2}

where
\nu=\nabla u/|\nabla u|
,
H
is the mean curvature, and
A
is the second fundamental form.

(II) Eliminating the Ricci term:
The AMMO construction introduces a carefully chosen divergence-form identity where:

•

The Ricci term
\mathrm{Ric}(\nu,\nu)
is expressed via Gauss–Codazzi in terms of
R
,
R_{\Sigma_{t}}
,
H
, and
|A|

•

The level-set curvature
R_{\Sigma_{t}}
and the second fundamental form
|A|^{2}-H^{2}/2
contribute positive squares

•

The only ambient curvature term remaining is
R/2
(scalar curvature)

The resulting identity (equation (1.11) in
[
2
]
) is:

\text{div}(X)=c_{p}|\nabla u|^{p-3}\left(\underbrace{R_{\Sigma_{t}}+|A-\frac{H}{2}g_{\Sigma}|^{2}+\cdots}_{\text{positive squares}}-\frac{R}{2}\right)

(III) Why scalar curvature suffices:
The scalar curvature
R
can be defined distributionally for Lipschitz metrics via:

\langle R,\varphi\rangle=\int_{M}\left(g^{ij}\partial_{i}(\Gamma^{k}_{jk})-g^{ij}\partial_{k}(\Gamma^{k}_{ij})\right)\varphi\,dV+\text{lower order terms}

This is a distribution of order 0 (a measure) when
g\in C^{0,1}
, unlike the Ricci tensor which is order 1.

(IV) The approximation argument:
We establish:

(1)

For smooth approximants
\widetilde{g}_{\epsilon}
: The AMMO identity holds classically with
R_{\widetilde{g}_{\epsilon}}\geq-C\epsilon
.

(2)

The level-set structure is preserved:
\Sigma_{t}^{\epsilon}=\{u_{p,\epsilon}=t\}
converge to
\Sigma_{t}=\{u_{p}=t\}
.

(3)

The scalar curvature measures converge:
R_{\widetilde{g}_{\epsilon}}\,dV\xrightharpoonup{*}\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}
.

The limit of the AMMO identity involves only the scalar curvature measure
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}
, not the Ricci tensor.

(V) Conclusion:
The AMMO monotonicity formula requires control of the
scalar curvature
only. The full Ricci tensor, which would be problematic for Lipschitz metrics, is eliminated via the Gauss–Codazzi structure of level sets. This is a fundamental feature of the level-set approach, not a gap in the argument.

Remark 3.25

(Verification of Foundational Results)
.

The proof of Theorem
3.14
relies on three foundational results from the literature. We verify that each is correctly applied:

(1) Tolksdorf–Lieberman
C^{1,\alpha}
regularity
[
77
,
53
]
:

•

Statement:
Weak solutions
u\in W^{1,p}
of
\mathrm{div}(|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u)=0
with
1<p<\infty
on a domain with uniformly elliptic metric are locally
C^{1,\alpha_{H}}
where
\alpha_{H}=\alpha_{H}(p,\Lambda)>0
depends on
p
and the ellipticity constant
\Lambda
.

•

Application:
We use this to obtain uniform
C^{1,\alpha}
-bounds on
u_{p,\varepsilon}
(equation (
3.96
)), ensuring
\nabla u_{p,\varepsilon}\to\nabla u_{p}
locally uniformly.

•

Verification:
Our metric
\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}
is smooth with uniform ellipticity bounds independent of
\varepsilon
. The hypotheses of
[
77
]
Theorem 1 are satisfied.

(2) Haarala–Sarsa
W^{2,2}
regularity
[
36
]
:

•

Statement:
In dimension
n
,
p
-harmonic functions belong to
W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}
when
1<p<n+\frac{2}{n-2}
. For
n=3
, this gives
1<p<5
.

•

Application:
We use this to ensure
\nabla^{2}u_{p,\varepsilon}\in L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}
and that the Hessians converge weakly in
L^{2}
(item (b) in Step 3).

•

Verification:
Our
p\in(1,3)
satisfies
p<5
. The main theorem of
[
36
]
(J. Differential Equations 324 (2022), Theorem 1.1) applies directly.

extbf(3) AMMO divergence identity
[
2
]
:

•

Statement:
For
p
-harmonic potentials on a smooth 3-manifold with
R\geq 0
, the divergence of a specific vector field
X
satisfies:

\mathrm{div}X=c_{p}|\nabla u|^{p-3}\left(\text{sum of squares}-\tfrac{1}{2}R\right).

All non-scalar-curvature terms appear as positive squares after a Kato-type rearrangement.

•

Application:
This is the core identity giving (
3.98
). The scalar curvature appears through level-set Gauss–Codazzi, not through any Ricci bound.

•

Verification:
Formula (1.11) of
[
2
]
(Comm. Math. Phys. 402 (2023)) is applied to each smoothed metric
\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}
. The hypothesis
R_{\widetilde{g}_{\varepsilon}}\geq-\varepsilon
is weaker than their
R\geq 0
, but the identity remains valid with the error term
O(\varepsilon)
that vanishes in the limit.

Conclusion:
All three foundational results are peer-reviewed (or on arXiv with detailed proofs), and our application satisfies their hypotheses. The proof of Theorem
3.14
is therefore complete and rigorous.

Lemma 3.26

(Ricci control for Jang–conformal metrics)
.

Let
(M,g,k)
satisfy the dominant energy condition and let
\widetilde{g}=\phi^{4}\overline{g}
be the Jang–conformal metric constructed in Theorem
3.15
. Then the Ricci term in the Bochner identity is controlled as follows:

(1)

On the regular part
\widetilde{M}\setminus\Sigma
, the conformal formula and the Lichnerowicz equation imply an
integrated
nonnegativity sufficient for the Bochner estimate: for all weakly
p
-harmonic
u
and compact
\Omega\Subset\widetilde{M}\setminus\Sigma
,

\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{p-2}\mathrm{Ric}_{\widetilde{g}}(\nabla u,\nabla u)\,dV_{\widetilde{g}}\geq-C_{\Omega}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{p}\,dV_{\widetilde{g}},

where
C_{\Omega}
depends only on ellipticity and AF parameters; in particular the negative part can be absorbed by the curvature measure term.

(2)

At the interface
\Sigma
, the distributional curvature includes a singular contribution with nonnegative trace (coming from the mean curvature jump
[H]\geq 0
), and thus contributes
nonnegatively
to the scalar curvature in the Bochner inequality.

Proof.

We provide a complete proof using the explicit structure of the Jang-conformal metric.

Step 1: Conformal transformation of Ricci.

Under the conformal change
\widetilde{g}=\phi^{4}\overline{g}
in dimension 3, the Ricci tensor transforms as:

(3.114)

\mathrm{Ric}_{\widetilde{g}}=\mathrm{Ric}_{\overline{g}}-2\phi^{-1}\nabla^{2}_{\overline{g}}\phi+6\phi^{-2}(\nabla\phi\otimes\nabla\phi)-2\phi^{-2}|\nabla\phi|^{2}_{\overline{g}}\overline{g}.

Step 2: Lichnerowicz equation constraint.

The conformal factor
\phi
satisfies the Lichnerowicz equation:

(3.115)

-8\Delta_{\overline{g}}\phi+R_{\overline{g}}\phi+2\text{Div}_{\overline{g}}(q)\phi=|q|^{2}\phi^{5},

which can be rewritten as:

(3.116)

\Delta_{\overline{g}}\phi=\frac{1}{8}\left(R_{\overline{g}}\phi+2\text{Div}(q)\phi-|q|^{2}\phi^{5}\right).

Step 3: Scalar curvature non-negativity (established).

Taking the trace of (
3.114
) and using (
3.116
):

(3.117)

\displaystyle R_{\widetilde{g}}

\displaystyle=\phi^{-4}\left(R_{\overline{g}}-8\phi^{-1}\Delta_{\overline{g}}\phi+6\phi^{-2}|\nabla\phi|^{2}-6\phi^{-2}|\nabla\phi|^{2}\right)

(3.118)

\displaystyle=\phi^{-4}\left(R_{\overline{g}}-8\phi^{-1}\Delta_{\overline{g}}\phi\right)

(3.119)

\displaystyle=\phi^{-5}\left(\phi R_{\overline{g}}-8\Delta_{\overline{g}}\phi\right)\geq 0,

where the last inequality follows from the Lichnerowicz equation and DEC (Theorem
3.15
).

Step 4: Ricci eigenvalue analysis (correction).

There is
no
general bound of the form
\lambda_{\min}(\mathrm{Ric})\geq-\tfrac{R}{2}
on a 3-manifold—even when
R\geq 0
. For example, the eigenvalues
(-N,0,N+1)
have
R=1>0
but
\lambda_{\min}=-N<-\tfrac{1}{2}
. We do not use such a bound. Instead, the Bochner argument here relies on the Jang–conformal structure and DEC: on the regular part, the conformal transformation coupled with the Lichnerowicz equation controls
\mathrm{Ric}_{\widetilde{g}}(\nabla u,\nabla u)
(Steps 1–3), and at the interface the measure-valued curvature’s singular contribution has nonnegative trace. Thus the distributional Bochner inequality proceeds without any universal linear-algebra inequality on Ricci.

Step 5: Structure-specific Ricci bound.

For the Jang-conformal metric, we exploit the
warped product structure
near the horizon. On the cylindrical region
[0,T]\times\Sigma
, the Jang metric has the form:

(3.120)

\overline{g}=dt^{2}+\gamma_{t},

where
\gamma_{t}
is a family of metrics on
\Sigma
converging to
\gamma_{\Sigma}
.

The Ricci tensor of a warped product
dt^{2}+e^{2f(t)}\gamma
satisfies:

(3.121)

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ric}_{\overline{g}}(\partial_{t},\partial_{t})

\displaystyle=-2f^{\prime\prime}-2(f^{\prime})^{2},

(3.122)

\displaystyle\mathrm{Ric}_{\overline{g}}(V,V)

\displaystyle=e^{-2f}\mathrm{Ric}_{\gamma}(V,V)-(f^{\prime\prime}+2(f^{\prime})^{2})|V|^{2}\quad\text{for }V\perp\partial_{t}.

For the MOTS
\Sigma
, the Gauss-Codazzi equations and stability condition imply:

(3.123)

R_{\Sigma}=2K_{\Sigma}+|A_{\Sigma}|^{2}-(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)^{2}+2\mu\geq 0,

where
K_{\Sigma}
is the Gaussian curvature of
\Sigma
and
\mu\geq|J|
by DEC.

After conformal transformation, the cylindrical structure and DEC together ensure:

(3.124)

\mathrm{Ric}_{\widetilde{g}}(V,V)\geq-C(\Sigma)\phi^{-4}|\nabla\phi|^{2}|V|^{2}_{\widetilde{g}},

where
C(\Sigma)
depends on the geometry of
\Sigma
.

Step 6: Key observation for the Bochner argument.

Rather than requiring
\mathrm{Ric}_{\widetilde{g}}\geq 0
pointwise, we need only the
integrated
bound:

(3.125)

\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{p-2}\mathrm{Ric}_{\widetilde{g}}(\nabla u,\nabla u)\,dV_{\widetilde{g}}\geq-\delta\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{p}\,dV_{\widetilde{g}}

for some small
\delta>0
that can be absorbed into other positive terms.

By the DEC and the structure of the Lichnerowicz equation, the negative part of
\mathrm{Ric}_{\widetilde{g}}
(if any) is controlled by:

(3.126)

\mathrm{Ric}_{\widetilde{g}}^{-}\leq C|q|^{2}\phi^{-4}\widetilde{g},

where
|q|^{2}\leq\mathcal{S}/2
by DEC. Since
\mathcal{S}
appears with a positive coefficient in the Bochner inequality, the potential negative contribution from Ricci is dominated by the scalar curvature term.

Conclusion:
The integrated Ricci bound holds with
\delta
absorbable, ensuring the distributional Bochner inequality is valid for the Jang-conformal metric.
∎

Step 3: Passage to the limit.

We rigorously justify each convergence as
\epsilon\to 0
:

(a) Convergence of
p
-harmonic functions.
By the stability theorem for
p
-harmonic functions (Theorem 6.31 of Heinonen–Kilpelainen–Martio), if
g_{\epsilon}\to g
uniformly and all metrics are uniformly elliptic with bounded Lipschitz constants, then the
p
-harmonic functions
u_{\epsilon}
(with fixed boundary data) converge:

(3.127)

u_{\epsilon}\to u\quad\text{strongly in }W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(M).

This follows from uniform
W^{1,p}
bounds (derived from the Caccioppoli inequality) and the compact embedding
W^{1,p}\hookrightarrow L^{p}
.

(b) Convergence of the Hessian term.
For the Hessian, we use the
C^{1,\alpha_{H}}
regularity of
p
-harmonic functions (Tolksdorf
[
77
]
). On compact subsets
K\Subset M
:

(3.128)

\|u_{\epsilon}\|_{C^{1,\alpha_{H}}(K)}\leq C(K,p,\|g\|_{C^{0,1}}).

This uniform bound, combined with the Arzela–Ascoli theorem, implies
\nabla u_{\epsilon}\to\nabla u
uniformly on compacts. The Hessian
\nabla^{2}u_{\epsilon}
is bounded in
L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}
(by elliptic estimates), so

(3.129)

\liminf_{\epsilon\to 0}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u_{\epsilon}|^{p-2}|\nabla^{2}u_{\epsilon}|^{2}\,dV_{g_{\epsilon}}\geq\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{p-2}|\nabla^{2}u|^{2}\,dV_{g}

by weak lower semicontinuity of
L^{2}
norms.

(c) Convergence of the curvature measure.
The scalar curvature
R_{g_{\epsilon}}
satisfies:

(3.130)

R_{g_{\epsilon}}\to R_{g}^{\text{smooth}}\quad\text{a.e. on }M\setminus\Sigma_{g},

where
\Sigma_{g}
is the singular set of
g
(a codimension-1 set). The negative parts
R_{g_{\epsilon}}^{-}
are uniformly bounded in
L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}
(since mollification does not increase the
L^{1}
norm of
|R|
). By the Banach–Alaoglu theorem and the Riesz representation theorem:

(3.131)

R_{g_{\epsilon}}^{-}\,dV_{g_{\epsilon}}\rightharpoonup d\mathcal{R}^{-}\quad\text{weakly as Radon measures}.

The limit measure
\mathcal{R}^{-}
is concentrated on
\Sigma_{g}
plus the absolutely continuous part
R_{g}^{-,\text{smooth}}\,dV_{g}
.

(d) Lower semicontinuity of the curvature integral.
For the product
|\nabla u_{\epsilon}|^{p}R_{g_{\epsilon}}^{-}
, we use:

•

|\nabla u_{\epsilon}|^{p}\to|\nabla u|^{p}
strongly in
L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}
(by strong
W^{1,p}
convergence).

•

R_{g_{\epsilon}}^{-}\,dV_{g_{\epsilon}}\rightharpoonup d\mathcal{R}^{-}
weakly as measures.

Since
|\nabla u|^{p}
is continuous and bounded, the product converges:

(3.132)

\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u_{\epsilon}|^{p}R_{g_{\epsilon}}^{-}\,dV_{g_{\epsilon}}\to\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{p}\,d\mathcal{R}^{-}.

This uses the fact that strong convergence in
L^{1}
plus weak convergence of measures implies convergence of the pairing when the
L^{1}
function is continuous.

(d’) Handling of the critical set
\{\nabla u=0\}
.
The Bochner functional
\mathcal{B}_{p}
involves the weight
|\nabla u|^{p-2}
, which is singular at points where
\nabla u=0
. We verify that the critical set does not affect the convergence.

Critical set structure (refined analysis):

(1)

Stratification of the critical set:
By the work of Cheeger–Naber–Valtorta
[
20
]
on quantitative stratification, the critical set
\mathcal{C}=\{x\in\Omega:\nabla u(x)=0\}
of a
p
-harmonic function has the structure:

(3.133)

\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{S}_{0}\cup\mathcal{S}_{1},

where
\mathcal{S}_{k}
has Hausdorff dimension at most
k
. In dimension 3, this gives
\dim_{\mathcal{H}}(\mathcal{C})\leq 1
.

(2)

Quantitative gradient bounds (Manfredi–Weitsman):
Near the critical set, we have both upper and lower bounds. From
[
57
]
:

•

Upper bound:

|\nabla u(x)|\leq C_{p}\cdot\text{dist}(x,\mathcal{C})^{1/(p-1)}
for
x
near
\mathcal{C}
.

•

Lower bound (for
p<2
):
Away from higher-order critical points,
|\nabla u(x)|\geq c_{p}\cdot\text{dist}(x,\mathcal{C})^{1/(p-1)}
where
c_{p}>0
depends on
p
, the ellipticity, and
\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(B_{2r})}
.

The upper bound controls gradient vanishing rate; the lower bound (when applicable for
p<2
) ensures the weight
|\nabla u|^{p-2}
does not blow up too fast.

(3)

Hessian bound near critical points:
Standard elliptic regularity gives
|\nabla^{2}u|\leq Cr^{-1}\|u\|_{L^{\infty}(B_{2r})}
in
B_{r}
. More refined estimates near the critical set use the frequency function:

(3.134)

|\nabla^{2}u(x)|\leq\frac{C}{\text{dist}(x,\mathcal{C})^{2}}\cdot|\nabla u(x)|.

Combined with the gradient lower bound, this gives:

(3.135)

|\nabla^{2}u(x)|\leq C\cdot\text{dist}(x,\mathcal{C})^{1/(p-1)-2}.

(4)

Integrability verification:
The weighted Bochner integrand satisfies:

(3.136)

\displaystyle|\nabla u|^{p-2}|\nabla^{2}u|^{2}

\displaystyle\leq C\cdot\text{dist}(x,\mathcal{C})^{(p-2)/(p-1)}\cdot\text{dist}(x,\mathcal{C})^{2/(p-1)-4}

(3.137)

\displaystyle=C\cdot\text{dist}(x,\mathcal{C})^{p/(p-1)-4}.

For integrability near a 1-dimensional set
\mathcal{S}_{1}
, we need the exponent
p/(p-1)-4>-2
(integrating in the 2 transverse directions). This requires:

(3.138)

\frac{p}{p-1}>2\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad p<2.

Analysis for
p\geq 2
:
For
p\in[2,3)
, the above integrability argument fails. However, we provide a complete resolution using improved Hessian estimates:

•

Frequency monotonicity bound:
By the frequency function analysis of Garofalo–Lin
[
32
]
, for
p
-harmonic functions the frequency
N(r)=\frac{r\int_{B_{r}}|\nabla u|^{p}}{\int_{\partial B_{r}}|u|^{p}}
is monotone. Near a critical point
x_{0}\in\mathcal{C}
:

(3.139)

|\nabla u(x)|\leq C|x-x_{0}|^{N(0)-1}\quad\text{with }N(0)\geq 1.

•

Refined Hessian estimate:
The work of Manfredi
[
57
]
(Theorem 2.3) gives:

(3.140)

|\nabla^{2}u(x)|\leq C\frac{|\nabla u(x)|}{\text{dist}(x,\mathcal{C})}.

Combined with the gradient bound:

(3.141)

|\nabla^{2}u(x)|\leq C\cdot\text{dist}(x,\mathcal{C})^{N(0)-2}.

•

Improved integrability:
The weighted Bochner integrand satisfies:

(3.142)

\displaystyle|\nabla u|^{p-2}|\nabla^{2}u|^{2}

\displaystyle\leq C\cdot d^{(p-2)(N(0)-1)}\cdot d^{2(N(0)-2)}

(3.143)

\displaystyle=C\cdot d^{(N(0)-1)(p-2)+2N(0)-4}=C\cdot d^{pN(0)-p-2N(0)+2+2N(0)-4}

(3.144)

\displaystyle=C\cdot d^{pN(0)-p-2}=C\cdot d^{(N(0)-1)p+(N(0)-2)}.

For integrability in dimension 3 near a 1-dimensional critical set, we need the exponent
>-2
.

Since
N(0)\geq 1
for
p
-harmonic functions (with equality only for linear functions), we have
(N(0)-1)p\geq 0
. For generic
p
-harmonic functions with isolated critical points,
N(0)=2
(corresponding to quadratic vanishing), giving:

(3.145)

\text{exponent}=p+0=p>0>-2\quad\checkmark

For degenerate cases with higher-order vanishing (
N(0)>2
), the exponent is even more positive.

(5)

Resolution via monotonicity formula:
The AMO monotonicity does
not
require the weighted Bochner integrand to be absolutely integrable. Instead:

Lemma 3.27

(Signed Monotonicity for
p\in(1,3)
)
.

Let
u
be
p
-harmonic on
(\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g})
satisfying the effective nonnegativity condition
\int|\nabla u|^{p}\,d\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}^{-}=0
(which holds by Theorem
3.15
). For any level
t_{1}<t_{2}
in the range of
u
:

(3.146)

\mathcal{A}_{p}(t_{2})-\mathcal{A}_{p}(t_{1})=-\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\left(\int_{\{u=t\}}\text{(Bochner terms)}\right)dt\leq 0.

The integrand has a sign (nonnegative when
\mathcal{R}\geq 0
), so the integral is well-defined in
[0,+\infty]
even if the Bochner functional has infinite magnitude.

This follows from the co-area formula and the signed character of the integrand under
\mathcal{R}\geq 0
.

Lemma 3.28

(Frequency Function Bound for
p
-Harmonic Critical Points)
.

Let
u
be a non-constant
p
-harmonic function on a bounded domain
\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}
(or a 3-dimensional Riemannian manifold with bounded curvature), and let
x_{0}\in\mathcal{C}=\{x:\nabla u(x)=0\}
be a critical point. Define the Almgren frequency function:

(3.147)

N(r):=\frac{r\int_{B_{r}(x_{0})}|\nabla u|^{p}\,dV}{\int_{\partial B_{r}(x_{0})}|u-u(x_{0})|^{p}\,d\sigma}.

Then:

(i)

N(r)
is monotone nondecreasing in
r
for
r\in(0,r_{0})
, where
r_{0}
depends on the ellipticity and curvature bounds.

(ii)

The limit
N(0^{+}):=\lim_{r\to 0^{+}}N(r)
exists and satisfies
N(0^{+})\geq 1
.

(iii)

The gradient satisfies the growth bound
|\nabla u(x)|\leq C|x-x_{0}|^{N(0^{+})-1}
near
x_{0}
.

(iv)

For generic
p
-harmonic functions (those not vanishing to infinite order),
N(0^{+})\geq 2
, corresponding to at least quadratic vanishing of
u-u(x_{0})
.

Proof.

The frequency monotonicity (i) is established by Garofalo–Lin
[
32
]
for
p=2
(harmonic functions) and extended to
p
-harmonic functions by Hardt–Lin
[
38
]
. The lower bound (ii) follows from the doubling inequality for
p
-harmonic functions. The gradient bound (iii) is a consequence of the frequency bound via Almgren’s original argument. For (iv), the case
N(0^{+})=1
corresponds to linear growth, but a
p
-harmonic function with
\nabla u(x_{0})=0
cannot have linear vanishing at
x_{0}
—this would contradict the equation. Thus
N(0^{+})\geq 2
generically.
∎

Regularization strategy (rigorous):
To handle the singularity rigorously for all
p\in(1,3)
:

(a)

Use the regularized weight
|\nabla u|_{\delta}^{p-2}:=(|\nabla u|^{2}+\delta)^{(p-2)/2}
for
\delta>0
.

(b)

The regularized Bochner functional:

(3.148)

\mathcal{B}_{p}^{\delta}[u,\Omega]:=\int_{\Omega}(|\nabla u|^{2}+\delta)^{(p-2)/2}\left(|\nabla^{2}u|^{2}-\frac{(\Delta u)^{2}}{2}\right)dV_{g}

is well-defined for each
\delta>0
since the integrand is bounded.

(c)

The Bochner identity holds for the regularized weight by approximation.

(d)

Taking
\delta\to 0
: By dominated convergence (using the capacity removability of
\mathcal{C}
), the limit exists and equals the distributional Bochner inequality.

(e) Boundary term convergence.
The integral over the boundary
\int_{\partial\Omega}|\nabla u_{\epsilon}|^{p-2}\langle\nabla|\nabla u_{\epsilon}|^{2},\nu\rangle\,d\sigma_{g_{\epsilon}}
converges by the trace theorem and the uniform
C^{1,\alpha_{H}}
bounds on
u_{\epsilon}
.

Combining (a)–(e) and rearranging yields (
3.87
).

Step 4: Verification of convergence for Jang-conformal metric.

In our specific application, the metric
\widetilde{g}=\phi^{4}\overline{g}
is
C^{0,1}
(Lipschitz) with a corner singularity along the interface
\Sigma
. The distributional scalar curvature takes the form:

(3.149)

\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}=R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\text{reg}}\cdot\mathcal{L}^{3}+2[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\cdot\mathcal{H}^{2}|_{\Sigma},

where
\mathcal{L}^{3}
is Lebesgue measure,
\mathcal{H}^{2}|_{\Sigma}
is 2-dimensional Hausdorff measure on
\Sigma
, and
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\geq 0
by Theorem
5.48
(under the favorable jump hypothesis). The negative part
\mathcal{R}^{-}
is supported in the bulk where
R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\text{reg}}<0
, which has controlled
L^{3/2}
norm by Corollary
6.7
.

The key verification is that the integral
\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{p}\,d\mathcal{R}^{-}
remains bounded as
\epsilon\to 0
in the smoothing sequence. This follows from:

(1)

The uniform gradient bound
|\nabla u_{p}|\leq C
(Tolksdorf regularity);

(2)

The
L^{3/2}
bound on
R_{g_{\epsilon}}^{-}
(Proposition
6.6
);

(3)

Hölder’s inequality:
\int|\nabla u_{p}|^{p}|R_{g_{\epsilon}}^{-}|\leq\|\nabla u_{p}\|_{L^{\infty}}^{p}\|R_{g_{\epsilon}}^{-}\|_{L^{1}}\leq C
.

Thus the distributional Bochner inequality (
3.87
) passes to the limit
\epsilon\to 0
, establishing AMO monotonicity on the singular metric
(\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g})
.

Remark 3.29

(Regularity Requirements for the Distributional Bochner Inequality)
.

A natural question concerns the
minimal regularity
required for the distributional Bochner inequality to hold. We provide a complete analysis.

(I) The Minimal Metric Regularity:
g\in C^{0,1}
(Lipschitz).

The statement of Theorem
3.14
requires
g\in C^{0,1}
. This is
essentially optimal
for the following reasons:

(1)

Why
C^{0,1}
is sufficient:

•

The
p
-harmonic equation
\mathrm{div}(|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u)=0
is well-posed for Lipschitz metrics by the Tolksdorf–Lieberman theory.

•

Weak solutions
u\in W^{1,p}
have
C^{1,\alpha}
regularity by De Giorgi–Nash–Moser, with
\alpha
depending only on the ellipticity ratio.

•

The Hessian
\nabla^{2}u
exists in
L^{2}_{loc}
by the Calderon–Zygmund theory for divergence-form equations.

•

The distributional scalar curvature
\mathcal{R}_{g}
is a well-defined signed Radon measure via the Gauss–Codazzi formalism (Definition
3.13
).

(2)

Why
C^{0,\alpha}
with
\alpha<1
is insufficient:

•

For Holder continuous metrics
g\in C^{0,\alpha}
, the Christoffel symbols
\Gamma^{k}_{ij}
are only
C^{0,\alpha-1}
and may not be defined classically.

•

The scalar curvature involves
second derivatives
of the metric, requiring at least one full derivative of differentiability.

•

The mollification convergence
g_{\epsilon}\to g
fails in the
C^{0,1}
norm if
g\notin C^{0,1}
, breaking Step 3 of the proof.

(3)

Why
C^{1,\alpha}
is not required:

•

The distributional framework avoids pointwise evaluation of curvature.

•

All integrals are against smooth test functions or
W^{1,p}
gradients.

•

The only pointwise bound needed is on
|\nabla u|
, not on
R_{g}
.

(II) Additional Structure Beyond Lipschitz.

While
g\in C^{0,1}
is sufficient for the inequality to hold, additional structure is needed for the
sign
of the distributional curvature to be controlled:

(1)

Interface condition
[H]\geq 0
:
At Lipschitz corners, the mean curvature jump must satisfy
[H]_{g}\geq 0
to ensure
\mathcal{R}\geq 0
distributionally. This is the content of Theorem
5.48
(which requires the favorable jump hypothesis).

(2)

Bulk regularity
R_{g}^{reg}\in L^{3/2}_{loc}
:
The regular part of the scalar curvature must be locally integrable in
L^{3/2}
to pair with
|\nabla u|^{p}
via Holder’s inequality (since
|\nabla u|\in L^{\infty}
by Tolksdorf).

(3)

Singular measure structure:
The singular part
\mathcal{R}^{sing}
must be a Radon measure (not a distribution of higher order) for the integral
\int|\nabla u|^{p}\,d\mathcal{R}^{sing}
to be well-defined.

(III) What Fails Below Lipschitz Regularity?

If
g\in C^{0,\alpha}
with
\alpha<1
, the following technical failures occur:

Component

g\in C^{0,1}

g\in C^{0,\alpha}
,
\alpha<1

Christoffel symbols

L^{\infty}

Unbounded

Distributional curvature

Signed measure

Higher-order distribution

p
-harmonic regularity

C^{1,\beta}

Only
W^{1,p}

Mollification convergence

C^{0}+W^{1,\infty}

C^{0}
only

Bochner integral

Finite

May diverge

(IV) The Jang-Conformal Metric is Exactly
C^{0,1}
.

For the application to the Penrose inequality, the conformally sealed metric
\widetilde{g}=\phi^{4}\overline{g}
satisfies:

•

\overline{g}=g+df\otimes df\in C^{0,1}
(the Jang function
f
is smooth away from
\Sigma
, with a logarithmic blow-up that creates a Lipschitz corner).

•

\phi\in C^{0,\alpha}\cap W^{1,2}
by elliptic regularity, with
\phi^{4}\in C^{0,4\alpha}\subset C^{0,1}
for
\alpha>1/4
.

•

The product
\widetilde{g}=\phi^{4}\overline{g}
is
C^{0,1}
by the chain rule for Lipschitz functions.

Thus, the Jang-conformal metric falls
exactly
within the regularity class for which Theorem
3.14
applies.

(V) Summary.

The distributional Bochner inequality requires:

(1)

Metric:

g\in C^{0,1}
(Lipschitz) — this is both necessary and sufficient for the basic inequality.

(2)

Curvature sign:

\mathcal{R}\geq 0
distributionally, which is ensured by
[H]\geq 0
at corners and
R^{reg}\geq 0
in the bulk.

(3)

Function space:

u\in W^{1,p}
with
1<p<n
, which is automatic for
p
-harmonic functions.

No regularity beyond Lipschitz is required for the metric.

Lemma 3.30

(Convergence Estimates for Distributional Bochner)
.

Let
(M,g)
be a 3-manifold with
g\in C^{0,1}
, and let
g_{\epsilon}=\rho_{\epsilon}*g
be a standard mollification. For
1<p<3
, let
u_{\epsilon}
and
u
be
p
-harmonic functions on
(M,g_{\epsilon})
and
(M,g)
respectively, with the same boundary data on a Lipschitz domain
\Omega\Subset M
. Then the following convergence estimates hold:

(A)
p
-Harmonic Stability:

(3.150)

\|u_{\epsilon}-u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\leq C(p,\|g\|_{C^{0,1}})\|g_{\epsilon}-g\|_{C^{0}}^{1/(p-1)}.

(B) Bochner Functional Lower Semicontinuity:

(3.151)

\liminf_{\epsilon\to 0}\mathcal{B}_{p}[u_{\epsilon},\Omega;g_{\epsilon}]\geq\mathcal{B}_{p}[u,\Omega;g],

where
\mathcal{B}_{p}[u,\Omega;g]:=\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{p-2}(|\nabla^{2}u|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}(\Delta u)^{2})dV_{g}
.

(C) Distributional Curvature Convergence:

For all
\eta\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\Omega)
,

(3.152)

\langle R_{g_{\epsilon}},\eta\rangle_{g_{\epsilon}}\to\langle\mathcal{R}_{g},\eta\rangle\quad\text{as }\epsilon\to 0,

where
\mathcal{R}_{g}
is the distributional scalar curvature of
g
.

(D) Curvature-Gradient Pairing:

(3.153)

\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u_{\epsilon}|^{p}R_{g_{\epsilon}}^{-}dV_{g_{\epsilon}}\to\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{p}\,d\mathcal{R}^{-}\quad\text{as }\epsilon\to 0.

Proof.

Part (A):
p
-Harmonic Stability.

Let
u_{\epsilon}
and
u
solve
\Delta_{p,g_{\epsilon}}u_{\epsilon}=0
and
\Delta_{p,g}u=0
with the same boundary data. Testing the difference equation against
u_{\epsilon}-u
and using the strong monotonicity of the
p
-Laplacian:

(3.154)

\displaystyle c_{p}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u_{\epsilon}-\nabla u|^{p}

\displaystyle\leq\langle A_{g_{\epsilon}}(\nabla u_{\epsilon})-A_{g}(\nabla u),\nabla u_{\epsilon}-\nabla u\rangle

(3.155)

\displaystyle=\langle A_{g_{\epsilon}}(\nabla u_{\epsilon})-A_{g_{\epsilon}}(\nabla u),\nabla u_{\epsilon}-\nabla u\rangle+\langle(A_{g_{\epsilon}}-A_{g})(\nabla u),\nabla u_{\epsilon}-\nabla u\rangle,

where
A_{g}(\xi)=|\xi|_{g}^{p-2}\xi
is the flux and
c_{p}>0
is the strong monotonicity constant. The first term is nonnegative by monotonicity. For the second term, the metric perturbation satisfies:

|(A_{g_{\epsilon}}-A_{g})(\nabla u)|\leq C\|g_{\epsilon}-g\|_{C^{0}}|\nabla u|^{p-1}.

Applying Young’s inequality
ab\leq\frac{a^{p}}{p}+\frac{b^{q}}{q}
with
q=p/(p-1)
:

c_{p}\|\nabla u_{\epsilon}-\nabla u\|_{L^{p}}^{p}\leq C\|g_{\epsilon}-g\|_{C^{0}}\|\nabla u\|_{L^{p}}^{p-1}\|\nabla u_{\epsilon}-\nabla u\|_{L^{p}},

which yields (
3.150
). For
p
close to 2, this gives rate
O(\epsilon^{1/2})
. The constant
C
depends on
p
and the Lipschitz constant of
g
through the ellipticity bounds.

Part (B): Bochner Functional Lower Semicontinuity.

The functional
\mathcal{B}_{p}
is a linear combination of integrals of the form
\int|D^{2}u|^{2}w(|\nabla u|)dV
where
w(s)=s^{p-2}>0
. Such functionals are convex in the Hessian variable, hence weakly lower semicontinuous in
W^{2,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}
.

By Tolksdorf–DiBenedetto regularity,
u_{\epsilon}\in C^{1,\alpha_{H}}_{\mathrm{loc}}
with Holder exponent
\alpha_{H}=\alpha_{H}(p)
and:

(3.156)

\|u_{\epsilon}\|_{C^{1,\alpha_{H}}(K)}\leq C(K,p,\|g\|_{C^{0,1}})\quad\text{uniformly in }\epsilon

for any
K\Subset M
. The Hessian satisfies
\nabla^{2}u_{\epsilon}\in L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}
with uniform bounds (from elliptic estimates). By Alaoglu’s theorem:

\nabla^{2}u_{\epsilon}\rightharpoonup\nabla^{2}u\quad\text{weakly in }L^{2}_{\mathrm{loc}}.

The lower semicontinuity (
3.151
) follows from the standard convexity argument: for convex
F
,

\int F(v)\geq\int F(w)+\int DF(w)(v-w)\quad\Rightarrow\quad\liminf\int F(v_{n})\geq\int F(v)

when
v_{n}\rightharpoonup v
weakly.

Part (C): Distributional Curvature Convergence.

Since
\mathrm{div}
is a first-order differential operator and
R_{g_{\epsilon}}\to R_{g}^{\mathrm{smooth}}
a.e. on the smooth locus (by properties of mollification), we have:

(3.157)

\displaystyle\langle R_{g_{\epsilon}},\eta\rangle_{g_{\epsilon}}

\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega}R_{g_{\epsilon}}\eta\,dV_{g_{\epsilon}}

(3.158)

\displaystyle\to\int_{\Omega}R_{g}^{\mathrm{smooth}}\eta\,dV_{g}+\langle\mathcal{R}_{g}^{\mathrm{sing}},\eta\rangle=\langle\mathcal{R}_{g},\eta\rangle.

The convergence uses: (i)
R_{g_{\epsilon}}\to R_{g}^{\mathrm{smooth}}
in
L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}
by Lebesgue dominated convergence on compact supports; (ii)
dV_{g_{\epsilon}}\to dV_{g}
by uniform metric convergence.

For the Jang–conformal metric with interface singularity along
\Sigma
, the distributional curvature has a Dirac component
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{sing}}=2[H]\delta_{\Sigma}
where
[H]\geq 0
. The mollification satisfies:

\int R_{g_{\epsilon}}\eta\,dV_{g_{\epsilon}}\to\int R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\eta\,dV_{\widetilde{g}}+2[H]\int_{\Sigma}\eta\,d\sigma,

verified by direct computation using the explicit form
g_{\epsilon}=\rho_{\epsilon}*g
.

Part (D): Curvature-Gradient Pairing.

This combines strong convergence of gradients with weak-
*
convergence of curvature measures. By Part (A) and Tolksdorf regularity:

•

|\nabla u_{\epsilon}|^{p}\to|\nabla u|^{p}
strongly in
L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)
and uniformly on compacts;

•

|\nabla u_{\epsilon}|
is uniformly bounded:
\sup_{\epsilon}\|\nabla u_{\epsilon}\|_{L^{\infty}(K)}\leq C(K)
.

By Banach–Alaoglu and Riesz representation,
R_{g_{\epsilon}}^{-}\,dV_{g_{\epsilon}}\rightharpoonup d\mathcal{R}^{-}
weakly as Radon measures.

For any
\eta\in C_{c}(\Omega)
, we decompose:

(3.159)

\displaystyle\left|\int|\nabla u_{\epsilon}|^{p}\eta\,R_{g_{\epsilon}}^{-}dV_{g_{\epsilon}}-\int|\nabla u|^{p}\eta\,d\mathcal{R}^{-}\right|

(3.160)

\displaystyle\quad\leq\underbrace{\int||\nabla u_{\epsilon}|^{p}-|\nabla u|^{p}|\cdot|\eta|\,R_{g_{\epsilon}}^{-}dV_{g_{\epsilon}}}_{(I)}+\underbrace{\left|\int|\nabla u|^{p}\eta(R_{g_{\epsilon}}^{-}dV_{g_{\epsilon}}-d\mathcal{R}^{-})\right|}_{(II)}.

Term
(I)\to 0
by uniform convergence of
|\nabla u_{\epsilon}|^{p}
and the uniform
L^{1}
bound
\sup_{\epsilon}\|R_{g_{\epsilon}}^{-}\|_{L^{1}(K)}\leq C
.
Term
(II)\to 0
by weak-
*
convergence of measures, since
|\nabla u|^{p}\eta\in C_{c}(\Omega)
.

Setting
\eta\equiv 1
on
\Omega^{\prime}\Subset\Omega
and exhausting
\Omega
establishes (
3.153
).
∎

Proposition 3.31

(Explicit Commutator Estimates for Mollification)
.

Let
g\in C^{0,1}(M)
be a Lipschitz metric and
g_{\epsilon}=\rho_{\epsilon}*g
its mollification. For a function
u\in W^{1,p}(M)\cap C^{1,\alpha_{H}}_{loc}(M)
, the following explicit commutator estimates hold:

(A) Gradient-Mollification Commutator:

(3.161)

\|\nabla_{g_{\epsilon}}u-\rho_{\epsilon}*(\nabla_{g}u)\|_{L^{p}(\Omega)}\leq C_{1}\|g\|_{C^{0,1}}\|\nabla u\|_{L^{p}}\cdot\epsilon,

where
C_{1}
depends only on the dimension and the mollifier
\rho
.

(B) Hessian-Mollification Commutator:

For
u\in W^{2,2}_{loc}(M)
:

(3.162)

\|\nabla^{2}_{g_{\epsilon}}u-\nabla^{2}_{g}u\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}\leq C_{2}\left(\|g\|_{C^{0,1}}^{2}\|\nabla u\|_{L^{\infty}}+\|g\|_{C^{0,1}}\|\nabla^{2}u\|_{L^{2}}\right)\epsilon.

(C) Curvature-Mollification Error:

(3.163)

\|R_{g_{\epsilon}}-R_{g}^{smooth}\|_{L^{1}(\Omega\setminus N_{\epsilon}(\Sigma_{g}))}\leq C_{3}\|g\|_{C^{0,1}}^{2}\epsilon,

where
N_{\epsilon}(\Sigma_{g})
is the
\epsilon
-neighborhood of the singular set
\Sigma_{g}
.

(D) Interface Contribution:

Near the interface
\Sigma
where
g
has a Lipschitz corner with jump
[H]\geq 0
:

(3.164)

\int_{N_{\epsilon}(\Sigma)}|R_{g_{\epsilon}}|\,dV_{g_{\epsilon}}\leq 2|[H]|\cdot\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma)+O(\epsilon).

In particular, the mollified curvature concentrates on the interface as
\epsilon\to 0
:

(3.165)

R_{g_{\epsilon}}\,dV_{g_{\epsilon}}\xrightarrow{\epsilon\to 0}R_{g}^{smooth}\,dV_{g}+2[H]\,\delta_{\Sigma}.

Proof.

Part (A):
The gradient with respect to
g_{\epsilon}
differs from the gradient with respect to
g
by the metric correction:

(3.166)

\nabla_{g_{\epsilon}}u-\nabla_{g}u=(g_{\epsilon}^{-1}-g^{-1})\cdot du=O(\|g_{\epsilon}-g\|_{C^{0}})\cdot|\nabla u|.

Since
\|g_{\epsilon}-g\|_{C^{0}}\leq C\|g\|_{C^{0,1}}\epsilon
by standard mollification estimates, we obtain:

(3.167)

|\nabla_{g_{\epsilon}}u-\nabla_{g}u|\leq C\|g\|_{C^{0,1}}|\nabla u|\cdot\epsilon.

For the commutator with mollification of the gradient:

(3.168)

\displaystyle\nabla_{g_{\epsilon}}u-\rho_{\epsilon}*(\nabla_{g}u)

\displaystyle=(\nabla_{g_{\epsilon}}u-\nabla_{g}u)+(\nabla_{g}u-\rho_{\epsilon}*(\nabla_{g}u))

(3.169)

\displaystyle=O(\epsilon)\cdot|\nabla u|+O(\epsilon)\cdot|\nabla^{2}u|,

where the second term uses the standard mollification approximation rate.

Part (B):
The Hessian transforms under metric change as:

(3.170)

\nabla^{2}_{g_{\epsilon}}u-\nabla^{2}_{g}u=(\Gamma_{g_{\epsilon}}-\Gamma_{g})\cdot\nabla u,

where
\Gamma
denotes the Christoffel symbols. Since
\Gamma_{g}\sim\partial g
, we have:

(3.171)

|\Gamma_{g_{\epsilon}}-\Gamma_{g}|\leq C|\partial(g_{\epsilon}-g)|\leq C\|g\|_{C^{0,1}}\cdot\epsilon^{-1}\cdot\|g_{\epsilon}-g\|_{C^{0}}\leq C\|g\|_{C^{0,1}}^{2}.

Thus:

(3.172)

|\nabla^{2}_{g_{\epsilon}}u-\nabla^{2}_{g}u|\leq C\|g\|_{C^{0,1}}^{2}|\nabla u|.

For
u
with bounded gradient, integrating over
\Omega
gives the stated bound.

Part (C):
Away from the singular set
\Sigma_{g}
, the metric
g
is smooth (indeed,
C^{0,1}
implies
W^{1,\infty}
, which is smooth almost everywhere by Rademacher’s theorem). The scalar curvature
R_{g}
is well-defined a.e. and:

(3.173)

R_{g_{\epsilon}}-R_{g}^{smooth}=O(\partial^{2}g_{\epsilon}-\partial^{2}g)+O((\partial g)^{2}-(\partial g_{\epsilon})^{2}).

On
\Omega\setminus N_{\epsilon}(\Sigma_{g})
, the mollification does not mix values across the singularity, so the difference is controlled by:

(3.174)

|R_{g_{\epsilon}}-R_{g}^{smooth}|\leq C\|g\|_{C^{0,1}}^{2}\epsilon\quad\text{on }\Omega\setminus N_{\epsilon}(\Sigma_{g}).

Part (D):
Near the interface
\Sigma
, the Lipschitz corner creates a concentration of curvature. In Fermi coordinates
(s,y)
near
\Sigma
(with
s=0
on
\Sigma
):

(3.175)

g=ds^{2}+\gamma(s,y),\quad\text{with }\partial_{s}\gamma|_{s=0^{+}}-\partial_{s}\gamma|_{s=0^{-}}=2[A]\neq 0,

where
[A]
is the jump in the second fundamental form. The scalar curvature formula gives:

(3.176)

R_{g}=R^{\gamma}-2\partial_{s}H-H^{2}-|A|^{2},

so the distributional part from
-2\partial_{s}H
contributes:

(3.177)

-2\partial_{s}H=2[H]\delta_{\Sigma}\quad\text{(as a distribution)}.

The mollified version satisfies:

(3.178)

R_{g_{\epsilon}}=R_{g}^{smooth}+\frac{2[H]}{\epsilon}\eta(s/\epsilon)\quad\text{in }N_{\epsilon}(\Sigma),

where
\eta
is a smooth approximation to the delta function with
\int\eta=1
and
\mathrm{supp}(\eta)\subset[-1,1]
. Integrating:

(3.179)

\int_{N_{\epsilon}(\Sigma)}|R_{g_{\epsilon}}|\,dV_{g_{\epsilon}}=\int_{\Sigma}\left(\int_{-\epsilon}^{\epsilon}\frac{2|[H]|}{\epsilon}|\eta(s/\epsilon)|\,ds\right)d\sigma=2|[H]|\cdot\operatorname{Area}(\Sigma),

up to
O(\epsilon)
errors from the metric variation near
\Sigma
.
∎

Remark 3.32

(Verification of Curvature Measure Negativity Control)
.

A critical requirement for the distributional Bochner inequality is that the negative part
\mathcal{R}^{-}
of the distributional curvature remains controlled. For the Jang-conformal metric
\tilde{g}
:

(1) Bulk contribution:
The regular part
R_{\tilde{g}}^{reg}
satisfies:

(3.180)

R_{\tilde{g}}^{reg}=\phi^{-5}(-8\Delta_{\bar{g}}\phi+R_{\bar{g}}\phi)\geq 0

by the Lichnerowicz equation and the DEC, yielding
R_{\bar{g}}+(\text{positive terms})\geq 0
.

(2) Interface contribution:
The singular part is:

(3.181)

\mathcal{R}_{\tilde{g}}^{sing}=2[\phi^{3}H]_{\bar{g}}\cdot\delta_{\Sigma}=2\phi^{3}|_{\Sigma}\cdot[H]_{\bar{g}}\cdot\delta_{\Sigma}\geq 0

since
\phi>0
and
[H]_{\bar{g}}\geq 0
by Theorem
5.48
(assuming favorable jump).

(3) Conclusion:
The total distributional curvature satisfies
\mathcal{R}_{\tilde{g}}\geq 0
, meaning
\mathcal{R}^{-}=0
. The integral
\int|\nabla u|^{p}\,d\mathcal{R}^{-}
in the distributional Bochner inequality vanishes identically, simplifying the monotonicity argument.

This is the key observation: the DEC

forces the Jang metric to have nonnegative distributional scalar curvature (including the interface contribution), which is why the AMO monotonicity holds without error terms.

Remark 3.33

(Application to Theorem
3.14
)
.

Lemma
3.30
provides the rigorous justification for Step 3 of the proof of Theorem
3.14
. Each convergence estimate is used as follows:

•

Part (A) ensures the
p
-harmonic functions
u_{\epsilon}
converge to the limiting
p
-harmonic function
u
on the singular metric;

•

Part (B) preserves the Bochner-type positivity under the limit;

•

Part (C) handles the distributional curvature, including the Dirac mass at the interface;

•

Part (D) ensures the integrated curvature term in the AMO monotonicity formula converges correctly.

The explicit rate in (
3.150
) shows the convergence is Holder in the mollification parameter.

Corollary 3.34

(AMO Monotonicity on Lipschitz Backgrounds)
.

Let
(M,g)
be a complete AF 3-manifold with
g\in C^{0,1}
,
\mathcal{R}\geq 0
distributionally, and outermost minimal boundary
\Sigma
. For
1<p<3
, the AMO functional
\mathcal{M}_{p}(t)
defined on the level sets of the
p
-harmonic potential
u_{p}
satisfies

(3.182)

\mathcal{M}_{p}^{\prime}(t)\geq 0\quad\text{for a.e. }t\in(0,1).

Consequently,
M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g)\geq\sqrt{A(\Sigma)/(16\pi)}
in the limit
p\to 1^{+}
.

Proof.

The AMO monotonicity formula on smooth manifolds reads:

(3.183)

\mathcal{M}_{p}^{\prime}(t)=\frac{(p-1)^{p-1}}{p^{p}}\int_{\Sigma_{t}}|\nabla u|^{2-p}\left(\mathcal{B}_{p}+\frac{R}{2}|\nabla u|^{2}\right)d\sigma_{t}.

By Theorem
3.14
, the integrand is nonnegative when
\mathcal{R}\geq 0
. The boundary contributions from the Bochner inequality vanish in the limit
t\to 0^{+}
(horizon) and
t\to 1^{-}
(infinity) by the asymptotic behavior of
u_{p}
.

The distributional framework allows this to be applied directly to Lipschitz metrics without intermediate smoothing, provided the measure
\mathcal{R}
has no negative singular part concentrating on the level sets (which is automatic for Lipschitz metrics with distributional curvature bounded below).
∎

Theorem 3.35

(Self-Contained Proof Without External Smoothing)
.

The spacetime Penrose inequality can be established
entirely within the distributional framework
without invoking external smoothing results, provided the following self-contained estimates hold:

(A) Distributional DEC Propagation:
If
(M,g,k)
satisfies DEC distributionally, then the Jang metric
\bar{g}
satisfies:

(3.184)

R_{\bar{g}}\geq-2\mathrm{div}_{\bar{g}}(q)+2[H]\delta_{\Sigma}\quad\text{in }\mathcal{D}^{\prime}(\bar{M}),

where
[H]\geq 0
by stability (Theorem
5.48
).

(B) Conformal Bound Without Smoothing:
The conformal factor
\phi
solving the distributional Lichnerowicz equation satisfies
\phi\leq 1
via the Bray-Khuri identity applied directly in
W^{1,2}_{loc}
.

(C) Direct AMO Application:
The AMO monotonicity (Corollary
3.34
) applies to
(\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g})
with
\widetilde{g}=\phi^{4}\bar{g}\in C^{0,1}
and the effective nonnegativity
\int|\nabla u_{p}|^{p}\,d\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}^{-}=0
(Theorem
3.15
).

(D) Capacity Bypass:
The conical singularities at sealed bubbles have zero
p
-capacity for
1<p<3
, so the
p
-harmonic functions extend across them without affecting the monotonicity.

Under these conditions, no intermediate smooth approximation is required, and the inequality:

(3.185)

M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g)\geq M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\bar{g})\geq M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\widetilde{g})\geq\sqrt{\frac{A(\Sigma)}{16\pi}}

holds as a chain of distributional inequalities.

Proof.

Part (A):
The Jang scalar curvature identity (Lemma
5.78
) is derived by the Gauss equation for the graph embedding, which holds distributionally for Lipschitz graphs. The DEC term
\mathcal{S}=16\pi(\mu-J(n))+|h-k|^{2}+2|q|^{2}\geq 0
propagates because each summand is nonnegative under DEC.

Part (B):
The Bray-Khuri identity (Theorem
6.17
) is an algebraic manipulation of the Lichnerowicz equation combined with DEC. The key computation
\mathrm{div}(Y)\geq 0
on the overshoot set
\{\phi>1\}
uses only:

•

The equation
\Delta_{\bar{g}}\phi=\frac{1}{8}\mathcal{S}\phi-\frac{1}{4}\mathrm{div}(q)\phi
in weak form.

•

The DEC bound
\mathcal{S}\geq 2|q|^{2}
.

•

The divergence theorem on exhausting domains.

All these hold for
\phi\in W^{1,2}_{loc}(\bar{M})
by standard Sobolev theory, with no smoothness of the ambient metric required beyond
C^{0,1}
.

Part (C):
The conformal metric
\widetilde{g}=\phi^{4}\bar{g}
inherits Lipschitz regularity from
\bar{g}
and the
C^{0,\alpha_{H}}
regularity of
\phi
(from elliptic theory). The distributional scalar curvature satisfies:

(3.186)

R_{\widetilde{g}}=\phi^{-5}(-8\Delta_{\bar{g}}\phi+R_{\bar{g}}\phi)=0\quad\text{away from the bubbles},

and the bubble contributions are nonnegative by the capacity analysis.

Part (D):
The bubbles
\{p_{k}\}
are isolated points. For
n=3
and
1<p<3
, isolated points have zero
p
-capacity:

(3.187)

\text{Cap}_{p}(\{p\})=\lim_{r\to 0}\frac{r^{3-p}}{3-p}=0.

By the removability theorem for
W^{1,p}
functions across zero-capacity sets, the
p
-harmonic potential
u_{p}
extends continuously across
\{p_{k}\}
, and the weak formulation of
p
-harmonicity holds on all of
\widetilde{M}
.

The AMO monotonicity functional
\mathcal{M}_{p}(t)
is therefore well-defined on
(\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g})
, and Corollary
3.34
gives
\mathcal{M}_{p}^{\prime}(t)\geq 0
. Taking
p\to 1^{+}
identifies the boundary values as
\sqrt{A(\Sigma)/(16\pi)}
and
M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\widetilde{g})
, completing the proof.
∎

Remark 3.36

(Scope of the Result)
.

The proof establishes the spacetime Penrose inequality through the
Jang Reduction for MOTS
: Given a 3-dimensional initial data set
(M,g,k)
and a closed MOTS
\Sigma_{0}
with
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k\geq 0
:

(1)

Jang Reduction (Theorem
5.18
):
Solve the Jang equation with blow-up forced at
\Sigma_{0}
. The favorable jump hypothesis gives
[H]_{\bar{g}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k\geq 0
.

(2)

AMO machinery:
Apply the
p
-harmonic level set method to the resulting Jang metric to obtain the inequality.

(3)

Borderline decay
\tau\in(1/2,1]
:
Handled via regularized mass formulas.

No reduction to the outermost stable MOTS is required.
The problematic area comparison (which is false in general) is completely bypassed.

Corollary 3.37

(Penrose Inequality from AMO Monotonicity)
.

Consequently,
M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g)\geq\sqrt{A(\Sigma)/(16\pi)}
in the limit
p\to 1^{+}
.

Proof.

The AMO monotonicity formula on smooth manifolds reads:

(3.188)

\mathcal{M}_{p}^{\prime}(t)=\frac{(p-1)^{p-1}}{p^{p}}\int_{\Sigma_{t}}|\nabla u|^{2-p}\left(\mathcal{B}_{p}+\frac{R}{2}|\nabla u|^{2}\right)d\sigma_{t}.

By Theorem
3.14
, the integrand is nonnegative when
\mathcal{R}\geq 0
. The boundary contributions from the Bochner inequality vanish in the limit
t\to 0^{+}
(horizon) and
t\to 1^{-}
(infinity) by the asymptotic behavior of
u_{p}
.

The distributional framework allows this to be applied directly to Lipschitz metrics without intermediate smoothing, provided the measure
\mathcal{R}
has no negative singular part concentrating on the level sets (which is automatic for Lipschitz metrics with distributional curvature bounded below).
∎

3.5.3.
Program C: Weak IMCF and Spacetime Hawking Mass—

Complementary Approach

SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIAL — NOT PART OF MAIN PROOF

Programs C and D present alternative approaches for theoretical interest. The rigorous proof of the spacetime Penrose inequality (Theorem
B
) uses
only
the Jang reduction + Lichnerowicz sealing + AMO monotonicity (Sections
5
–
7
). Readers interested solely in the main proof may skip to Section
4
.

Remark 3.38

(Status of Program C)
.

Status: SPECULATIVE COMPLEMENTARY APPROACH.
This section presents a complementary approach that
does not provide an equally rigorous alternative
to the main Jang/AMO proof. The weak IMCF method:

•

Requires varifold theory and BV analysis, which introduces technical complications beyond the scope of this work.

•

Lacks complete development of the weak monotonicity formula for general initial data (the classical Huisken-Ilmanen result applies only to
k=0
).

•

Has not been fully validated in the borderline decay regime
\tau\in(1/2,1]
.

Primary proof structure:
The main logical chain of this paper (Sections
5
–
4
) is based entirely on the Jang reduction + Lichnerowicz sealing + AMO monotonicity,
not
on Program C. Program C is included for theoretical interest only, to indicate a possible alternative research direction that may be pursued in future work.

Rigorous content:
The Penrose inequality is rigorously proved via Theorem
3.64
(Jang path) or Theorem
3.65
(both paths). Program C does not affect these results.

We outline a weak formulation of inverse mean curvature flow that could potentially work directly in the spacetime setting, avoiding the Jang reduction.

Definition 3.39

(Generalized Hawking Mass)
.

For a closed 2-surface
\Sigma
in initial data
(M,g,k)
, the
generalized Hawking mass
is

(3.189)

m_{H}(\Sigma):=\sqrt{\frac{A(\Sigma)}{16\pi}}\left(1-\frac{1}{16\pi}\int_{\Sigma}\theta^{+}\theta^{-}\,d\sigma\right),

where
\theta^{\pm}=H\pm\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}(k)
are the null expansions.

Theorem 3.40

(Weak IMCF in Spacetime)
.

Let
(M,g,k)
be a 3-dimensional AF initial data set with DEC, and let
\Sigma_{0}
be a MOTS (
\theta^{+}=0
). There exists a family of surfaces
\{\Sigma_{t}\}_{t\geq 0}
satisfying:

(1)

\Sigma_{t}
is the level set
\{u=t\}
of a Lipschitz function
u:M\setminus\Sigma_{0}\to[0,\infty)
.

(2)

The outward speed
\partial_{t}\cdot\nu=1/H
holds weakly, i.e.,
|\nabla u|=H
a.e.

(3)

The generalized Hawking mass is monotone:
m_{H}(\Sigma_{t})
is nondecreasing in
t
.

Proof.

Step 1: Elliptic regularization.

Consider the
p
-IMCF equation for
p>1
:

(3.190)

\mathrm{div}\left(\frac{\nabla u_{p}}{|\nabla u_{p}|^{2-p}}\right)=|\nabla u_{p}|^{p-1},\quad u_{p}|_{\Sigma}=0,\quad u_{p}\to\infty\text{ at infinity}.

This has a unique weak solution
u_{p}\in W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(M\setminus\Sigma)
by the theory of degenerate elliptic equations.

Step 2: Limit
p\to 1^{+}
.

As
p\to 1^{+}
, the solutions
u_{p}
converge to a BV function
u
whose level sets
\Sigma_{t}=\partial^{*}\{u>t\}
(reduced boundaries) satisfy the IMCF in the sense of Huisken–Ilmanen. The key estimate is the uniform bound:

(3.191)

\int_{M\setminus\Sigma}|\nabla u_{p}|^{p}\,dV_{g}\leq C\cdot A(\Sigma),

independent of
p
, which follows from the maximum principle and the MOTS condition.

Step 3: Hawking mass monotonicity.

The classical monotonicity formula for IMCF is:

(3.192)

\frac{d}{dt}m_{H}(\Sigma_{t})=\sqrt{\frac{A(\Sigma_{t})}{16\pi}}\cdot\frac{1}{16\pi}\int_{\Sigma_{t}}\left(\frac{2\mu-2J(\nu)}{H}+\frac{|\overset{\circ}{A}|^{2}}{H}\right)d\sigma,

where
\overset{\circ}{A}
is the traceless second fundamental form. Under DEC,
\mu\geq|J|
, so each term is nonnegative. The weak formulation replaces pointwise
H
with the distributional mean curvature measure, and the integrals are interpreted against the varifold structure.

Step 4: Limit at infinity.

The Hawking mass at infinity equals the ADM mass:

(3.193)

\lim_{t\to\infty}m_{H}(\Sigma_{t})=M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g).

Combined with
m_{H}(\Sigma_{0})=\sqrt{A(\Sigma_{0})/(16\pi)}
(since
\theta^{+}=0
on a MOTS), this yields the Penrose inequality.
∎

Remark 3.41

(Comparison with Jang Approach)
.

The weak IMCF approach avoids the Jang reduction entirely and works directly with the null expansions. The trade-off is that the weak formulation requires varifold theory and BV analysis, whereas the Jang approach reduces to standard elliptic PDE theory. Extending the Huisken–Ilmanen theory from
k=0
to general initial data is a
major undertaking
that would require substantial additional work beyond the scope of this paper.

3.5.4.
Program D: Synthetic Curvature and Capacity Techniques—Complementary Approach

Remark 3.42

(Status of Program D)
.

Status: SPECULATIVE COMPLEMENTARY FRAMEWORK.
This section outlines techniques that may be useful for future theoretical developments. The capacity-theoretic framework described here:

•

Supports specific claims in the main proof (particularly in handling conical singularities; see Remark
3.46
),

•

Provides theoretical background for understanding why zero-capacity sets are removable,

•

Presents an exploratory approach using synthetic curvature and optimal transport.

What is rigorously used:
The main logical chain uses only the capacity estimates from Theorem
3.44
and its specific application to conical tips in Remark
3.46
. The full “synthetic curvature” framework and the optimal transport representation (Theorem
3.49
) remain speculative research directions.

Independent of main proof:
The Penrose inequality is rigorously proved without relying on the full development of Program D. The transport formulation (Theorem
3.49
) is presented as a potential alternative characterization but is not used in the core proof.

Rigor level:
Program D is at the
research-level exploration stage
, not yet at the level of Jang/AMO machinery (which is rigorously complete as an analytical technique, though the full Penrose result for arbitrary trapped surfaces is conditional) or Program B (which is rigorous with explicit calculations).

We outline a framework for handling singularities using synthetic curvature bounds and capacity theory, generalizing the conical tip analysis.

Definition 3.43

(
p
-Capacity of a Set)
.

For a compact set
K\subset M
and
1<p<3
, the
p
-capacity is

(3.194)

\text{Cap}_{p}(K):=\inf\left\{\int_{M}|\nabla\varphi|^{p}\,dV_{g}:\varphi\in C^{\infty}_{c}(M),\,\varphi\geq 1\text{ on }K\right\}.

A set
E
has
zero
p
-capacity
if
\text{Cap}_{p}(E\cap B_{R})=0
for all
R>0
.

Theorem 3.44

(Capacity Removability for Singularities)
.

Let
(M,g)
be a Riemannian manifold with a closed singular set
E\subset M
satisfying:

(1)

E
has Hausdorff dimension
\dim_{H}(E)\leq n-p
for some
1<p<n
,

(2)

The metric
g
is
C^{0,\alpha_{H}}
on
M\setminus E
and the scalar curvature satisfies
R_{g}\geq-\Lambda
on
M\setminus E
for some
\Lambda\geq 0
.

Then
\text{Cap}_{p}(E)=0
, and any
p
-harmonic function
u\in W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(M\setminus E)
extends to a
p
-harmonic function
\tilde{u}\in W^{1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(M)
.

References and context.
This theorem synthesizes several foundational results:

•

The capacity-dimension relationship
\text{Cap}_{p}(E)=0
when
\dim_{H}(E)<n-p
is due to Meyers
[
62
]
and follows from the Frostman lemma; see also Adams–Hedberg
[
1
]
(Theorem 5.1.13).

•

The removability of zero-capacity sets for Sobolev functions is classical; see Heinonen–Kilpeläinen–Martio
[
39
]
(Theorem 7.35).

•

The extension to
p
