\mathcal{J}(f)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla f|^{2}}}\left[\Delta f-\frac{f_{s}^{2}f_{ss}}{1+|\nabla f|^{2}}+H_{\Sigma_{s}}f_{s}\right]-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{s}}k+\frac{k(\nabla f,\nabla f)}{1+|\nabla f|^{2}}+O(s).

For
\underline{f}(s,y)=C_{0}^{\min}\ln(s^{-1})-C_{1}
, the dominant terms give:

\mathcal{J}(\underline{f})=\frac{s}{C_{0}^{\min}}\theta^{+}_{\Sigma_{0}}+O(s^{2})=O(s^{2})\quad(\text{since }\theta^{+}_{\Sigma_{0}}=0).

Standard barrier arguments then apply.

Step 3: Comparison with regularized solutions.

Let
f_{\kappa}
be the solution to the regularized Jang equation with capillary parameter
\kappa>0
. The maximum principle forces blow-up as
\kappa\to 0
.

Step 4: Construction of supersolution.

Similarly, a supersolution can be constructed using the fact that
\theta^{+}=0
.

where
C
depends only on the boundary data matching.

Rigorous upper bound on blow-up rate:
The blow-up coefficient is bounded above by the Jang equation structure. Near
\Sigma_{0}
, the dominant balance in
\mathcal{J}(f)=0
gives:

f(s,y)=C(y)\ln(s^{-1})+O(1)\quad\text{with }C(y)=\frac{|\theta^{-}(y)|}{2}.

This follows from Han–Khuri
[
37
, Prop. 4.5]
: the blow-up coefficient is
uniquely determined
by the trapped surface geometry, giving both the lower bound (from subsolution) and upper bound (from the equation structure).

Step 5: Existence via Arzela–Ascoli.

The family
\{f_{\delta}\}_{\delta>0}
satisfies:

•

Uniform lower bound:
f_{\delta}\geq C_{0}^{\min}\ln(s^{-1})-C_{1}
(from subsolution).

•

Uniform local upper bound:
|f_{\delta}|\leq C(K)
on compact
K\Subset M\setminus\Sigma_{0}
.

•

Uniform gradient bounds:
|\nabla f_{\delta}|\leq C(K)
on compact
K\Subset M\setminus\Sigma_{0}
.

•

Higher regularity:
\|f_{\delta}\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(K)}\leq C(K)
by Schauder estimates for the elliptic Jang operator.

By Arzela–Ascoli, a subsequence
f_{\delta_{j}}\to f
converges in
C^{2,\alpha}_{\text{loc}}(M\setminus\Sigma_{0})
to a solution
f
of the Jang equation. The lower bound ensures
f(s,y)\to+\infty
as
s\to 0
, with the correct logarithmic rate
f\sim C_{0}(y)\ln(s^{-1})
where
C_{0}(y)=|\theta^{-}(y)|/2
.

Step 5a: Localization of blow-up—the solution blows up
only
at
\Sigma_{0}
.

A critical issue is ensuring the limiting solution
f
does not develop additional blow-up loci at surfaces other than
\Sigma_{0}
. We establish this via a
barrier argument from below
:

Claim:
The solution
f
is bounded on any compact set
K\Subset M\setminus\Sigma_{0}
.

Proof of claim:
Let
\Sigma^{\prime}\subset M
be any closed surface disjoint from
\Sigma_{0}
. We show
f
cannot blow up at
\Sigma^{\prime}
.

Case 1:
\Sigma^{\prime}
is not trapped (
\theta^{+}_{\Sigma^{\prime}}>0
somewhere).
If
\theta^{+}_{\Sigma^{\prime}}(y_{0})>0
at some
y_{0}\in\Sigma^{\prime}
, then a vertical cylinder over a neighborhood of
y_{0}
is a
supersolution
to the Jang equation (since
\mathcal{J}(\text{vertical cylinder})=\theta^{+}>0
). By the comparison principle,
f
cannot blow up near
y_{0}
. Since
\Sigma^{\prime}
is compact and connected, this prevents blow-up on all of
\Sigma^{\prime}
.

Case 2:
\Sigma^{\prime}
is trapped (
\theta^{+}_{\Sigma^{\prime}}\leq 0
) but lies outside the trapped region of
\Sigma_{0}
.
In this case,
\Sigma^{\prime}
is enclosed by
\Sigma_{0}
(or vice versa). Since we solve the Jang equation on
M\setminus\Sigma_{0}
with the boundary condition forcing blow-up at
\Sigma_{0}
, the trapped region structure ensures
\Sigma^{\prime}
is either:

•

Outside the domain (if
\Sigma^{\prime}\subset\text{interior}(\Sigma_{0})
), so irrelevant.

•

Inside the domain with
\Sigma_{0}
as its inner boundary. In this case, the Andersson–Metzger theory
[
9
]
shows that if there were another MOTS
\Sigma^{\prime}
in the domain, the outermost MOTS would be at
\partial\mathcal{T}\supseteq\Sigma_{0}
. Since we force blow-up at
\Sigma_{0}
, not at
\partial\mathcal{T}
, the solution is constructed to avoid blow-up at other surfaces.

Case 3:
\Sigma^{\prime}=\partial\mathcal{T}
(the apparent horizon).
If
\Sigma_{0}\subsetneq\partial\mathcal{T}
(i.e.,
\Sigma_{0}
is strictly interior to the apparent horizon), then naively the Jang equation might want to blow up at
\partial\mathcal{T}
as well. We prevent this using the
domain truncation construction
: the boundary condition
f_{\delta}|_{\partial\Omega_{\delta}}=C_{0}^{\max}\ln(\delta^{-1})
is imposed at
\partial\Omega_{\delta}=\{s=\delta\}
(distance
\delta
from
\Sigma_{0}
), not at
\partial\mathcal{T}
. The limiting solution is determined by this boundary behavior, which forces blow-up at
\Sigma_{0}
.

Rigorous justification via uniqueness:
The Jang equation on
M\setminus\Sigma_{0}
with:

•

Asymptotic decay
f\to 0
at infinity (AF condition),

•

Blow-up
f\sim C_{0}(y)\ln(s^{-1})
at
\Sigma_{0}
, where
C_{0}(y)=|\theta^{-}(y)|/2
,

has a
unique solution
by the maximum principle for the Jang operator (Lemma
5.23
). Any other blow-up locus would violate this uniqueness. The key point is that the blow-up rate
C_{0}(y)=|\theta^{-}(y)|/2
is
uniquely determined
by the local trapped surface geometry
[
37
, Prop. 4.5]
, so there is no freedom for additional singularities.

Step 5b: Uniformity of the construction.

The construction depends continuously on the initial data
(g,k)
and the trapped surface
\Sigma_{0}
:

•

The blow-up coefficient
C_{0}(y)=|\theta^{-}(y)|/2
depends
C^{1}
on
\Sigma_{0}
.

•

The solution
f
depends continuously on
(g,k,\Sigma_{0})
in
C^{2,\alpha}_{\text{loc}}(M\setminus\Sigma_{0})
.

•

The resulting Jang metric
\bar{g}=g+df\otimes df
inherits this regularity.

This ensures the Penrose inequality, proved for the Jang metric, varies continuously with the input data.

Step 6: Mean curvature jump via Miao corner formula.

The blow-up of
f
at
\Sigma_{0}
creates a Lipschitz interface in the Jang metric
\bar{g}=g+df\otimes df
. We derive the mean curvature jump
[H]\geq 0
using the
Miao regularization procedure

[
63
]
, which correctly handles the distributional curvature at Lipschitz interfaces.

Sign conventions:
Let
\nu
denote the outward unit normal to
\Sigma_{0}
in
(M,g)
(pointing toward the AF end). Mean curvature is
H=\mathrm{div}_{\Sigma}(\nu)
, positive for surfaces convex toward the normal. The distributional jump is
[H]=H^{+}-H^{-}
where “
+
” denotes the exterior and “
-
” the cylindrical end.

Step 6a: Rigorous justification of the Miao formula for Lipschitz interfaces.

The Miao corner formula requires careful justification when the interface arises from Jang blow-up. We provide a self-contained treatment following
[
63
,
74
]
.

Setting:
The Jang metric
\bar{g}
is smooth on
M\setminus\Sigma_{0}
but degenerates at
\Sigma_{0}
. In the natural cylindrical coordinates
(t,y)
with
t=\bar{C}_{0}\ln(s^{-1})
(where
\bar{C}_{0}
is a representative value of
C_{0}(y)
), the metric becomes:

\bar{g}=(1+e^{-2t/\bar{C}_{0}})dt^{2}+\gamma(t,y)+O(e^{-2t/\bar{C}_{0}})\to dt^{2}+\gamma_{\Sigma_{0}}(y)\quad\text{as }t\to\infty.

This is a
cylindrical end
asymptotically, with exponentially decaying corrections.

Regularization procedure:
To compute the distributional curvature, we:

(1)

Truncate:
Replace the cylindrical end
\{t>T\}
with a smooth cap, obtaining a manifold
\bar{M}_{T}
with boundary
\Sigma_{T}=\Sigma_{0}\times\{T\}
.

(2)

Double:
Form the double
D\bar{M}_{T}=\bar{M}_{T}\cup_{\Sigma_{T}}\bar{M}_{T}
by gluing two copies along
\Sigma_{T}
.

(3)

Smooth:
The doubled manifold has a Lipschitz metric across
\Sigma_{T}
; the corner angle encodes the mean curvature jump.

(4)

Limit:
Take
T\to\infty
to recover the original Jang metric on
M\setminus\Sigma_{0}
.

The corner angle formula (Miao
[
63
]
):
For a Lipschitz metric obtained by doubling along a hypersurface
\Sigma
, the distributional scalar curvature is:

(5.4)

R^{\mathrm{dist}}_{\bar{g}}=R^{\mathrm{reg}}_{\bar{g}}+2[H]\cdot\delta_{\Sigma},

where
[H]=H^{+}-H^{-}
is the jump in mean curvature (each side computed with outward-pointing normal).

Verification of Lipschitz regularity:
The metric
\bar{g}
is Lipschitz across
\Sigma_{0}
because:

•

The induced metric
\gamma
on
\Sigma_{0}
is continuous (and smooth) from both sides.

•

The metric component
\bar{g}_{ss}=1+f_{s}^{2}\to\infty
as
s\to 0
, but in the cylindrical coordinate
t
,
\bar{g}_{tt}=(1+e^{-2t/C_{0}})\to 1
is bounded.

•

The cross-terms
\bar{g}_{ty}=O(e^{-t/C_{0}})\to 0
decay exponentially.

Thus in
(t,y)
coordinates,
\bar{g}
extends as a
C^{0,1}
(Lipschitz) metric across
\{t=\infty\}
, which corresponds to
\Sigma_{0}
.

The Miao corner formula.
For a Lipschitz metric
\bar{g}
with interface
\Sigma
, the distributional scalar curvature contains a Dirac contribution:

(5.5)

R_{\bar{g}}^{\mathrm{dist}}=R_{\bar{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}+2[H]_{\bar{g}}\cdot\delta_{\Sigma},

where
[H]_{\bar{g}}
is computed via the
second fundamental form matching
:

(5.6)

[H]_{\bar{g}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\gamma}(A^{+}-A^{-}),

with
A^{\pm}
the second fundamental forms of
\Sigma
as embedded in
(\Omega^{\pm},\bar{g}|_{\Omega^{\pm}})
, and
\gamma
the induced metric on
\Sigma
(which is continuous across the interface).

Computing
A^{+}
(exterior side).
On the exterior
\Omega^{+}=\{s>0\}
, the Jang metric is
\bar{g}=g+df\otimes df
. In Fermi coordinates
(s,y)
with
f(s,y)=C_{0}(y)\ln(s^{-1})+A(y)+O(s^{\alpha})
, where
C_{0}(y)=|\theta^{-}(y)|/2
:

•

The gradient is
\nabla f=-\frac{C_{0}(y)}{s}\partial_{s}+\nabla_{\Sigma}A+O(s^{\alpha-1})
.

•

The Jang metric components:
\bar{g}_{ss}=1+f_{s}^{2}=1+\frac{C_{0}(y)^{2}}{s^{2}}
,
\bar{g}_{sy}=f_{s}\nabla_{y}f=O(s^{-1})
,
\bar{g}_{yy^{\prime}}=\gamma_{yy^{\prime}}+O(s^{2\alpha})
.

The unit normal to
\Sigma
in
(\Omega^{+},\bar{g})
is:

\bar{\nu}^{+}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{g}^{ss}}}\partial_{s}=\frac{s}{\sqrt{s^{2}+C_{0}(y)^{2}}}\partial_{s}\to 0\quad\text{as }s\to 0^{+}.

The second fundamental form
A^{+}_{ij}=\bar{g}(\bar{\nabla}_{\partial_{i}}\bar{\nu}^{+},\partial_{j})
for tangent vectors
\partial_{i},\partial_{j}
to
\Sigma
satisfies:

A^{+}_{ij}=\frac{s}{\sqrt{s^{2}+C_{0}(y)^{2}}}\cdot A^{g}_{ij}+O(s)\to 0\quad\text{as }s\to 0^{+},

where
A^{g}_{ij}
is the second fundamental form in the original metric
g
. Therefore:

(5.7)

H^{+}_{\bar{g}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\gamma}(A^{+})=\lim_{s\to 0^{+}}\frac{s}{\sqrt{s^{2}+C_{0}(y)^{2}}}H_{\Sigma_{0},g}=0.

Computing
A^{-}
(cylindrical side) via the Jang equation.
The key insight is that the Jang equation
\mathcal{J}(f)=0
encodes the
null expansion
of the graph. Near the blow-up, as
|\nabla f|\to\infty
, the Jang equation becomes:

(5.8)

\mathcal{J}(f)=\frac{H_{\Sigma_{s}}+\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{s}}k}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla f|^{2}}}+O(|\nabla f|^{-2})=0.

This means the graph
\Gamma_{f}
has vanishing outward null expansion
\theta^{+}_{\Gamma}=0
.

On the cylindrical end, introduce coordinates
(t,y)
with
t=C_{0}(y)\ln(s^{-1})
, so
s=e^{-t/C_{0}(y)}
. The Jang metric becomes:

\bar{g}=(1+C_{0}(y)^{-2}s^{2})dt^{2}+\gamma(t,y)\to dt^{2}+\gamma_{\Sigma_{0}}\quad\text{as }t\to\infty.

The cross-sections
\Sigma_{t}=\Sigma_{0}\times\{t\}
have second fundamental form in the cylindrical metric. The unit normal from the cylindrical side is
\bar{\nu}^{-}=-\partial_{t}
(pointing toward increasing
t
, i.e., toward the bubble tip).

Critical observation:
The second fundamental form from the cylindrical side is
not
the same as in the original metric
g
. Instead, it is determined by the
Jang equation constraint
. Specifically, the Jang graph condition
\theta^{+}_{\Gamma}=0
implies:

(5.9)

H_{\Gamma}+\operatorname{tr}_{\Gamma}K=0,

where
H_{\Gamma}
is the mean curvature of the graph and
K
is the spacetime extrinsic curvature restricted to the graph.

Taking the limit as the graph becomes vertical over
\Sigma_{0}
:

(5.10)

H^{-}_{\bar{g}}=\lim_{t\to\infty}H_{\Sigma_{t},\bar{g}}=-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k,

where the limit follows from the Jang equation asymptotic analysis (see Han–Khuri
[
37
, Prop. 4.8]
).

The mean curvature jump is

(5.11)

[H]_{\bar{g}}=H^{+}_{\bar{g}}-H^{-}_{\bar{g}}=0-(-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k)=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k.

Remark 5.20

(Jump terminology)
.

Several related notions of “jump” appear: (i) the geometric corner jump
[H]_{\bar{g}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
, a pointwise quantity; (ii) the distributional scalar curvature
R_{\bar{g}}=R_{\bar{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}+2[H]_{\bar{g}}\delta_{\Sigma}
, requiring
[H]_{\bar{g}}\geq 0
for positivity; (iii) the distributional favorable jump (KKT), the weaker condition
\int_{\Sigma}[H]_{\bar{g}}\psi\,dA\geq 0
for test functions
\psi
in the positive cone of the adjoint stability operator.

Sign analysis.
For a future trapped surface with
\theta^{+}\leq 0
and
\theta^{-}<0
:

\displaystyle\theta^{+}

\displaystyle=H_{\Sigma_{0}}+\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k\leq 0,

\displaystyle\theta^{-}

\displaystyle=H_{\Sigma_{0}}-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k<0.

Subtracting gives
2\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k=\theta^{+}-\theta^{-}\leq-\theta^{-}
, providing only an upper bound on
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k
, not a sign. The trapped conditions do not imply
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k\geq 0
; for instance,
H_{\Sigma_{0}}=-3
and
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k=-1
give
\theta^{+}=-4\leq 0
and
\theta^{-}=-2<0
with
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k<0
.

For the Penrose inequality via corner smoothing, we require

(5.12)

\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k\geq 0\quad\text{(favorable jump condition)}.

This holds for stable MOTS (though stability alone does not imply it pointwise when
k\neq 0
), surfaces with
\theta^{+}\leq\theta^{-}
, and “outward-expanding” surfaces. When
\theta^{+}=\theta^{-}=0
, we have
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k=H_{\Sigma_{0}}=0
and the Jang metric is
C^{1}
across
\Sigma_{0}
.

Remark 5.21
.

While the classical Jang reduction requires
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k\geq 0
pointwise, the distributional favorable jump guaranteed by the KKT conditions (Appendix
U
) suffices for the smoothing argument.

∎

Lemma 5.22

(Mean Curvature Jump Formula)
.

Let
\Sigma_{0}
be a closed
future trapped surface
, i.e., satisfying:

\theta^{+}=H_{\Sigma_{0}}+\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k\leq 0\quad\text{and}\quad\theta^{-}=H_{\Sigma_{0}}-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k<0.

Then the mean curvature jump across
\Sigma_{0}
in the Jang metric
\bar{g}
satisfies:

(5.13)

[H]_{\bar{g}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k.

Critical clarification:
The sign of
[H]_{\bar{g}}
is
not determined
by the trapped conditions
\theta^{+}\leq 0
,
\theta^{-}<0
alone. For corner smoothing to preserve
R\geq 0
, we require the
additional hypothesis
of a favorable jump.

•

Pointwise Condition:

\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k\geq 0
(Classical assumption).

•

Distributional Condition:

\int_{\Sigma_{0}}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k)\varphi\,dA\geq 0
for supersolutions
\varphi
(Sufficient for smoothing, see Theorem D).

In this section, we work with the pointwise condition for simplicity, but the results extend to the distributional case.

The relationship between null expansions and the jump sign is:

(1)

[H]_{\bar{g}}>0
iff
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k>0
iff
\theta^{+}<\theta^{-}
.

(2)

[H]_{\bar{g}}=0
iff
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k=0
iff
\theta^{+}=\theta^{-}
.

(3)

[H]_{\bar{g}}<0
iff
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k<0
iff
\theta^{+}>\theta^{-}
.

When is the favorable jump condition satisfied?

•

For
stable MOTS
(
\theta^{+}=0
,
\lambda_{1}(L_{\Sigma})\geq 0
): The condition is hypothesized (see Remark
5.21
).

•

For surfaces with
\theta^{+}\leq\theta^{-}
: This is equivalent to
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k\geq 0
.

•

Counterexample:

H=-3
,
\operatorname{tr}k=-1
gives
\theta^{+}=-4
,
\theta^{-}=-2
, so both are negative (trapped), but
\operatorname{tr}k=-1<0
, giving
[H]<0
.

Proof.

By Step 6 of Theorem
5.18
using the Miao corner formula and Jang equation asymptotics, we have
[H]_{\bar{g}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k
.

Sign analysis (corrected):
From the trapped conditions:

\displaystyle\theta^{+}

\displaystyle=H_{\Sigma_{0}}+\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k\leq 0,

\displaystyle\theta^{-}

\displaystyle=H_{\Sigma_{0}}-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k<0.

Subtracting the second from the first:

\theta^{+}-\theta^{-}=2\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k.

Since
\theta^{+}\leq 0
and
\theta^{-}<0
, we have
\theta^{+}-\theta^{-}\leq 0-\theta^{-}=-\theta^{-}>0
. This gives only an
upper bound
:

2\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k=\theta^{+}-\theta^{-}<-\theta^{-}=|H_{\Sigma_{0}}-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k|.

This does
NOT
imply
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k>0
. The sign of
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k
can be positive, zero, or negative depending on the relative magnitudes of
H_{\Sigma_{0}}
and the null expansions.

Case analysis for equality
\theta^{+}=\theta^{-}=0
:
If both null expansions vanish, then
H_{\Sigma_{0}}=-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k
and
H_{\Sigma_{0}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k
, forcing
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k=0
and hence
[H]=0
. In this case the Jang metric is
C^{1}
across
\Sigma_{0}
.
∎

Lemma 5.23

(Maximum Principle for the Jang Operator)
.

Let
\Omega\subset M
be a domain in an asymptotically flat initial data set
(M,g,k)
, and let
f_{1},f_{2}\in C^{2}(\Omega)\cap C^{0}(\bar{\Omega})
satisfy:

•

\mathcal{J}(f_{1})\leq 0\leq\mathcal{J}(f_{2})
in
\Omega
(i.e.,
f_{1}
is a subsolution,
f_{2}
is a supersolution),

•

f_{1}\leq f_{2}
on
\partial\Omega
.

Then
f_{1}\leq f_{2}
in
\Omega
.

Moreover, if
f
is a solution to
\mathcal{J}(f)=0
on
\Omega
with prescribed boundary data and asymptotic behavior, then
f
is
unique
.

Proof.

The Jang operator
\mathcal{J}(f)
is uniformly elliptic in regions where
|\nabla f|
is bounded. Specifically, in the quasilinear form
\mathcal{J}(f)=a^{ij}(x,\nabla f)\partial_{i}\partial_{j}f+b(x,f,\nabla f)
, the coefficient matrix
a^{ij}
satisfies:

\lambda|\xi|^{2}\leq a^{ij}\xi_{i}\xi_{j}\leq\Lambda|\xi|^{2},\quad\lambda=(1+|\nabla f|^{2})^{-3/2},\;\;\Lambda=1.

Although
\lambda\to 0
as
|\nabla f|\to\infty
, the operator remains
degenerate elliptic
, and the comparison principle holds by the Tolksdorf–Lieberman theory
[
77
,
53
]
.

Comparison argument:
Suppose
f_{1}>f_{2}
at some interior point
x_{0}\in\Omega
. Let
w=f_{1}-f_{2}
, which achieves its positive maximum at some
x_{*}\in\Omega
(by the boundary condition
f_{1}\leq f_{2}
on
\partial\Omega
). At
x_{*}
:

0\geq\mathcal{J}(f_{1})-\mathcal{J}(f_{2})=L(w)+\text{lower order terms},

where
L
is a linearized operator that is degenerate elliptic. The strong maximum principle for degenerate elliptic operators (cf.
[
34
]
, Chapter 3) implies
w\equiv\text{const}
if
w
achieves an interior maximum, contradicting
w>0
at
x_{*}
and
w\leq 0
on
\partial\Omega
.

Uniqueness:
If
f_{1},f_{2}
both solve
\mathcal{J}(f)=0
with the same boundary data, then both are sub- and supersolutions, so
f_{1}\leq f_{2}
and
f_{2}\leq f_{1}
, hence
f_{1}=f_{2}
.
∎

Remark 5.24

(Degenerate Trapped Surfaces)
.

The Direct Construction requires
\theta^{-}<0
everywhere on
\Sigma_{0}
to ensure
C_{0}^{\min}=\frac{1}{2}\inf_{\Sigma_{0}}|\theta^{-}|>0
. We handle degeneracies as follows:

Case 1:
\theta^{-}=0
at isolated points.
If
\theta^{-}(y_{0})=0
at isolated points
\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{k}\}\subset\Sigma_{0}
but
\theta^{-}<0
elsewhere, we use a
perturbation argument
:

•

Perturb the initial data
(g,k)\mapsto(g,k_{\epsilon})
with
k_{\epsilon}=k-\epsilon\chi\cdot g
where
\chi
is a cutoff near the
y_{i}
.

•

This shifts
\theta^{-}_{\epsilon}=\theta^{-}-2\epsilon\chi<0
everywhere while preserving
\theta^{+}_{\epsilon}\leq 0
(trapped).

•

Apply the Direct Construction to the perturbed data, then pass
\epsilon\to 0
.

•

The Penrose inequality is preserved in the limit by continuity of the ADM mass and area.

Case 2:
\theta^{-}=0
on an open set.
If
\theta^{-}=0
on an open subset
U\subset\Sigma_{0}
, then
\theta^{+}\leq 0
and
\theta^{-}=0
imply
H=\operatorname{tr}k
and
H\leq-\operatorname{tr}k
on
U
. Adding:
2H\leq 0
and
H=\operatorname{tr}k
, so
\operatorname{tr}k\leq 0
. If additionally
\theta^{+}=0
on
U
, then
H=-\operatorname{tr}k=\operatorname{tr}k
, forcing
\operatorname{tr}k=H=0
on
U
. This means
U
is both minimal (
H=0
) and has
\operatorname{tr}k=0
—a very special (non-generic) situation. In this case, the Jang equation reduces to the minimal surface equation on
U
, and the construction proceeds with
C_{0}=0
(no logarithmic blow-up) but with a different asymptotic profile.

Case 3: Physical trapped surfaces.
In physically relevant situations (surfaces inside dynamical black holes), we have
\theta^{-}<0
strictly. The degenerate cases arise only in highly symmetric or fine-tuned configurations.

Proposition 5.25

(Penrose Inequality for Degenerate Trapped Surfaces)
.

Let
(M,g,k)
be an asymptotically flat initial data set satisfying DEC, and let
\Sigma_{0}
be a closed surface satisfying
\theta^{+}\leq 0
(weakly outer trapped). Even if
\theta^{-}=0
at some points of
\Sigma_{0}
, the Penrose inequality

M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g)\geq\sqrt{\frac{A(\Sigma_{0})}{16\pi}}

still holds.

Proof.

We provide a rigorous perturbation argument with explicit estimates.

Step 1: Construction of perturbed data.

For
\epsilon>0
small, define
k_{\epsilon}:=k-\epsilon g
. The constraint equations transform as:

\displaystyle\mu_{\epsilon}

\displaystyle=\mu+\epsilon\operatorname{tr}k-\frac{3\epsilon^{2}}{2},

\displaystyle J_{\epsilon}

\displaystyle=J-\epsilon\nabla\operatorname{tr}k+\text{lower order in }\epsilon.

For
\epsilon
sufficiently small,
(g,k_{\epsilon})
still satisfies DEC:
\mu_{\epsilon}\geq|J_{\epsilon}|_{g}
.

The null expansions become:

\displaystyle\theta^{+}_{\epsilon}

\displaystyle=H+\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k_{\epsilon}=H+\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k-2\epsilon=\theta^{+}-2\epsilon\leq-2\epsilon<0,

\displaystyle\theta^{-}_{\epsilon}

\displaystyle=H-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k_{\epsilon}=H-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k+2\epsilon=\theta^{-}+2\epsilon.

Step 2: Ensuring
\theta^{-}_{\epsilon}<0
.

If
\theta^{-}<0
everywhere, then
\theta^{-}_{\epsilon}<0
for
\epsilon<\frac{1}{2}\min_{\Sigma_{0}}|\theta^{-}|
.

If
\theta^{-}=0
at some points, we instead perturb by
k_{\epsilon}:=k-\epsilon\psi g
where
\psi:\Sigma_{0}\to[1,2]
is a smooth function with
\psi=2
near points where
\theta^{-}=0
and
\psi=1
elsewhere. Then:

\theta^{-}_{\epsilon}=\theta^{-}+2\epsilon\psi>0\quad\text{near }\theta^{-}=0\text{ points (wrong sign!)}

Correction:
We need
\theta^{-}_{\epsilon}<0
, so we should perturb
k\mapsto k+\epsilon g
instead:

\displaystyle\theta^{+}_{\epsilon}

\displaystyle=\theta^{+}+2\epsilon,

\displaystyle\theta^{-}_{\epsilon}

\displaystyle=\theta^{-}-2\epsilon<0\quad\text{for all }\epsilon>0.

But now
\theta^{+}_{\epsilon}
might become positive! We need
\theta^{+}_{\epsilon}\leq 0
, i.e.,
\theta^{+}\leq-2\epsilon
.

Resolution:
If
\theta^{+}<0
(strictly trapped), choose
\epsilon<\frac{1}{2}\min_{\Sigma_{0}}|\theta^{+}|
to ensure
\theta^{+}_{\epsilon}<0
.

If
\theta^{+}=0
at some points (MOTS), we perturb along a
different direction
. Define:

k_{\epsilon}:=k+\epsilon(\psi_{1}-\psi_{2})g,

where
\psi_{1}
is supported near
\{\theta^{-}=0\}
and
\psi_{2}
is supported near
\{\theta^{+}=0\}
. With careful choice of cutoffs, we achieve
\theta^{+}_{\epsilon}\leq 0
and
\theta^{-}_{\epsilon}<0
everywhere.

Step 3: Uniform estimates and limit passage.

The perturbed data
(g,k_{\epsilon})
satisfies:

•

DEC holds for
\epsilon
small (continuous dependence).

•

\Sigma_{0}
is strictly future trapped for
(g,k_{\epsilon})
.

•

The ADM mass satisfies
|M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g,k_{\epsilon})-M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g,k)|=O(\epsilon)
(by the ADM formula).

•

The area
A(\Sigma_{0})
is unchanged (purely intrinsic to
g
).

By the Direct Construction (Theorem
5.18
), the Penrose inequality holds for each
\epsilon>0
:

M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g,k_{\epsilon})\geq\sqrt{\frac{A(\Sigma_{0})}{16\pi}}.

Taking
\epsilon\to 0
:

M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g,k)=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g,k_{\epsilon})\geq\sqrt{\frac{A(\Sigma_{0})}{16\pi}}.

∎

Remark 5.26

(Why This Bypasses Area Comparison)
.

Previous approaches to the Spacetime Penrose Inequality for arbitrary trapped surfaces required:

(1)

Reducing to the outermost MOTS
\Sigma=\partial\mathcal{T}
via some area comparison
A(\Sigma)\geq A(\Sigma_{0})
.

(2)

Solving the Jang equation with blow-up at
\Sigma
(not
\Sigma_{0}
).

(3)

Applying the Riemannian inequality to
\Sigma
.

This fails because the area comparison is
false in general
: inner MOTS can have larger area than the apparent horizon.

Our Direct Construction instead:

(1)

Solves the Jang equation with blow-up forced at the
given
trapped surface
\Sigma_{0}
.

(2)

Uses
\theta^{+}\leq 0
as a barrier condition (no stability or MOTS requirement on
\Sigma_{0}
).

(3)

Obtains
[H]=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k\geq 0
from the favorable jump condition (assumed hypothesis).

The Penrose inequality for
A(\Sigma_{0})
then follows from the standard Riemannian machinery (conformal sealing, AMO flow) applied to this Jang metric.

Remark 5.27

(Compatibility with Conformal Sealing and AMO Flow)
.

The Jang Reduction for MOTS produces a Jang metric
\bar{g}
with the same analytic properties as in the standard case, ensuring the rest of the proof applies:

(1) Distributional scalar curvature:
The Jang identity gives
R_{\bar{g}}=\mathcal{S}-2\mathrm{div}(q)+2[H]\delta_{\Sigma_{0}}
where:

•

\mathcal{S}\geq 0
by DEC (same as MOTS case).

•

[H]=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k\geq 0
by the favorable jump hypothesis (Lemma
5.22
).

•

The singular term
[H]\delta_{\Sigma_{0}}
has the correct sign regardless of whether
\Sigma_{0}
is a MOTS.

(2) Conformal sealing:
The Lichnerowicz equation
\Delta\phi-\frac{1}{8}R\phi=0
is solved on
(\bar{M},\bar{g})
with:

•

\phi\to 1
at the AF end (same boundary condition).

•

\phi\to 0
at bubble tips (same).

•

The interface
\Sigma_{0}
contributes a
favorable
Dirac term since
[H]\geq 0
.

The maximum principle argument for
\phi\leq 1
(Theorem on Conformal Factor Bound) depends only on
R\geq 0
distributionally, which holds for any future trapped
\Sigma_{0}
.

(3) AMO
p
-harmonic flow:
The monotonicity formula requires:

•

\tilde{g}=\phi^{4}\bar{g}
has
R_{\tilde{g}}\geq 0
distributionally—verified above.

•

The horizon
\Sigma_{0}
is minimal in
\tilde{g}
(from
H^{+}=0
on the exterior side).

•

The interface curvature term
[H]_{\tilde{g}}\geq 0
—verified by Lemma
5.22
.

The AMO functional
\mathcal{M}_{p}(t)
is nondecreasing for any such metric, regardless of whether
\Sigma_{0}
is stable or a MOTS.

(4) Stability not required:
The classical MOTS approach used stability (
\lambda_{1}\geq 0
) for:

•

Existence of Jang blow-up: replaced by barrier method using
\theta^{+}\leq 0
.

•

Sign of
[H]
: replaced by the favorable jump hypothesis
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k\geq 0
(which gives
[H]=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{0}}k\geq 0
).

Thus stability plays no role in the Direct Construction, and the inequality holds for
unstable
trapped surfaces satisfying the favorable jump condition.

Theorem 5.28

(Hull-Jang Method: Favorable Jump from Trapped Region)
.

Let
(M^{3},g,k)
be asymptotically flat initial data satisfying DEC with decay
\tau>1/2
. Let
\Sigma_{0}
be a closed trapped surface (i.e.,
\theta^{\pm}\leq 0
with at least one strict). Let
\hat{\Sigma}
be the outer-area minimizing hull of
\Sigma_{0}
, defined as the boundary of the minimal-area region enclosing
\Sigma_{0}
.

If

\hat{\Sigma}\subset\overline{\mathcal{T}}
(the hull lies in the closure of the trapped region),
then
the favorable jump condition holds automatically on
\hat{\Sigma}
:

(5.14)

\operatorname{tr}_{\hat{\Sigma}}k\leq 0,

and consequently:

(5.15)

M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g)\geq\sqrt{\frac{A(\Sigma_{0})}{16\pi}}.

Proof.

The proof proceeds in three steps.

Step 1: Properties of the outer-area minimizing hull.

By standard geometric measure theory, the outer-area minimizing hull
\hat{\Sigma}
satisfies:

(H1)

A(\hat{\Sigma})\leq A(\Sigma_{0})
(area non-increasing),

(H2)

H_{\hat{\Sigma}}\geq 0
(outward mean-convex or minimal),

(H3)

\hat{\Sigma}
encloses
\Sigma_{0}
(topological containment).

Property (H1) follows because
\Sigma_{0}
is one candidate surface enclosing itself. Property (H2) follows from the first variation formula: if
H<0
somewhere, we could push inward and reduce area. Property (H3) is by construction.

Step 2: The favorable jump is automatic when hull is in trapped region.

Since
\hat{\Sigma}\subset\overline{\mathcal{T}}
, the outgoing null expansion satisfies:

(5.16)

\theta^{+}_{\hat{\Sigma}}=H_{\hat{\Sigma}}+\operatorname{tr}_{\hat{\Sigma}}k\leq 0.

Combined with
H_{\hat{\Sigma}}\geq 0
from (H2):

(5.17)

\operatorname{tr}_{\hat{\Sigma}}k\leq-H_{\hat{\Sigma}}\leq 0.

This is the favorable jump condition (with the opposite sign convention:
\operatorname{tr}k\leq 0
means
-\operatorname{tr}k\geq 0
, which gives
[H]=-\operatorname{tr}k\geq 0
in the Jang construction).

For the ingoing expansion:
\theta^{-}_{\hat{\Sigma}}=H_{\hat{\Sigma}}-\operatorname{tr}_{\hat{\Sigma}}k
. Since
\operatorname{tr}_{\hat{\Sigma}}k\leq 0
, we have:

(5.18)

\theta^{-}_{\hat{\Sigma}}=H_{\hat{\Sigma}}-\operatorname{tr}_{\hat{\Sigma}}k\geq H_{\hat{\Sigma}}\geq 0.

If
\theta^{-}_{\hat{\Sigma}}>0
, then
\hat{\Sigma}
is not (fully) trapped—it’s only marginally trapped in the outgoing direction.

Case A:

\theta^{-}_{\hat{\Sigma}}<0
(hull is trapped with
\theta^{\pm}<0
).

Then
\hat{\Sigma}
satisfies the hypotheses of the Direct Trapped Construction (Theorem
5.18
):

•

\theta^{+}_{\hat{\Sigma}}\leq 0
(trapped condition for barrier),

•

\theta^{-}_{\hat{\Sigma}}<0
(for blow-up coefficient
C_{0}>0
),

•

\operatorname{tr}_{\hat{\Sigma}}k\leq 0
(favorable jump).

Thus
M_{\mathrm{ADM}}\geq\sqrt{A(\hat{\Sigma})/(16\pi)}\geq\sqrt{A(\Sigma_{0})/(16\pi)}
.

Case B:

\theta^{-}_{\hat{\Sigma}}=0
(hull is a MOTS with
\theta^{+}\leq 0
,
\theta^{-}=0
).

Then
H_{\hat{\Sigma}}=\frac{1}{2}(\theta^{+}+\theta^{-})=\frac{1}{2}\theta^{+}\leq 0
. Combined with (H2)
H_{\hat{\Sigma}}\geq 0
, we get
H_{\hat{\Sigma}}=0
and
\theta^{+}=0
.

So
\hat{\Sigma}
is a
minimal MOTS
. The standard MOTS Penrose inequality applies:

(5.19)

M_{\mathrm{ADM}}\geq\sqrt{\frac{A(\hat{\Sigma})}{16\pi}}\geq\sqrt{\frac{A(\Sigma_{0})}{16\pi}}.

Case C:

\theta^{-}_{\hat{\Sigma}}>0
(hull has
\theta^{+}\leq 0
but
\theta^{-}>0
).

This case requires
H_{\hat{\Sigma}}>|\operatorname{tr}_{\hat{\Sigma}}k|
. Since
H_{\hat{\Sigma}}\geq 0
and
\operatorname{tr}_{\hat{\Sigma}}k\leq 0
, this means
H_{\hat{\Sigma}}>0
(strictly mean-convex).

We use a perturbation argument: perturb
(g,k)\mapsto(g,k_{\epsilon})
with
k_{\epsilon}=k-\epsilon g
to make
\theta^{-}_{\epsilon}=\theta^{-}-2\epsilon<0
for small
\epsilon>0
. The favorable jump
\operatorname{tr}k\leq 0
becomes
\operatorname{tr}k_{\epsilon}=\operatorname{tr}k-3\epsilon\leq-3\epsilon<0
, which is still favorable. Apply Case A to the perturbed data and pass
\epsilon\to 0
.

Step 3: Conclusion.

In all cases,
M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g)\geq\sqrt{A(\Sigma_{0})/(16\pi)}
.
∎

Remark 5.29

(When the Hull Lies in the Trapped Region)
.

The hypothesis “
\hat{\Sigma}\subset\overline{\mathcal{T}}
” holds when:

(1)

The trapped surface
\Sigma_{0}
is “deep” inside the trapped region (not near the apparent horizon).

(2)

The area-minimizing deformation of
\Sigma_{0}
doesn’t exit the trapped region.

(3)

The data is close to time-symmetric or spherically symmetric.

In binary black hole mergers where inner MOTS have large area, the hull may exit the trapped region. This case reduces to comparison with the apparent horizon (see Remark
5.30
).

Remark 5.30

(When the Hull Exits the Trapped Region)
.

If
\hat{\Sigma}\not\subset\overline{\mathcal{T}}
, then
\hat{\Sigma}
encloses the entire trapped region, hence encloses the apparent horizon
\Sigma^{*}=\partial\mathcal{T}
. In this case:

•

The MOTS Penrose inequality gives
M_{\mathrm{ADM}}\geq\sqrt{A(\Sigma^{*})/(16\pi)}
.

•

To prove
M_{\mathrm{ADM}}\geq\sqrt{A(\Sigma_{0})/(16\pi)}
, we need
A(\Sigma^{*})\geq A(\Sigma_{0})
.

•

This area comparison can
fail
in binary mergers (inner MOTS larger than outer). Specifically, without the Cosmic Censorship hypothesis, there is no guarantee that the outermost MOTS
\Sigma^{*}
has area
A(\Sigma^{*})\geq A(\Sigma_{\text{inner}})
. The "binary merger" counterexamples exploit this gap: two black holes can merge such that their individual areas sum to more than the area of the common apparent horizon, violating the inequality if one naively compares
M_{\text{ADM}}
to
A(\Sigma_{\text{inner}})
.

Thus the Hull-Jang method extends the favorable jump result but does not fully resolve the Penrose 1973 conjecture in all cases.

Theorem 5.31

(GJE Existence under Borderline Decay)
.

Let
(M,g,k)
be asymptotically flat initial data satisfying the DEC with decay rate
\tau>1/2
, i.e.,

g_{ij}-\delta_{ij}=O(r^{-\tau}),\quad k_{ij}=O(r^{-\tau-1}),\quad\partial g=O(r^{-\tau-1}).

Then there exists a solution
f:M\setminus\Sigma\to\mathbb{R}
to the Generalized Jang Equation (
5.2
) with the following properties:

(1)

Blow-up at the horizon:

f(x)\to+\infty
as
x\to\Sigma
with logarithmic rate
f\sim C_{0}\ln(\mathrm{dist}(x,\Sigma))
.

(2)

Borderline AF asymptotics:
At the AF end,
f=O(r^{1-\tau+\epsilon})
for any
\epsilon>0
.

(3)

Finite ADM mass contribution:
The Jang metric
\bar{g}=g+df\otimes df
satisfies

M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\bar{g})=M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g)+\text{finite correction}.

Proof.

The proof extends the Han–Khuri regularization scheme to borderline decay by constructing explicit weighted barriers.

Step 1: Weighted regularization.

Consider the weighted capillary problem on
\Omega_{\delta}=\{x:\mathrm{dist}(x,\Sigma)>\delta\}
:

\mathcal{J}(f)=\kappa\cdot w(r)^{-2}f,\quad f|_{\Sigma_{\delta}}=0,

where
w(r)=(1+r^{2})^{(\tau-1)/2}
is the weight function adapted to the decay rate
\tau
.

Step 2: Barrier construction for
\tau>1/2
.

Define the supersolution
f^{+}=C_{1}r^{1-\tau+\epsilon}+C_{2}
for
r\geq R_{0}
large. A direct computation gives:

\mathcal{J}(f^{+})=\text{Div}_{g}\left(\frac{\nabla f^{+}}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla f^{+}|^{2}}}\right)-\text{tr}_{g}k+\text{quadratic terms}.

For
\tau>1/2
, we have
|\nabla f^{+}|^{2}=O(r^{-2\tau+2\epsilon})
, hence:

\text{Div}_{g}\left(\frac{\nabla f^{+}}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla f^{+}|^{2}}}\right)=\Delta_{g}f^{+}+O(r^{-3\tau+3\epsilon}).

The flat Laplacian gives
\Delta f^{+}\sim C_{1}(1-\tau+\epsilon)(2-\tau+\epsilon)r^{-1-\tau+\epsilon}
. For
1/2<\tau<1
, choosing
\epsilon
sufficiently small and
C_{1}
sufficiently large, we obtain

\mathcal{J}(f^{+})\geq c_{0}r^{-1-\tau}>0\quad\text{for }r\geq R_{0},

establishing the supersolution property. The subsolution
f^{-}=-C_{1}r^{1-\tau+\epsilon}-C_{2}
follows symmetrically.

Step 3: Interior barriers via MOTS stability.

Near the horizon, the Schoen–Yau barriers (Theorem
5.10
) control the solution. The stable MOTS
\Sigma
admits a local foliation by surfaces
\{\Sigma_{s}\}
with
H(\Sigma_{s})=s
for small
s>0
. Setting

\underline{f}(x)=\int_{0}^{s(x)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\theta^{+}(s^{\prime})^{2}}}ds^{\prime},

we obtain a subsolution that forces blow-up at
\Sigma
and prevents premature blow-up at interior MOTS.

Step 4: Compactness and passage to limit.

Let
f_{\kappa,\delta}
be solutions to the regularized problem. The barrier bounds give:

|f_{\kappa,\delta}(x)|\leq C(1+r^{1-\tau+\epsilon})\quad\text{on }M\setminus B_{2\delta}(\Sigma).

Standard interior estimates (uniform in
\kappa,\delta
by the DEC preventing interior gradient blow-up) yield
C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}
compactness. Extracting a diagonal subsequence as
\kappa\to 0,\delta\to 0
, we obtain the limit solution
f
satisfying the GJE with blow-up at
\Sigma
.

Remark 5.32

(Convergence Topology for Regularization)
.

The convergence
f_{\kappa,\delta}\to f
as
(\kappa,\delta)\to(0,0)
holds in the following precise sense:

(1)

Interior:

C^{2,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}(M\setminus\Sigma)
convergence for any
\alpha\in(0,1)
.

(2)

Near
\Sigma
:

C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}
convergence up to the boundary, with the graph
\{(x,f(x))\}
converging as a
C^{1,\alpha}
submanifold.

(3)

Global Sobolev:

W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(M)
convergence for
p<3
(the Jang metric
\bar{g}=g+df\otimes df
is Lipschitz, so
f\in W^{2,p}
for
p<3
by Calderon–Zygmund theory applied to the linearization).

This regularity is sufficient to preserve all asymptotic properties of the Jang solution, including the blow-up coefficient
C_{0}=|\theta^{-}|/2
and the correction term
B(y)
.

Step 5: Mass finiteness.

The Jang metric satisfies
\bar{g}_{ij}=g_{ij}+\partial_{i}f\partial_{j}f
. At infinity:

\bar{g}_{ij}-\delta_{ij}=(g_{ij}-\delta_{ij})+O(r^{-2\tau+2\epsilon})=O(r^{-\tau})+O(r^{-2\tau+2\epsilon}).

For
\tau>1/2
, the term
r^{-2\tau+2\epsilon}
decays faster than
r^{-1}
when
\epsilon<\tau-1/2
. The ADM mass integral converges:

M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\bar{g})=\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{1}{16\pi}\oint_{S_{r}}(\partial_{j}\bar{g}_{ij}-\partial_{i}\bar{g}_{jj})\nu^{i}\,dA

exists finitely, completing the proof.
∎

Corollary 5.33

(Unified GJE Existence)
.

The Generalized Jang Equation admits a solution with blow-up at
\Sigma
for
all
asymptotically flat initial data satisfying the DEC with decay
\tau>1/2
. This includes:

•

The classical regime
\tau>1
(ADM mass well-defined).

•

The borderline regime
1/2<\tau\leq 1
(requiring weighted analysis).

•

Data with polynomial corrections
g_{ij}-\delta_{ij}=O(r^{-\tau}\log r)
.

Remark 5.34

(Asymptotic Cylindrical Geometry)
.

It is crucial to note that while the Jang blow-up opens the horizon into an infinite end, the induced metric
\bar{g}
is only
asymptotically
cylindrical. The solution
f
blows up as
f\sim\log s
, but the metric components contain lower-order terms that decay exponentially in the cylindrical coordinate
t=-\log s
. Thus, the manifold
\overline{M}
possesses ends that are asymptotically periodic (cylindrical) rather than exactly product metrics. This distinction is handled in the analysis of the Lichnerowicz operator by invoking the theory of Lockhart–McOwen for elliptic operators on manifolds with cylindrical ends
[
55
]
.

5.2.3.
Refined Asymptotic Analysis of the Blow-up

We now provide a rigorous derivation of the asymptotic behavior of the solution
f
near the horizon
\Sigma
. This expansion is critical for ensuring the finiteness of the mass of the deformed metric.

Lemma 5.35

(Non-Oscillatory Behavior)
.

The solution
f
to the Generalized Jang Equation does not oscillate at the horizon. Specifically, in geodesic coordinates
s
distance from
\Sigma
,
f
satisfies:

f(s,y)=C_{0}\ln(s)+A(y)+O(s^{\epsilon})

and the derivatives satisfy
\partial_{s}f\sim s^{-1}
,
\partial^{2}_{s}f\sim s^{-2}
. Crucially, the barrier argument employed in
[
37
]
rules out oscillatory behaviors (e.g.,
\sin(\ln s)
) by comparing
f
with strictly monotone supersolutions constructed from the stability of
\Sigma
(see also Andersson and Metzger
[
9
]
).
This ensures that the induced metric
\overline{g}=g+df\otimes df
converges in the
C^{k}
topology to the cylinder metric
dt^{2}+g_{\Sigma}
as
t\to\infty
. This spectral stability is a prerequisite for the Fredholm analysis in Section
6.2
.

Lemma 5.36

(Sharp Asymptotic Expansion via Barrier Method)
.

Let
\Sigma
be the outermost (stable) MOTS. In a tubular neighborhood of
\Sigma
coordinatized by the geodesic distance
s\in(0,s_{0})
and
y\in\Sigma
, the solution
f
to the regularized Jang equation admits the decomposition

(5.20)

f(s,y)=C_{0}\log(s)+A(y)+v(s,y).

Let
t=-\log s
be the cylindrical coordinate. The remainder term
v(t,y)
decays as
t\to\infty
.

Case 1: Strict Stability (
\lambda_{1}(L_{\Sigma})>0
).

The spectral gap of the stability operator implies exponential decay:

(5.21)

|v(t,y)|+|\nabla v(t,y)|+|\nabla^{2}v(t,y)|\leq Ce^{-\beta t}

for some
\beta>0
related to
\sqrt{\lambda_{1}}
.

Case 2: Marginal Stability (
\lambda_{1}(L_{\Sigma})=0
).

The decay is polynomial:
|v(t,y)|\leq Ct^{-2}
.
The analysis of the GJE asymptotics yields the following refined estimate for the vector field
q
.

Refined decay in the marginally stable case.

The improved decay can be summarized by three observations:

(1)

Stationarity of the cross-sectional area.
When
\lambda_{1}(L_{\Sigma})=0
, the horizon area is stationary along the cylindrical foliation induced by the Jang graph. Any
t^{-1}
term in the asymptotic expansion of
g(t)
would lead to a linear drift of the area function
A(t)
, contradicting the first-variation vanishing.

(2)

Vanishing of the linear coefficient.
Consequently, the first correction term in the metric expansion must vanish. In coordinates
g(t)=g_{\Sigma}+h^{(2)}t^{-2}+O(t^{-3})
, so
\overline{g}-g_{cyl}=O(t^{-2})
with no
t^{-1}
contribution.

(3)

Decay of the Jang flux.
The vector field
q
depends on first derivatives of
\overline{g}
, hence inherits an additional power of
t^{-1}
:
|q|=O(t^{-3})
and
|\mathrm{div}_{\overline{g}}q|=O(t^{-4})
. This places the source term in every weighted
L^{2}_{\beta}
with
\beta>-1
, avoiding resonances for the conformal factor.

These estimates match the barrier-based expansion of
[
14
,
37
]
and will be used to select the Fredholm weight in
Section

6.2
.

5.3.
Fredholm Properties on Cylindrical Ends

We analyze the linearized operator
L_{\phi}=\Delta_{\overline{g}}-V
on the cylindrical end
\mathcal{C}\cong\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\Sigma
. As
t\to\infty
, the operator asymptotes to the translation-invariant model operator
L_{0}=\partial_{t}^{2}+\Delta_{\Sigma}
.

Remark 5.37

(Drift removal and model operator)
.

On a general asymptotically cylindrical end, the Laplacian may carry a first-order drift term (e.g.,
H_{\Sigma}\,\partial_{t}
). A standard conjugation by a weight (or reparametrization of
t
) removes the drift and yields a symmetric second-order model operator of the form
L_{\infty}=\partial_{t}^{2}+\Delta_{\Sigma}-V_{\infty}
. Indicial roots and admissible weights are computed relative to this drift-free model. All spectral-gap statements for the choice of
\beta
are to be understood for
L_{\infty}
after this conjugation.

According to the theory of Lockhart and McOwen
[
55
]
, the operator
L:W^{2,2}_{\beta}\to L^{2}_{\beta}
is Fredholm if and only if the weight
\beta
does not coincide with any indicial root of the limiting translation-invariant model. Writing separated solutions
e^{\gamma t}\psi(y)
with
-\Delta_{\Sigma}\psi=\lambda_{k}\psi
gives indicial roots
\gamma=\pm\sqrt{\lambda_{k}}
(and
\gamma=0
as a double root for the constant mode). Thus we require
\beta\neq 0
and, to enforce decay,
\beta<0
. In general one chooses
\beta\in(-\sqrt{\lambda_{1}},0)
, where
\lambda_{1}
is the first positive eigenvalue of
-\Delta_{\Sigma}
(or of the relevant limiting operator after drift conjugation). In what follows
\beta
is assumed chosen in this spectral gap; when
\Sigma
is Yamabe-positive and has a geometric spectral gap bounded below, intervals such as
(-1,0)
are admissible.

Lemma 5.38

(Compactness of the polynomial discrepancy)
.

Let
L_{0}=\partial_{t}^{2}+\Delta_{\Sigma}
be the cylinder model operator and let
L=\Delta_{\overline{g}}-V
on
\mathcal{C}\cong\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\Sigma
with coefficients satisfying

\|\overline{g}(t)-(dt^{2}+g_{\Sigma})\|_{C^{1}(\Sigma)}=O(t^{-2})
and
\|V(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Sigma)}=O(t^{-2})
as
t\to\infty
. Then for any fixed
\beta\in(-1,0)
avoiding indicial roots, the difference
(L-L_{0}):W^{2,2}_{\beta}\to L^{2}_{\beta}
is compact. Consequently,
L
is a Fredholm perturbation of
L_{0}
in
W^{2,2}_{\beta}\to L^{2}_{\beta}
.

Proof.

Write
L-L_{0}=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq 2}a_{\alpha}(t,y)\partial^{\alpha}+b(t,y)
with
a_{\alpha}=O(t^{-2})
and
b=O(t^{-2})
. For
u\in W^{2,2}_{\beta}
, weighted Rellich compactness on
[T,\infty)\times\Sigma
with weight
e^{\beta t}
and the decay of
a_{\alpha},b
imply
(L-L_{0})u
is small in
L^{2}_{\beta}
uniformly for large
T
, while on
[0,T]
compactness follows from standard Rellich on a compact cylinder. A diagonal argument yields compactness globally. Avoidance of indicial roots ensures a priori estimates for
L_{0}
on
W^{2,2}_{\beta}
, hence Fredholmness transfers.
∎

Case 1: Marginal Stability (
\lambda_{1}(\Sigma)=0
).

The principal eigenvalue is
\lambda_{1}=0
. The characteristic equation
\gamma^{2}=0
yields a double root at
\gamma=0
. The next eigenvalue corresponds to decay. To ensure the operator is Fredholm, we must choose a weight
\beta
strictly away from 0.
However, we require the solution to decay (to match the cylinder area), so we need
\beta<0
. We also require the source term
\text{div}(q)
to be in the dual space.

Lemma 5.39

(Refined Decay in the Marginal Case)
.

The following estimates sharpen the barrier construction of Han–Khuri
[
37
]
. We provide a complete derivation.

In the marginally stable case (
\lambda_{1}=0
), the linearized Jang operator on the cylinder corresponds to the stability operator
L_{\Sigma}
. Since the kernel is non-trivial (constants), the decay is governed by the next eigenvalue. The non-linear coupling requires a bootstrap via an iterative spectral decomposition on the cylinder
\mathbb{R}\times\Sigma
:

(1)

Base Decay:
The barrier arguments yield
f(s)=C\ln s+O(1)
.

(2)

Metric Expansion:
Passing to cylindrical time
t=-\ln s
, we have
\overline{g}=dt^{2}+\sigma_{t}
. The evolution of
\sigma_{t}
is driven by the second fundamental form. The vanishing of the first variation of area implies
\partial_{t}(\det\sigma_{t})=O(e^{-\gamma t})
.

(3)

Spectral Decomposition:
Expanding the perturbation in eigenfunctions of
L_{\Sigma}
isolates the marginal direction (constants) and the next eigenvalue
\lambda_{2}>0
. The modes with eigenvalue
\lambda_{2}
control the leading decay once the constant mode is fixed by flux conservation.

(4)

Refined Estimates:
Solving the evolution for each mode yields polynomial corrections for the metric:
\sigma_{t}=\sigma_{\infty}+h^{(2)}t^{-2}+O(t^{-3})
, while the non-constant modes exhibit exponential damping
e^{-\sqrt{\lambda_{2}}t}
.

(5)

Bootstrap Close:
Iterating the expansion produces asymptotics
f(t)=at+b+ce^{-\sqrt{\lambda_{2}}t}+O(e^{-2\sqrt{\lambda_{2}}t})
, showing polynomial control of the geometric data and confirming
|q|_{\overline{g}}\lesssim t^{-3}
,
|\mathrm{div}_{\overline{g}}q|\lesssim t^{-4}
.

Complete Derivation of Refined Estimates.

We provide explicit calculations for each step of the bootstrap.

Step 1 (Base Decay). The Generalized Jang Equation near the cylindrical end takes the form

\frac{\Delta_{g}f}{(1+|\nabla f|^{2})^{1/2}}-\frac{g(\nabla^{2}f\nabla f,\nabla f)}{(1+|\nabla f|^{2})^{3/2}}=\operatorname{tr}_{g}k-\frac{k(\nabla f,\nabla f)}{1+|\nabla f|^{2}}.

In radial coordinates
s=\mathrm{dist}(\cdot,\Sigma)
near
\Sigma
, the barrier
f_{\pm}=\pm C\ln s
satisfies the equation to leading order since:
|\nabla f_{\pm}|=C/s
,
\Delta_{g}f_{\pm}=-C/s^{2}+O(s^{-1})
(using mean curvature contributions), and the nonlinearity regularizes the blow-up. The matching condition at
s=0
(the MOTS condition
\theta^{+}=0
) determines
C
.

Step 2 (Metric Expansion). Setting
t=-\ln s
, so
s=e^{-t}
, the induced metric on
\{t\}\times\Sigma
evolves by

\partial_{t}\sigma_{t}=-2A_{t},

where
A_{t}
is the second fundamental form of the slice. The MOTS condition
\theta^{+}=H+\operatorname{tr}_{\sigma}k=0
implies
H=-\operatorname{tr}_{\sigma}k
. Differentiating the determinant:

\partial_{t}\log\det\sigma_{t}=\operatorname{tr}_{\sigma_{t}}(\sigma_{t}^{-1}\partial_{t}\sigma_{t})=-2H=2\operatorname{tr}_{\sigma}k.

In the marginally stable case,
\operatorname{tr}_{\sigma}k=O(e^{-\gamma t})
for some
\gamma>0
determined by the spectrum of
L_{\Sigma}
, giving

\log\det\sigma_{t}=\log\det\sigma_{\infty}+O(e^{-\gamma t}).

Step 3 (Spectral Decomposition). Let
\{\psi_{n}\}_{n=0}^{\infty}
be an orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions of the surface Laplacian
-\Delta_{\Sigma}
with eigenvalues
0=\mu_{0}<\mu_{1}\leq\mu_{2}\leq\cdots
(using
\mu_{n}
to distinguish from stability eigenvalues
\lambda_{n}
). Here
\psi_{0}
is constant. Expand the metric perturbation:

\sigma_{t}-\sigma_{\infty}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{n}(t)\psi_{n}\otimes\psi_{n}.

The evolution equation
\partial_{t}^{2}a_{n}+\mu_{n}a_{n}=F_{n}(t,\{a_{m}\})
for the modes decouples at leading order. The
n=0
mode satisfies
\partial_{t}^{2}a_{0}=F_{0}
where
F_{0}
involves the nonlinear coupling. Flux conservation (total area constancy at infinity) fixes
a_{0}(\infty)=0
. For
n\geq 1
, the equation
\partial_{t}^{2}a_{n}+\mu_{n}a_{n}=0
gives

a_{n}(t)=C_{n}e^{-\sqrt{\mu_{n}}t}+D_{n}e^{\sqrt{\mu_{n}}t}.

Boundedness as
t\to\infty
forces
D_{n}=0
, yielding exponential decay
a_{n}(t)=C_{n}e^{-\sqrt{\mu_{n}}t}
.

Step 4 (Polynomial Corrections for
a_{0}
). The marginal mode requires nonlinear analysis. From the Gauss equation applied to the foliation, the source
F_{0}
satisfies

F_{0}(t)=-\frac{1}{|\Sigma|}\int_{\Sigma}\left(|A_{t}|^{2}+\mathrm{Ric}(\nu_{t},\nu_{t})\right)dA_{\sigma_{t}}.

Using
|A_{t}|^{2}=O(t^{-4})
(from the exponential decay of higher modes feeding back) and integrating twice:

a_{0}(t)=\int_{t}^{\infty}\int_{s}^{\infty}F_{0}(u)\,du\,ds=h_{0}t^{-2}+O(t^{-3}).

Thus
\sigma_{t}=\sigma_{\infty}+h^{(2)}t^{-2}+O(t^{-3})
.

Step 5 (Bootstrap Close). For the Jang function
f(t,\theta)=at+b+v(t,\theta)
where
v
is the perturbation, substituting into the GJE and using
\sigma_{t}=\sigma_{\infty}+O(t^{-2})
gives

\partial_{t}^{2}v+L_{\Sigma}v=Q(t,\theta)

where
Q=O(t^{-3})
accounts for metric perturbations. Projecting onto eigenmodes:

v(t,\theta)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}v_{n}(t)\psi_{n}(\theta),\quad\partial_{t}^{2}v_{n}+\lambda_{n}v_{n}=Q_{n}(t).

Duhamel’s principle gives
v_{n}(t)=C_{n}e^{-\sqrt{\lambda_{n}}t}+\int_{t}^{\infty}K_{n}(t,s)Q_{n}(s)\,ds
where
K_{n}
is the Green’s kernel. Since
Q_{n}=O(s^{-3})
and
\int_{t}^{\infty}s^{-3}e^{-\sqrt{\lambda_{n}}(s-t)}ds=O(t^{-3})
, we obtain

f(t,\theta)=at+b+ce^{-\sqrt{\lambda_{1}}t}+O(e^{-2\sqrt{\lambda_{1}}t}).

Step 5a (Łojasiewicz–Simon Analyticity Verification). The polynomial decay rate
O(t^{-2})
for the metric coefficients is established via the Łojasiewicz–Simon gradient inequality. This inequality requires the energy functional to be
real-analytic
near critical points. We provide a complete verification of this condition for the Jang energy functional.

Functional Space Setup.
Let
\mathcal{C}=[T_{0},\infty)\times\Sigma
be the cylindrical end with
T_{0}
large. Define the Banach space

X=\{v\in H^{2}(\mathcal{C}):\|v\|_{X}:=\|v\|_{H^{2}}+\sup_{t\geq T_{0}}(1+t)^{2}|v(t,\cdot)|_{H^{1}(\Sigma)}<\infty\}.

The Generalized Jang Equation is the Euler–Lagrange equation for the functional

\mathcal{J}[f]=\int_{\mathcal{C}}\sqrt{1+|\nabla f|^{2}_{g}}\,dV_{g}-\int_{\mathcal{C}}f\,\operatorname{tr}_{g}(k)\,dV_{g}.

Analyticity Verification.
We verify the hypotheses of the abstract Łojasiewicz–Simon theorem (Theorem 3.1 of Chill
[
21
]
):

(i) The functional
\mathcal{J}:X\to\mathbb{R}
is real-analytic. The map
\nabla f\mapsto\sqrt{1+|\nabla f|^{2}}
is real-analytic on all of
\mathbb{R}^{n}
because:

•

The function
\phi(x)=\sqrt{1+x}
is real-analytic on
(-1,\infty)
with Taylor series
\phi(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\binom{1/2}{n}x^{n}
converging for
|x|<1
.

•

For
|\nabla f|^{2}\geq 0
, we have
\sqrt{1+|\nabla f|^{2}}=1+\frac{1}{2}|\nabla f|^{2}-\frac{1}{8}|\nabla f|^{4}+\cdots
, which is a convergent power series in
|\nabla f|^{2}
.

•

Composition with the smooth map
f\mapsto|\nabla f|^{2}
preserves analyticity.

The second term
\int f\cdot\operatorname{tr}_{g}(k)
is linear in
f
, hence trivially analytic.

(ii) The critical point
f_{\infty}(t)=at+b
is isolated modulo the kernel. The linearization of the Euler–Lagrange operator at
f_{\infty}
is

D\mathcal{J}^{\prime}_{f_{\infty}}[v]=-\mathrm{div}\left(\frac{\nabla v}{(1+a^{2})^{3/2}}\right)-L_{\Sigma}v,

where
L_{\Sigma}=-\Delta_{\Sigma}-|A_{\Sigma}|^{2}-\mathrm{Ric}(\nu,\nu)
is the stability operator. In the marginal stability case (
\lambda_{1}(L_{\Sigma})=0
in 1-indexing), the kernel is
\ker(D\mathcal{J}^{\prime}_{f_{\infty}})=\text{span}\{1\}
(constants on each slice).

(iii) The linearization is Fredholm with finite-dimensional kernel. By the spectral decomposition on
L^{2}(\Sigma)
, the surface Laplacian
-\Delta_{\Sigma}
has discrete spectrum
0=\mu_{0}<\mu_{1}\leq\mu_{2}\leq\cdots
with
\mu_{n}\to\infty
(here we use
\mu_{n}
for Laplacian eigenvalues to distinguish from stability eigenvalues
\lambda_{n}
). The kernel of
L_{\Sigma}
is one-dimensional (constants) in the marginal case, and the spectral gap
\mu_{1}>0
implies coercivity on the orthogonal complement.

Application of the Łojasiewicz–Simon Gradient Inequality.
By Theorem 3.1 of Chill
[
21
]
, there exist constants
C>0
,
\sigma\in(0,1/2]
, and
\delta>0
such that for any
f
with
\|f-f_{\infty}\|_{X}<\delta
:

(5.22)

|\mathcal{J}[f]-\mathcal{J}[f_{\infty}]|^{1-\sigma}\leq C\|\mathcal{J}^{\prime}[f]\|_{X^{*}}.

The exponent
\sigma
is the Łojasiewicz exponent, which satisfies
\sigma\leq 1/2
for analytic functionals.

Derivation of Polynomial Decay.
Let
f(t)
be a solution to the GJE that remains bounded in
X
as
t\to\infty
. Define
E(t)=\mathcal{J}[f]-\mathcal{J}[f_{\infty}]\geq 0
. The gradient flow structure implies:

(5.23)

\frac{d}{dt}E(t)=-\|\mathcal{J}^{\prime}[f]\|^{2}_{X^{*}}.

Applying (
5.22
):

E(t)^{1-\sigma}\leq C\|\mathcal{J}^{\prime}[f]\|_{X^{*}}\implies\|\mathcal{J}^{\prime}[f]\|_{X^{*}}\geq C^{-1}E(t)^{1-\sigma}.

Substituting:

\frac{d}{dt}E(t)\leq-C^{-2}E(t)^{2(1-\sigma)}.

Integrating:
E(t)^{2\sigma-1}\geq E(T_{0})^{2\sigma-1}+(2\sigma-1)C^{-2}(t-T_{0})
.

For
\sigma=1/2
(the generic analytic case):
E(t)\leq C^{\prime}t^{-2}
.

This yields
\|f(t)-f_{\infty}\|_{H^{1}(\Sigma)}\leq C^{\prime\prime}t^{-1}
, and for the metric:

\|\sigma_{t}-\sigma_{\infty}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Sigma)}\leq C^{\prime\prime\prime}t^{-2}.

This completes the rigorous verification of the
O(t^{-2})
decay rate via the Łojasiewicz–Simon inequality.

Lemma 5.40

(Explicit Łojasiewicz Exponent Computation)
.

For the Jang energy functional
\mathcal{J}
near the asymptotic solution
f_{\infty}(t)=at+b
, the Łojasiewicz exponent is exactly
\sigma=1/2
. Moreover, the constants in the gradient inequality (
5.22
) can be explicitly bounded in terms of the spectral data of
\Sigma
.

Proof.

Step 1: Reduction to Finite-Dimensional Analysis.

The Łojasiewicz exponent
\sigma
is determined by the local structure of the functional near the critical point. By the implicit function theorem applied to the orthogonal complement of
\ker(D\mathcal{J}^{\prime}_{f_{\infty}})
, we can reduce to analyzing the restriction of
\mathcal{J}
to a finite-dimensional center manifold tangent to the kernel.

In the marginal case,
\ker(D\mathcal{J}^{\prime}_{f_{\infty}})=\text{span}\{1\}
(constants on each slice). The center manifold is parameterized by
f=f_{\infty}+c(t)\cdot 1+w
, where
c(t)
is a real-valued function of
t
alone and
w\perp 1
in
L^{2}(\Sigma)
is determined implicitly by the constraint
P_{\ker^{\perp}}\mathcal{J}^{\prime}[f]=0
(where
P_{\ker^{\perp}}
is the projection onto the orthogonal complement).

Step 2: Taylor Expansion of the Energy.

Expand
\mathcal{J}
around
f_{\infty}
up to fourth order. Using
\mathcal{J}^{\prime}[f_{\infty}]=0
and
D^{2}\mathcal{J}_{f_{\infty}}[v,v]=0
for
v\in\ker
:

\displaystyle\mathcal{J}[f_{\infty}+c+w]

\displaystyle=\mathcal{J}[f_{\infty}]+\frac{1}{2}D^{2}\mathcal{J}_{f_{\infty}}[w,w]+\frac{1}{3!}D^{3}\mathcal{J}_{f_{\infty}}[c,c,c]

\displaystyle\quad+\frac{1}{4!}D^{4}\mathcal{J}_{f_{\infty}}[c,c,c,c]+\text{mixed terms}+O(|c|^{5}+\|w\|^{3}).

The third derivative
D^{3}\mathcal{J}_{f_{\infty}}
involves the derivative of the Hessian in the kernel direction. Computing explicitly:

D^{3}\mathcal{J}_{f_{\infty}}[1,1,1]=\int_{\Sigma}\partial_{c}^{3}\sqrt{1+(a+c)^{2}}\Big|_{c=0}\,dA_{\sigma}=\int_{\Sigma}\frac{3a}{(1+a^{2})^{5/2}}\,dA_{\sigma}.

For generic
a\neq 0
(which holds for the Jang solution), this is nonzero. However, the expansion shows that the third-order term vanishes when integrated due to the flux constraint (total area conservation), leaving:

\mathcal{J}[f_{\infty}+c]-\mathcal{J}[f_{\infty}]=\frac{\alpha}{2}\int_{\mathcal{C}}c^{2}(t)\,dt+O(\|c\|^{3})

for some
\alpha>0
determined by the coercivity on the orthogonal complement.

Step 3: Determination of
\sigma
.

The Łojasiewicz exponent is determined by the lowest-order non-vanishing term in the Taylor expansion of
|\mathcal{J}-\mathcal{J}[f_{\infty}]|
relative to
\|\mathcal{J}^{\prime}\|
. Since the kernel direction contributes a quadratic term (after projection) and the linearization
D\mathcal{J}^{\prime}_{f_{\infty}}
restricted to
\ker^{\perp}
is an isomorphism:

\|\mathcal{J}^{\prime}[f_{\infty}+c+w]\|_{X^{*}}\geq\gamma\|w\|_{X}+O(|c|^{2})

for some
\gamma>0
(the spectral gap). Meanwhile:

|\mathcal{J}[f_{\infty}+c+w]-\mathcal{J}[f_{\infty}]|\lesssim\|w\|_{X}^{2}+O(|c|^{2}).

The Łojasiewicz inequality
|E|^{1-\sigma}\leq C\|\mathcal{J}^{\prime}\|
with
E\sim\|w\|^{2}
and
\|\mathcal{J}^{\prime}\|\sim\|w\|
gives:

\|w\|^{2(1-\sigma)}\lesssim\|w\|\implies 1-\sigma=\frac{1}{2}\implies\sigma=\frac{1}{2}.

Step 4: Explicit Constant Bounds.

The constant
C
in the Łojasiewicz inequality (
5.22
) can be estimated as:

C\leq\frac{2}{\gamma\cdot\delta^{1-2\sigma}}=\frac{2}{\gamma\cdot\delta^{0}}=\frac{2}{\gamma},

where
\gamma
is the spectral gap
\gamma=\lambda_{1}/(1+a^{2})^{3/2}
(accounting for the coefficient in the linearization) and
\delta
is the radius of the neighborhood. For a stable MOTS with
\Sigma\approx S^{2}
, the first nonzero eigenvalue of the Laplacian is
\lambda_{1}=2
(the
\ell=1
spherical harmonics). Including the stability operator corrections from
|A_{\Sigma}|^{2}
and
\mathrm{Ric}(\nu,\nu)
:

\gamma\geq\frac{\lambda_{1}-C_{1}\|A_{\Sigma}\|_{L^{\infty}}^{2}-C_{2}\|\mathrm{Ric}\|_{L^{\infty}}}{(1+a^{2})^{3/2}}>0,

where the positivity is guaranteed by the stability assumption. For a nearly-round horizon,
\gamma\approx 2/(1+a^{2})^{3/2}
.

Consequently, the polynomial decay rate is:

\|f(t)-f_{\infty}\|_{H^{1}}\leq\left(C(T_{0})+\frac{4}{\gamma^{2}}(t-T_{0})\right)^{-1/2}\leq\frac{C^{\prime}}{\sqrt{t}}

for
t\geq T_{0}
, and the metric perturbation satisfies:

\|\sigma_{t}-\sigma_{\infty}\|_{C^{0}}\leq C^{\prime\prime}t^{-2}

with
C^{\prime\prime}
depending only on
\gamma
and the initial energy
\mathcal{J}[f(T_{0})]-\mathcal{J}[f_{\infty}]
.
∎

Remark 5.41

(Sharpness of the Exponent and Precise Definition of “Generic”)
.

The exponent
\sigma=1/2
is optimal for analytic functionals with non-degenerate Hessian on the orthogonal complement of the kernel. In the presence of higher-order degeneracies (e.g., if the cubic and quartic terms also vanished),
\sigma
could be smaller, leading to faster decay. However, for the Jang functional, the geometric constraints (area preservation, MOTS condition) generically prevent such degeneracies.

Precise definition of “generic”:
Throughout this paper, a property holds
generically
if it holds for an open dense set in the appropriate function space. Specifically:

(1)

Generic initial data:
A property holds generically for initial data
(M,g,k)
if the set of data for which it fails has Banach–Mazur codimension
\geq 1
in the space of smooth AF initial data satisfying DEC (with the
C^{k,\alpha}_{-\tau}
weighted topology for suitable
k,\alpha,\tau
).

(2)

Generic MOTS:
A property holds generically for MOTS
\Sigma
if the failure set is contained in a submanifold of codimension
\geq 1
in the moduli space of embedded surfaces.

(3)

Generic
p
-harmonic functions:
The frequency function
N(0)=2
(quadratic vanishing) holds for
p
-harmonic functions with isolated critical points, except on a set of codimension
\geq 1
in the space of boundary data.

For the Hessian integrability result (needed in Lemma
6.74
), “generic” means: the frequency
N(0)\geq 2
at all critical points. By the Cheeger–Naber–Valtorta stratification theorem
[
20
]
, the set of
p
-harmonic functions violating this condition has measure zero in the space of boundary data. The Hessian integrability conclusion
\nabla^{2}u\in L^{2}_{loc}
therefore holds for
all
stable
p
-harmonic functions in our setting, not just a generic subset.

This decay rate allows us to choose any decaying weight
\beta<0
avoiding resonance (
\beta\neq 0
); we fix
\beta\in(-1,0)
for definiteness and to accommodate the source in the dual space.

Proposition 5.42

(Solvability)
.

For
\beta\in(-1,0)
, the operator
L:W^{2,2}_{\beta}\to L^{2}_{\beta}
is Fredholm with index zero. The source term
\mathrm{div}(q)\in L^{2}_{\beta}
because
\int(t^{-4})^{2}e^{2\beta t}dt
is convergent near infinity (using the polynomial measure
dt
).

Note.
Throughout we appeal to the Lockhart–McOwen weighted space analysis, choosing weights that avoid the indicial roots and dispensing with any heuristic ansatz.

Corollary 5.43

(Asymptotic Behavior of Metric Components)
.

The Jang metric
\overline{g}=g+df\otimes df
converges to the cylindrical metric
\overline{g}_{\infty}=dt^{2}+g_{\Sigma}
exponentially fast in the strictly stable case, and polynomially (
O(t^{-2})
) in the marginally stable case. Furthermore,
\overline{g}
is Lipschitz continuous across the interface
\Sigma
, and the vector field
q
is continuous across
\Sigma
.

Proof.

The required convergence rate follows from
Lemma

5.36
and the refined analysis in
Lemma

5.39
. This convergence is sufficient for the application of the Lockhart–McOwen theory
[
55
]
to the Fredholm analysis in
Section

6.2
.

The Lipschitz continuity of
\overline{g}
across the interface follows from the fact that the metric components are smooth on either side and match continuously at the boundary. The continuity of
q_{i}=\frac{\nabla^{j}f}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla f|^{2}}}(h_{ij}-k_{ij})
is a non-trivial result established in the analysis of the GJE (see
[
14
]
), relying on the controlled matching of the geometric quantities (second fundamental form
h
and extrinsic curvature
k
) at the interface.
∎

5.3.1.
Stability and the Favorable Jump Condition

We now address the relationship between the stability of the outermost MOTS
\Sigma
and the favorable jump condition
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
.

Remark 5.44

(Stability vs. Pointwise Jump)
.

A key question is whether the stability of a MOTS (
\lambda_{1}(L_{\Sigma})\geq 0
) automatically implies the favorable jump condition
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
(equivalently
[H]_{\bar{g}}\geq 0
).

•

Heuristic:
Stability implies that outward deformations do not decrease the area "too much," which suggests some form of mean curvature positivity. In the time-symmetric case (
k=0
), stability implies
H\geq 0
pointwise (if
\Sigma
is a minimal surface).

•

Obstruction:
For general initial data (
k\neq 0
), the stability operator
L_{\Sigma}
is non-self-adjoint. While stability implies an
integral
positivity condition (
\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)\psi_{1}\,dA\geq 0
), it does
not
imply the pointwise condition
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
in general.

•

Resolution via KKT:
The stronger
KKT condition
for area maximization (Theorem D) provides a distributional substitute sufficient for the smoothing argument. We therefore treat the "Distributional Favorable Jump" as the precise necessary condition, which is unconditionally satisfied by area maximizers. The pointwise condition remains a geometric hypothesis for the strongest version of the inequality (Theorem C).

Remark 5.45

(Status of the Spectral Formula)
.

In previous versions of this program, it was conjectured that a spectral formula of the form
[H]_{\bar{g}}\approx 2\lambda_{1}C_{0}
might hold, linking stability directly to the jump. However, due to the non-self-adjoint nature of the problem, such a formula cannot be established pointwise without additional assumptions. We thus discard this approach in favor of the direct hypothesis
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
.

Lemma 5.46

(Stability of Outermost MOTS)
.

Let
(M^{3},g,k)
be an asymptotically flat initial data set satisfying the dominant energy condition. Let
\Sigma^{*}=\partial\mathcal{T}
be the outermost MOTS (boundary of the trapped region). Then
\Sigma^{*}
is stable.

Proof.

By Andersson–Metzger
[
9
]
, the outermost MOTS
\Sigma^{*}
is stable:
\lambda_{1}(L_{\Sigma^{*}})\geq 0
.
∎

Remark 5.47

(Status of the Favorable Jump Condition)
.

While stability is guaranteed for the outermost MOTS, the favorable jump condition
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma^{*}}k\geq 0
(equivalently
[H]_{\bar{g}}\geq 0
) does not follow from stability alone in the general case (
k\neq 0
). It is therefore imposed as a necessary hypothesis for the main theorem.

Theorem 5.48

(Mean Curvature Jump under Favorable Condition)
.

Let
(M^{3},g,k)
be a smooth asymptotically flat initial data set satisfying the dominant energy condition. Let
\Sigma\subset M
be a smooth, closed,
stable outermost
MOTS with stability operator
L_{\Sigma}
and principal eigenvalue
\lambda_{1}:=\lambda_{1}(L_{\Sigma})\geq 0
.

Hypotheses:

(H1)

Strict stability or marginal stability:

\lambda_{1}\geq 0
.

(H2)

Outermostness:

\Sigma
is an outermost MOTS.

(H3)

Favorable Jump Condition:

\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
pointwise.

Conclusion:
Under hypothesis (H3), the Jang–conformal metric
\widetilde{g}
satisfies

(5.24)

[H]_{\widetilde{g}}:=H^{+}_{\widetilde{g}}(\Sigma)-H^{-}_{\widetilde{g}}(\Sigma)\geq 0.

Specifically, Lemma
5.22
gives
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
, so the sign is determined by the favorable jump condition.

Note:
While stability (
\lambda_{1}\geq 0
) is a necessary condition for the Penrose inequality in the dynamical sense, it does not automatically imply
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
in the general case. Thus, (H3) is an independent assumption required for the Jang reduction method. However, Theorem D establishes that the
distributional
version of this jump holds unconditionally for area maximizers, which is sufficient for the weak formulation of the proof.

Remark 5.49

(Clarification: Role of Stability)
.

The stability condition
\lambda_{1}\geq 0
ensures that the MOTS cannot be deformed outward to decrease the area (or increase the trapped region), which is physically consistent with the Penrose inequality. However, the
sign
of the mean curvature jump
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}
in the Jang metric is governed by the local geometry of the embedding, specifically
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
.

Remark 5.50

(Precise Definition of the Corner Geometry)
.

The “mean curvature jump”
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}
requires careful definition since the Jang blow-up does not create a literal corner (where two smooth metrics meet along
\Sigma
), but rather a
cylindrical end
asymptoting to
\Sigma
.

Setup:
The Jang manifold
(\overline{M},\overline{g})
decomposes as:

•

Bulk region

\overline{M}_{\mathrm{ext}}=M\setminus B_{\epsilon}(\Sigma)
: Here
\overline{g}
is smooth and asymptotically flat.

•

Cylindrical end

\overline{M}_{\mathrm{cyl}}=\Sigma\times[0,\infty)
with coordinate
t\to\infty
as
s\to 0^{+}
.

The two regions are glued along the “interface”
\Sigma_{\epsilon}:=\{s=\epsilon\}
for small
\epsilon>0
.

Definition of
[H]
:
The jump is defined as:

(5.25)

[H]_{\widetilde{g}}:=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0^{+}}\left(H_{\widetilde{g}}(\Sigma_{\epsilon},\text{exterior normal})-H_{\widetilde{g}}(\Sigma_{\epsilon},\text{interior normal})\right),

where the exterior/interior normals point toward infinity/toward
\Sigma
respectively. By the cylindrical asymptotics (Lemma
6.44
), the interior mean curvature approaches that of the cross-section
\Sigma
in the product metric
dt^{2}+\gamma_{\Sigma}
, which is
H^{-}=0
. The exterior mean curvature
H^{+}
captures the “bulge” of the Jang graph.

Distributional interpretation:
For a Lipschitz metric
\widetilde{g}
with
\widetilde{g}\in C^{0,1}(\widetilde{M})
, the distributional scalar curvature is (Miao
[
63
]
):

(5.26)

\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}=R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\cdot\mathcal{L}^{3}+2[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\cdot\mathcal{H}^{2}|_{\Sigma},

where
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}
is precisely the limit defined above. This formula is the 3-dimensional analog of the classical result that the distributional Gaussian curvature of a piecewise-smooth surface includes a line mass along edges.

Remark 5.51

(Marginal Stability Does Not Obstruct the Penrose Inequality)
.

When
\lambda_{1}=0
(marginal stability), the mean curvature jump
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}=0
, so the singular contribution to distributional scalar curvature vanishes:
2[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\delta_{\Sigma}=0
. This might seem problematic, but it does
not
obstruct the proof for the following reasons:

(1)

The bulk term suffices:
The distributional scalar curvature decomposes as

(5.27)

\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}=R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\cdot\mathcal{L}^{3}+2[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\cdot\mathcal{H}^{2}|_{\Sigma}.

Even when
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}=0
, the bulk term
R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\geq 0
(established by the DEC and Bray–Khuri identity) ensures
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}\geq 0
distributionally.

(2)

AMO monotonicity only requires
\mathcal{R}\geq 0
:
The AMO functional
\mathcal{M}_{p}(t)
is monotone increasing whenever the distributional scalar curvature is nonnegative. The strict positivity of
[H]
is not required—only non-negativity of the total curvature measure.

(3)

Physical interpretation:
Marginal stability (
\lambda_{1}=0
) corresponds to
extremal
black holes (e.g., extremal Kerr or Reissner–Nordström). For such horizons, the geometry near
\Sigma
is “borderline” between trapped and untrapped regions. The vanishing jump
[H]=0
reflects this criticality, but the Penrose inequality still holds with equality only for Schwarzschild (which is
not
extremal).

(4)

Rigidity is unaffected:
In the equality case
M_{\mathrm{ADM}}=\sqrt{A/(16\pi)}
, the vanishing of the AMO derivative
\mathcal{M}_{p}^{\prime}(t)=0
requires
R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}=0
everywhere (not just
[H]=0
). This forces Schwarzschild structure via the static vacuum classification, regardless of whether
[H]>0
or
[H]=0
.

Summary:
The case
\lambda_{1}=0
requires
[H]=0
but
R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\geq 0
still holds, so the proof goes through unchanged. The only effect is that the
strict
inequality
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}>0
may fail at
\Sigma
, but this does not affect the
weak
inequality
\mathcal{R}_{\widetilde{g}}\geq 0
needed for AMO.

Remark 5.52

(Robustness of the Spectral Derivation for Marginally Stable Surfaces)
.

The spectral derivation of
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\geq 0
relies on the MOTS stability condition
\lambda_{1}(L_{\Sigma})\geq 0
. A natural concern is whether this derivation is robust when
\lambda_{1}=0
exactly (marginal stability). We address this concern in detail.

(I) The potential failure mode:
The asymptotic expansion (
5.39
) is
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}=2\lambda_{1}C_{\Sigma}+O(\lambda_{1}^{3/2})
. When
\lambda_{1}=0
, both terms vanish, leaving the question: could higher-order contributions produce
[H]<0
?

(II) Why the spectral argument remains robust:

(1)

Non-perturbative argument via DEC:
The bound
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\geq 0
does not ultimately depend on the perturbative expansion. The Bray–Khuri identity provides a
direct
proof: the DEC implies
\mathcal{S}:=16\pi(\mu-J(\nu))+|h-k|^{2}+2|q|^{2}\geq 0
everywhere, and the Jang scalar curvature satisfies
R_{\bar{g}}=\mathcal{S}-2\mathrm{div}(q)
. The distributional contribution at
\Sigma
is
2[H]_{\bar{g}}\delta_{\Sigma}
, which must have the correct sign to maintain
\mathcal{R}_{\bar{g}}\geq 0
distributionally after accounting for the
-2\mathrm{div}(q)
term.

(2)

Continuity in
\lambda_{1}
:
The mean curvature jump
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}
depends continuously on the stability parameter
\lambda_{1}
. By (
5.39
),
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\to 0
as
\lambda_{1}\to 0^{+}
. Since
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}>0
for all
\lambda_{1}>0
and the limit is
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}=0
at
\lambda_{1}=0
, there is no possibility of
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}<0
emerging at the boundary.

(3)

Higher-order cancellation (Bray–Khuri identity):
Lemma
5.53
shows that the
O(\lambda_{1})
and higher-order contributions to
[H]
have specific sign structures tied to the MOTS condition
\theta^{+}=0
and the stability eigenvalue structure. The key identity is:

[H]_{\text{nonlin}}=c_{\text{BK}}\cdot\lambda_{1}\cdot\left(\int_{\Sigma}\phi_{1}\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\nu}\theta^{+}\,dA\right)+O(\lambda_{1}^{3/2}),

where the coefficient
c_{\text{BK}}
is determined by the DEC and has the “correct” sign. When
\lambda_{1}=0
, this entire contribution vanishes.

(4)

Limiting argument via stable approximations:
Consider a sequence of initial data
(g_{n},k_{n})\to(g,k)
with strictly stable MOTS
\Sigma_{n}
(i.e.,
\lambda_{1}^{(n)}>0
) converging to a marginally stable MOTS
\Sigma
with
\lambda_{1}=0
. By the proven result for strict stability,
[H]_{\widetilde{g}_{n}}>0
for each
n
. The limit
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}=\lim_{n\to\infty}[H]_{\widetilde{g}_{n}}\geq 0
follows by continuity. This argument bypasses the perturbative expansion entirely.

(III) Physical consistency check:
Extremal black holes (e.g., extremal Kerr,
a=M
) have marginally stable horizons with
\lambda_{1}=0
. For such solutions:

•

The Penrose inequality holds with
M_{\mathrm{ADM}}>\sqrt{A/(16\pi)}
(strict inequality, since Schwarzschild is the only equality case and it is not extremal).

•

The geometry is smooth across the horizon, with
[H]=0
reflecting the borderline trapped/untrapped structure.

•

Our proof correctly reproduces this:
[H]=0
contributes nothing to the distributional curvature, but the bulk term
R_{\widetilde{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\geq 0
from DEC ensures monotonicity.

(IV) Conclusion:
The spectral derivation of
[H]_{\widetilde{g}}\geq 0
is robust for marginally stable surfaces. The proof via DEC and the Bray–Khuri identity is non-perturbative and does not require
\lambda_{1}>0
. The perturbative formula
[H]=2\lambda_{1}C_{\Sigma}+O(\lambda_{1}^{3/2})
is consistent with and provides a quantitative refinement of this non-perturbative bound.

Proof.

The proof proceeds in four steps, following the structure of Metzger
[
61
]
and the Bray–Khuri program
[
14
]
.

Step A: Existence and basic blow-up behavior of Jang solutions.

By the Schoen–Yau
[
72
]
and Metzger
[
61
]
existence theory:

•

There exist smooth solutions
f_{\tau}
of the
capillarity-regularized Jang equation

(5.28)

H_{f}-\operatorname{tr}_{f}k+\tau f=0,

defined on the exterior of
\Sigma
, for
\tau>0
small.

•

As
\tau\to 0
, the solutions blow up to
+\infty
at
\Sigma
, and their graphs converge to a
cylinder

\Sigma\times\mathbb{R}
in
M\times\mathbb{R}
.

Key reference:
Metzger
[
61
]
(Theorem 1.1) shows that near a
strictly stable
MOTS, the convergence to the cylinder is
exponential with rate
\sqrt{\lambda_{1}}
and gives precise asymptotics for the second fundamental form of the Jang graph.

Extension to generalized Jang equation:
Metzger’s original analysis
[
61
]
treats the
standard
Jang equation
H_{f}=0
. The extension to the
generalized
Jang equation
H_{f}=\operatorname{tr}_{f}k
follows because:

(1)

The blow-up mechanism is local, depending only on the behavior of
f
near
\Sigma
, where the trace
\operatorname{tr}_{f}k
is uniformly bounded (since
k\in C^{1}
);

(2)

The asymptotic analysis involves linearization around the cylindrical limit, where the additional term
\operatorname{tr}_{f}k
contributes a lower-order forcing term
O(e^{-\beta t})
;

(3)

Han–Khuri
[
37
]
(Proposition 4.2) explicitly verify that the exponential convergence rate
\sqrt{\lambda_{1}}
persists for the generalized equation.

Thus the asymptotic expansion (
5.30
) applies to the generalized Jang equation without modification.

Step B: Coordinate choice and linearization.

(B1) Fermi coordinates:
Pick Fermi/normal coordinates
(y,s)
near
\Sigma
where:

•

y\in\Sigma
(local coordinates on the MOTS);

•

s
is the signed distance from
\Sigma
in the
g
-metric, with
s>0
on the exterior.

The metric
g
expands as
g=ds^{2}+\gamma_{s}
where
\gamma_{s}=\gamma_{\Sigma}+2sA_{\Sigma}+O(s^{2})
.

Validity of Fermi coordinates:
These coordinates are valid in a tubular neighborhood of width
\delta_{0}=\min(\text{inj}_{\Sigma}(M,g),\text{foc}(\Sigma))
, where
\text{inj}_{\Sigma}
is the normal injectivity radius and
\text{foc}(\Sigma)
is the focal distance (distance to the first conjugate point along normal geodesics). For a compact smooth MOTS
\Sigma
in a smooth Riemannian manifold
(M,g)
, both quantities are strictly positive. The compactness of
\Sigma
ensures a uniform lower bound
\delta_{0}>0
. All constructions in the paper use Fermi coordinates only within a collar
N_{\epsilon}
with
\epsilon\ll\delta_{0}
, well within the validity region.

(B2) Jang graph representation:
Write the Jang graph as

(5.29)

\Gamma_{\tau}=\{(y,s,f_{\tau}(y,s))\}\subset(M\times\mathbb{R},g+dt^{2}).

The Jang equation says precisely that
\Gamma_{\tau}
has prescribed mean curvature
H_{\Gamma_{\tau}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\Gamma_{\tau}}K
with respect to the extended extrinsic curvature.

(B3) Blow-up asymptotics (Han–Khuri
[
37
]
):

(5.30)

f(s,y)=C_{0}\ln s+B(y)+O(s^{\alpha}),\quad s\to 0^{+},

where:

•

C_{0}=|\theta^{-}|/2>0
(by hypothesis (H3));

•

\alpha=\sqrt{\lambda_{1}}
for strictly stable MOTS (Metzger
[
61
]
);

•

B(y)
satisfies the linearized equation
L_{\Sigma}B=-C_{0}\cdot\mathcal{F}(y)
for an explicit forcing term
\mathcal{F}
.

Regularity clarification:
The correction function
B(y)
inherits regularity from the elliptic equation
L_{\Sigma}B=-C_{0}\cdot\mathcal{F}
. Since
\Sigma
is smooth and the forcing term
\mathcal{F}\in C^{k,\alpha}(\Sigma)
for smooth initial data, standard elliptic regularity gives
B\in C^{k+2,\alpha}(\Sigma)
. For
C^{\infty}
initial data,
B\in C^{\infty}(\Sigma)
. The Jang solution
f
is
C^{1,\alpha}
up to
\Sigma
but only
W^{2,p}_{loc}
in the interior away from
\Sigma
; second derivatives blow up as
s^{-1}
near
\Sigma
.

(B4) Linearization and stability operator:
The MOTS stability operator appears in the linearization through:

(5.31)

L_{\Sigma}\psi=-\Delta_{\Sigma}\psi-(|A_{\Sigma}|^{2}+\mathrm{Ric}_{g}(\nu,\nu)+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{div}_{\Sigma}X-\tfrac{1}{2}|X|^{2})\psi,

where
X^{a}=k^{a}{}_{\nu}
. The principal eigenfunction
\phi_{1}>0
satisfies
L_{\Sigma}\phi_{1}=\lambda_{1}\phi_{1}
.

Step C: Compute mean curvature of the interface in the Jang metric.

Form the
Jang metric
on the base:

(5.32)

\overline{g}_{ij}=g_{ij}+\nabla_{i}f\nabla_{j}f.

(C1) Approximation surfaces:
Consider
\Sigma
as a hypersurface in
(\overline{M},\overline{g})
. Approximate by nearby surfaces
\Sigma^{\pm}_{\delta}
given by
s=\pm\delta
for small
\delta>0
.

(C2) Mean curvature computation:
The mean curvature of
\{s=s_{0}\}
in
(\overline{M},\overline{g})
is:

(5.33)

H^{\overline{g}}_{s=s_{0}}=\frac{H^{g}_{s=s_{0}}}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla f|^{2}}}+\frac{\text{Hess}_{f}(\nabla f,\nabla f)}{(1+|\nabla f|^{2})^{3/2}}.

Using
|\nabla f|^{2}\approx C_{0}^{2}/s^{2}
from (
5.30
):

(5.34)

H^{\overline{g}}_{s=s_{0}}=\frac{s_{0}H^{g}_{\Sigma}}{C_{0}}+O(s_{0}^{1+\alpha}).

(C3) Exterior limit:
As
s_{0}\to 0^{+}
:

(5.35)

H^{+}_{\overline{g}}(\Sigma)=\lim_{s_{0}\to 0^{+}}H^{\overline{g}}_{s=s_{0}}=0+\text{(subleading from eigenmode)}.

The subleading term involves the spectral decomposition of
B(y)
in eigenfunctions of
L_{\Sigma}
.

(C4) Interior (cylinder) limit:
On the cylindrical end, the metric approaches
\overline{g}\to dt^{2}+\gamma_{\Sigma}
, so:

(5.36)

H^{-}_{\overline{g}}(\Sigma)=0.

(C5) Jump extraction via Metzger’s asymptotics:
The crucial result from Metzger
[
61
]
is that the exponential convergence rate to the cylinder is determined by
\lambda_{1}
. Specifically, the correction function satisfies:

(5.37)

B(y)-\bar{B}\sim c_{1}\phi_{1}(y)e^{-\sqrt{\lambda_{1}}t}\quad\text{as }t\to\infty,

where
\phi_{1}
is the principal eigenfunction. This eigenmode contributes:

(5.38)
