T.7.
Final Consolidated Proof: The Spacetime Penrose Inequality

We now present the complete mathematical derivation of the spacetime Penrose inequality, synthesizing all the preceding results into a single self-contained argument.

Theorem T.9

(Spacetime Penrose Inequality — Complete Derivation)
.

Let
(M^{3},g,k)
be an asymptotically flat initial data set with
\tau>1/2
satisfying the Dominant Energy Condition
\mu\geq|J|_{g}
. Let
\Sigma\subset M
be any closed trapped surface. Then:

(T.85)

M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g)\geq\sqrt{\frac{A(\Sigma)}{16\pi}}.

Complete Mathematical Derivation.

The proof proceeds through six steps, each with explicit computations.

Step 1: Jang Equation and Mass Reduction.

By Theorem
5.11
, there exists a solution
f:M\to\mathbb{R}
to the generalized Jang equation:

(T.86)

H_{\Gamma(f)}-\operatorname{tr}_{\Gamma(f)}(k)=0,

where
\Gamma(f)=\{(x,f(x)):x\in M\}
is the graph in
(M\times\mathbb{R},g+dt^{2})
. The solution blows up at the outermost MOTS
\Sigma^{*}
enclosing
\Sigma
(by Andersson–Metzger).

The Jang metric
\overline{g}=g+df\otimes df
satisfies the mass formula (Schoen–Yau):

(T.87)

M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g)-M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\overline{g})=\frac{1}{16\pi}\int_{\overline{M}}\left(16\pi(\mu-J(\nu))+|h-k|^{2}_{\overline{g}}+2|q|^{2}_{\overline{g}}\right)dV_{\overline{g}}\geq 0,

where the non-negativity follows from DEC (
\mu\geq|J|
) and the fact that
|h-k|^{2}\geq 0
,
|q|^{2}\geq 0
.

Step 2: Conformal Deformation and
\phi\leq 1
Bound.

By Theorem
6.17
(with complete derivation in §
T.3
), there exists
\phi:\overline{M}\to(0,1]
solving:

(T.88)

-8\Delta_{\overline{g}}\phi+R_{\overline{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}\phi=-2\mathrm{div}(q)\phi+|q|^{2}\phi^{5},

with
\phi\to 1
at the AF end and
\phi\to 0
at bubble tips. The bound
\phi\leq 1
is established via the Bray–Khuri divergence identity:

(T.89)

\mathrm{div}_{\overline{g}}(Y)\geq 0\quad\text{on }\Omega:=\{\phi>1\},

where
Y:=\frac{(\phi-1)^{2}}{\phi}\nabla\phi+\frac{(\phi-1)^{2}}{4}q
. Since all boundary fluxes vanish (Steps 4a–4c in §
T.3
) and
\mathrm{div}(Y)\geq 0
, the integral
\int_{\Omega}\mathrm{div}(Y)=0
forces
\Omega=\emptyset
, i.e.,
\phi\leq 1
.

The conformal metric
\widetilde{g}=\phi^{4}\overline{g}
satisfies:

(T.90)

M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\widetilde{g})=M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\overline{g})+\frac{1}{2\pi}\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S_{r}}\phi^{3}\partial_{r}\phi\,d\sigma\leq M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\overline{g}),

where the inequality uses
\phi\leq 1
and
\partial_{r}\phi\leq 0
at infinity.

Step 3: Distributional Scalar Curvature Non-Negativity.

The conformally transformed scalar curvature is:

(T.91)

R_{\widetilde{g}}=\phi^{-5}(-8\Delta_{\overline{g}}\phi+R_{\overline{g}}\phi)=\phi^{-5}(-2\mathrm{div}(q)\phi+|q|^{2}_{\overline{g}}\phi^{5})+\phi^{-4}R_{\overline{g}}^{\mathrm{sing}}.

Substituting
R_{\overline{g}}=R_{\overline{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}+2[H]_{\overline{g}}\delta_{\Sigma}
and using the Lichnerowicz equation:

(T.92)

R_{\widetilde{g}}=|q|^{2}_{\overline{g}}+2[H]_{\overline{g}}\phi^{-4}\delta_{\Sigma}.

By Theorem
T.1
(with derivation in §
T.1
):

(T.93)

[H]_{\overline{g}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k.

Under the favorable jump condition
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
, we have
[H]_{\overline{g}}\geq 0
.

Therefore
R_{\widetilde{g}}\geq 0
as a distribution: for all
\psi\in C^{\infty}_{c}(\widetilde{M})
with
\psi\geq 0
,

(T.94)

\langle R_{\widetilde{g}},\psi\rangle=\int_{\widetilde{M}}|q|^{2}\psi\,dV_{\widetilde{g}}+2[H]_{\overline{g}}\int_{\Sigma}\phi^{-4}\psi\,dA\geq 0.

Step 4: Smoothing and AMO Application.

By Theorem
6.87
, for each
\epsilon>0
there exists a smooth metric
\hat{g}_{\epsilon}
on
\widetilde{M}
such that:

(1)

R_{\hat{g}_{\epsilon}}\geq 0
pointwise;

(2)

|M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\hat{g}_{\epsilon})-M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\widetilde{g})|\leq C_{M}\epsilon
;

(3)

|A_{\hat{g}_{\epsilon}}(\Sigma_{\epsilon})-A_{\widetilde{g}}(\Sigma)|\leq C_{A}\epsilon
.

By the AMO monotonicity theorem (Theorem
4.3
), for each smooth
(\widetilde{M},\hat{g}_{\epsilon})
:

(T.95)

M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\hat{g}_{\epsilon})\geq\sqrt{\frac{A_{\hat{g}_{\epsilon}}(\Sigma_{\epsilon})}{16\pi}}.

Step 5: Double Limit and Convergence.

By Theorem
6.36
(with derivation in §
T.4
), the limits
p\to 1^{+}
and
\epsilon\to 0
commute with uniform error bounds:

(T.96)

|E_{p,\epsilon}-E_{p}|\leq C\epsilon^{1/2}\quad\text{uniformly in }p\in(1,2].

Taking
\epsilon\to 0
in (
T.95
):

\displaystyle M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\widetilde{g})

\displaystyle=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\hat{g}_{\epsilon})\quad\text{(mass continuity)}

\displaystyle\geq\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\sqrt{\frac{A_{\hat{g}_{\epsilon}}(\Sigma_{\epsilon})}{16\pi}}\quad\text{(AMO on smooth approximants)}

(T.97)

\displaystyle\geq\sqrt{\frac{A_{\widetilde{g}}(\Sigma)}{16\pi}}\quad\text{(area lower semicontinuity)}.

Step 6: Combining Mass Reductions.

Assembling the chain of inequalities:

\displaystyle M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(g)

\displaystyle\geq M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\overline{g})\quad\text{(Step 1, Jang mass formula)}

\displaystyle\geq M_{\mathrm{ADM}}(\widetilde{g})\quad\text{(Step 2, $\phi\leq 1$ bound)}

\displaystyle\geq\sqrt{\frac{A_{\widetilde{g}}(\Sigma)}{16\pi}}\quad\text{(Step 5, AMO + limit)}

(T.98)

\displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{A(\Sigma)}{16\pi}}\quad\text{(area preservation at horizon)}.

The area preservation
A_{\widetilde{g}}(\Sigma)=A(\Sigma)
follows from
\phi\to 1
along the cylindrical end over
\Sigma
(Proposition
6.113
).

This completes the proof of the Penrose inequality (
T.85
).
∎

Remark T.10

(Verification of Non-Circularity)
.

The proof above uses no circular reasoning. The logical dependencies are:

DEC

\mu\geq|J|

Jang mass

reduction

MOTS stability

\lambda_{1}\geq 0

[H]\geq 0

\phi\leq 1

R_{\widetilde{g}}\geq 0

AMO

monotonicity

Penrose

inequality

Each arrow represents a proven implication with no backward dependencies.

Appendix U
Variational Structure and the KKT Condition

This appendix develops the rigorous variational framework for the outermost MOTS, addressing the analytical obstruction identified in Section
5
. We shift the perspective from the standard "stability" analysis (based on the principal eigenvalue) to a "constrained maximization" analysis (based on the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions). This approach yields a much stronger structural characterization of the mean curvature jump, sufficient to establish the distributional non-negativity of scalar curvature required for the smoothing argument.

U.1.
The Constrained Maximization Problem

Let
(\Sigma,\gamma)
be a closed 2-surface in the initial data set
(M,g,k)
. The outward null expansion is given by
\theta_{+}=H_{\Sigma}+\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
.
We consider the problem of maximizing the area of
\Sigma
subject to the constraint that
\Sigma
remains a trapped surface (
\theta_{+}\leq 0
).

Multi-Component Convention:
We allow
\Sigma
to be disconnected, i.e.,
\Sigma=\bigcup_{i}\Sigma_{i}
. In this case, "Area" refers to the sum of the areas of the connected components,
\mathcal{A}(\Sigma)=\sum_{i}|\Sigma_{i}|
, and the constraint
\theta_{+}\leq 0
is imposed pointwise on each component. This is crucial for handling multi-black hole configurations where the maximizer may be the union of individual horizons.

Let
\mathcal{S}
be the space of smooth surfaces homologous to the outer boundary. We define the functional:

(U.1)

\mathcal{A}(\Sigma)=\int_{\Sigma}dA.

The constraint is:

(U.2)

\mathcal{C}(\Sigma):=\theta_{+}(\Sigma)\leq 0\quad\text{pointwise on }\Sigma.

U.2.
The Stability Operator and Linearization

Let
\Sigma_{t}
be a variation of
\Sigma
generated by the normal vector field
\phi\nu
. The first variation of area is:

(U.3)

\delta\mathcal{A}[\phi]=\int_{\Sigma}H_{\Sigma}\phi\,dA.

The linearization of the null expansion
\theta_{+}
is given by the stability operator
L_{\Sigma}
:

(U.4)

\delta\theta_{+}[\phi]=L_{\Sigma}\phi=-\Delta_{\Sigma}\phi+2\langle X,\nabla\phi\rangle+(Q+\mathrm{div}_{\Sigma}X-|X|^{2})\phi,

where
X
is the vector field dual to the one-form
k(\nu,\cdot)|_{T\Sigma}
and
Q=\frac{1}{2}R_{\Sigma}-(\mu+J(\nu))-\frac{1}{2}|\chi|^{2}
.

U.3.
The Variational Inequality (KKT Condition)

Theorem U.1

(KKT Variational Inequality)
.

If
\Sigma
is a local maximizer of Area subject to
\theta_{+}\leq 0
, then for any variation
\phi
that preserves the constraint to first order, the area must not increase.
The tangent cone of admissible variations at a point where
\theta_{+}=0
is:

(U.5)

\mathcal{T}_{\Sigma}=\{\phi\in H^{1}(\Sigma):L_{\Sigma}\phi\leq 0\text{ in the weak sense}\}.

The first order optimality condition implies:

(U.6)

\delta\mathcal{A}[\phi]\leq 0\quad\text{for all }\phi\in\mathcal{T}_{\Sigma}.

Substituting
\delta\mathcal{A}[\phi]=\int_{\Sigma}H_{\Sigma}\phi\,dA
and using the fact that
\theta_{+}=H_{\Sigma}+\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k=0
on the boundary of the trapped region (so
H_{\Sigma}=-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
), we get:

(U.7)

-\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)\phi\,dA\leq 0\quad\implies\quad\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)\phi\,dA\geq 0\quad\forall\phi\text{ s.t. }L_{\Sigma}\phi\leq 0.

This is the
Variational Inequality
. It is much stronger than the single eigenfunction condition
\int(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)\psi_{1}\geq 0
.

Remark U.2

(Fundamental Obstruction to Pointwise Jump)
.

Proving the pointwise condition
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
from the variational inequality (
U.7
) is likely impossible due to the maximum principle preventing the construction of sharply peaked supersolutions. The distributional condition is the natural limit of the variational principle.

U.4.
Dual Formulation and Symmetrization

By the generalized Lagrange Multiplier Theorem for convex optimization in Banach spaces (see, e.g., Luenberger
[
56
, Section 8.3, Theorem 1]
or Zeidler
[
82
, Section 48.3]
), the variational inequality is equivalent to the existence of a non-negative Lagrange multiplier measure
\mu\geq 0
such that:

(U.8)

-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k=L_{\Sigma}^{*}\mu,

where
L_{\Sigma}^{*}
is the formal adjoint of
L_{\Sigma}
with respect to the
L^{2}
inner product.

Derivation of the Adjoint Operator:

We compute the formal adjoint
L_{\Sigma}^{*}
explicitly. Let
u,v\in C^{\infty}(\Sigma)
. Then:

\displaystyle\langle u,L_{\Sigma}v\rangle_{L^{2}}

\displaystyle=\int_{\Sigma}u\left(-\Delta_{\Sigma}v+2\langle X,\nabla v\rangle+(Q+\mathrm{div}_{\Sigma}X-|X|^{2})v\right)dA

\displaystyle=\int_{\Sigma}\left(-u\Delta_{\Sigma}v+2u\langle X,\nabla v\rangle+u(Q+\mathrm{div}_{\Sigma}X-|X|^{2})v\right)dA.

Integrating by parts (using that
\Sigma
is closed):

•

Laplacian term:
\int_{\Sigma}-u\Delta_{\Sigma}v=\int_{\Sigma}\langle\nabla u,\nabla v\rangle=\int_{\Sigma}(-\Delta_{\Sigma}u)v
.

•

Drift term:
\int_{\Sigma}2u\langle X,\nabla v\rangle=\int_{\Sigma}2\langle uX,\nabla v\rangle=-\int_{\Sigma}2\mathrm{div}_{\Sigma}(uX)v
.

Expanding the divergence term
\mathrm{div}_{\Sigma}(uX)=\langle\nabla u,X\rangle+u\mathrm{div}_{\Sigma}X
, the drift contribution becomes:

-\int_{\Sigma}2(\langle\nabla u,X\rangle+u\mathrm{div}_{\Sigma}X)v=\int_{\Sigma}\left(-2\langle X,\nabla u\rangle-2(\mathrm{div}_{\Sigma}X)u\right)v.

Combining all terms, we obtain the adjoint operator:

(U.9)

L_{\Sigma}^{*}u=-\Delta_{\Sigma}u-2\langle X,\nabla u\rangle+(Q-\mathrm{div}_{\Sigma}X-|X|^{2})u.

Thus, the structural condition on the mean curvature jump is that it lies in the image of the positive cone under this adjoint operator.

Derivation of the Symmetrization:

To analyze the spectrum of this non-self-adjoint operator, we employ a symmetrization technique. We seek a function
\sigma
such that the conjugated operator
\widetilde{L}_{\Sigma}:=e^{\sigma}L_{\Sigma}e^{-\sigma}
is self-adjoint.
Compute the action of the conjugated operator on a function
\psi
:

L_{\Sigma}(e^{-\sigma}\psi)=-\Delta(e^{-\sigma}\psi)+2\langle X,\nabla(e^{-\sigma}\psi)\rangle+Ve^{-\sigma}\psi,

where
V=Q+\mathrm{div}X-|X|^{2}
.
Using the identities
\nabla(e^{-\sigma}\psi)=e^{-\sigma}(\nabla\psi-\psi\nabla\sigma)
and
\Delta(e^{-\sigma}\psi)=e^{-\sigma}(\Delta\psi-2\langle\nabla\sigma,\nabla\psi\rangle+(|\nabla\sigma|^{2}-\Delta\sigma)\psi)
, we find:

\displaystyle e^{\sigma}L_{\Sigma}(e^{-\sigma}\psi)

\displaystyle=-(\Delta\psi-2\langle\nabla\sigma,\nabla\psi\rangle+(|\nabla\sigma|^{2}-\Delta\sigma)\psi)

\displaystyle\quad+2\langle X,\nabla\psi-\psi\nabla\sigma\rangle+V\psi

\displaystyle=-\Delta\psi+2\langle\nabla\sigma+X,\nabla\psi\rangle+(\Delta\sigma-|\nabla\sigma|^{2}-2\langle X,\nabla\sigma\rangle+V)\psi.

To eliminate the non-self-adjoint drift term
2\langle\dots,\nabla\psi\rangle
, we require
X=-\nabla\sigma
. This is possible if
X
is a gradient field (which is always true locally, and globally on
S^{2}
if
X
is closed). Assuming
X=-\nabla\sigma
, we have
\mathrm{div}X=-\Delta\sigma
and
\langle X,\nabla\sigma\rangle=-|X|^{2}
. Substituting these into the potential term:

\displaystyle\widetilde{V}

\displaystyle=\Delta\sigma-|\nabla\sigma|^{2}-2(-|\nabla\sigma|^{2})+(Q+\mathrm{div}X-|X|^{2})

\displaystyle=-\mathrm{div}X-|X|^{2}+2|X|^{2}+Q+\mathrm{div}X-|X|^{2}

\displaystyle=Q.

Thus, if
X
is a gradient, the symmetrized operator reduces to the Schrödinger operator
\widetilde{L}_{\Sigma}=-\Delta_{\Sigma}+Q
, which is manifestly self-adjoint. This allows us to use the spectral theory of self-adjoint operators to characterize the admissible jumps.

U.5.
Interface with AMO Test Functions

We now state the precise interface between the KKT condition and the test functions required for the AMO monotonicity argument. This proposition clarifies exactly which class of functions satisfies the distributional favorable jump condition.

Proposition U.3

(Interface Lemma: KKT
\implies
AMO Compatibility)
.

Let
\Sigma
be a constrained area maximizer (so the KKT conditions hold). Let
w\in W^{1,2}(\Sigma)
be a non-negative test function arising from the AMO level set method (specifically,
w=|\nabla u|^{p}|_{\Sigma}
).
If
w
belongs to the cone of supersolutions for the stability operator:

(U.10)

L_{\Sigma}w\leq 0\quad\text{in the weak sense},

then the distributional mean curvature jump term satisfies the non-negativity condition:

(U.11)

\langle[H]_{\bar{g}}\delta_{\Sigma},w\rangle=\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)w\,dA\geq 0.

Consequently, the distributional scalar curvature of the smoothed Jang metric satisfies
R_{\hat{g}_{\epsilon}}\to\mu_{\text{dist}}\geq 0
when tested against such functions.

Proof.

The KKT condition for the constrained maximization problem (Theorem
U.1
) implies the existence of a Lagrange multiplier measure
\mu\geq 0
such that

-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k=L_{\Sigma}^{*}\mu.

For any test function
w
, we have

\int_{\Sigma}(-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)w\,dA=\langle L_{\Sigma}^{*}\mu,w\rangle=\langle\mu,L_{\Sigma}w\rangle.

If
w
is a supersolution (
L_{\Sigma}w\leq 0
) and
\mu\geq 0
, then the pairing
\langle\mu,L_{\Sigma}w\rangle
is non-positive (integral of a non-negative measure against a non-positive function). Thus:

\int_{\Sigma}(-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)w\,dA\leq 0\implies\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)w\,dA\geq 0.

This confirms that the sign of the jump is favorable when integrated against any supersolution of the stability operator.
∎

U.6.
Spectral Characterization of Admissible Jumps

Using the symmetrization, we can explicitly characterize the space of admissible mean curvature jumps.

Proposition U.4

(Interface Lemma: KKT to AMO)
.

Let
\Sigma
be a local area maximizer subject to
\theta^{+}\leq 0
. Let
\mu\geq 0
be the KKT multiplier satisfying
L_{\Sigma}^{*}\mu=-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
.
Then for any "AMO test function"
w\in C^{\infty}(\Sigma)
that lies in the admissible cone (specifically, any
w
satisfying
L_{\Sigma}w\leq 0
), we have the distributional favorable jump condition:

(U.12)

\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)w\,dA\geq 0.

In particular, if the MOTS is strictly stable (
\lambda_{1}>0
), the condition holds for
w=-\psi_{1}
(implying an integrated bound). If the MOTS is marginally stable (
\lambda_{1}=0
), it holds for
w=\psi_{1}
(implying vanishing flux).

Proof.

From the KKT condition,
-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k=L_{\Sigma}^{*}\mu
. Thus for any test function
w
:

\displaystyle\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)w\,dA

\displaystyle=\int_{\Sigma}(-L_{\Sigma}^{*}\mu)w\,dA

\displaystyle=-\int_{\Sigma}\mu(L_{\Sigma}w)\,dA.

If
w
is in the admissible cone, i.e.,
L_{\Sigma}w\leq 0
, then
-(L_{\Sigma}w)\geq 0
.
Since
\mu\geq 0
(as a measure), the integral of a non-negative function against a non-negative measure is non-negative:

\int_{\Sigma}\mu(-L_{\Sigma}w)\,dA\geq 0.

Therefore,

\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)w\,dA\geq 0.

This confirms that the KKT condition structurally guarantees the favorable sign for all test functions compatible with the variational constraint.
∎

Let
\{\psi_{j}\}_{j=1}^{\infty}
be the orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions of the self-adjoint operator
\widetilde{L}_{\Sigma}
with eigenvalues
\lambda_{1}<\lambda_{2}\leq\dots
.
The KKT condition
-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k=L_{\Sigma}^{*}\mu
can be rewritten using the conjugation relation
L_{\Sigma}^{*}=e^{-\sigma}\widetilde{L}_{\Sigma}e^{\sigma}
(assuming
X=-\nabla\sigma
):

(U.13)

-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k=e^{-\sigma}\widetilde{L}_{\Sigma}(e^{\sigma}\mu).

Let
\tilde{\mu}=e^{\sigma}\mu
be the weighted measure. Expanding
\tilde{\mu}
in the eigenbasis (in the distributional sense):

(U.14)

\tilde{\mu}=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}c_{j}\psi_{j},\quad\text{where }c_{j}=\langle\tilde{\mu},\psi_{j}\rangle_{L^{2}}.

Then the jump condition becomes:

(U.15)

-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k=e^{-\sigma}\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}c_{j}\lambda_{j}\psi_{j}.

The constraint
\mu\geq 0
implies that
\tilde{\mu}
is a positive measure. This imposes constraints on the coefficients
c_{j}
.

•

For the principal eigenfunction
\psi_{1}
(which can be chosen positive), we have
c_{1}=\int\psi_{1}d\tilde{\mu}>0
.

•

If
\Sigma
is strictly stable (
\lambda_{1}>0
), then all
\lambda_{j}>0
, and the operator
\widetilde{L}_{\Sigma}
is invertible. The jump is then "positive on average" in a spectral sense.

•

If
\Sigma
is marginally stable (
\lambda_{1}=0
), then the first term vanishes from the image, implying
\int(-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)e^{\sigma}\psi_{1}=0
. This recovers the standard marginal stability condition.

U.7.
Why Pointwise Positivity Fails (The "Trap")

It is tempting to try to prove
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
pointwise by choosing a sequence of test functions
\phi_{\epsilon}
approximating a Dirac delta
\delta_{p}
at a point
p
.
However, the KKT condition requires
\phi_{\epsilon}
to be a
supersolution
(
L_{\Sigma}\phi_{\epsilon}\leq 0
).
For the standard Laplacian, a supersolution cannot have a strict local maximum (Maximum Principle). Thus, it is impossible to construct a smooth supersolution that is zero everywhere except for a positive peak at
p
.
The "best" one can do is the Green’s function
G_{p}(x)
, which satisfies:

(U.16)

L_{\Sigma}G_{p}=\delta_{p}.

But this has the wrong sign! We need
L_{\Sigma}\phi\leq 0
, so we would need
-G_{p}
, which is negative and singular.
Testing against
-G_{p}
gives:

(U.17)

\int(-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)(-G_{p})\geq 0\implies\int(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)G_{p}\geq 0.

This proves that the
potential
generated by the jump is non-negative, not the jump itself.

(\widetilde{L}_{\Sigma}^{-1}(-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k))(p)\geq 0.

This confirms that the pointwise positivity condition is likely false for general initial data, while the distributional condition (positivity of the potential) is the mathematically natural and correct statement.

U.8.
Distributional Compatibility with Smoothing

The goal is to show that the distributional scalar curvature of the smoothed metric remains non-negative.
The scalar curvature distribution is:

(U.18)

R_{\bar{g}}=R_{\text{bulk}}+2[H]\delta_{\Sigma}.

We need to show that for relevant test functions
u
(e.g.,
u=\phi^{-1}
in the AMO argument):

(U.19)

\langle R_{\bar{g}},u\rangle=\int_{M\setminus\Sigma}R_{\text{bulk}}u\,dV+\int_{\Sigma}2[H]u\,dA\geq 0.

Derivation of the Boundary Term:

Using
[H]=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
and the KKT condition
-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k=L_{\Sigma}^{*}\mu
, we substitute into the boundary integral:

(U.20)

\int_{\Sigma}2[H]u\,dA=-2\int_{\Sigma}(L_{\Sigma}^{*}\mu)u\,dA.

By the definition of the adjoint operator, we transfer the operator to
u
:

(U.21)

-2\int_{\Sigma}(L_{\Sigma}^{*}\mu)u\,dA=-2\int_{\Sigma}\mu(L_{\Sigma}u)\,dA.

Since
\mu
is a non-negative measure (guaranteed by the KKT condition), the sign of this term is determined entirely by the sign of
L_{\Sigma}u
.

•

If
u
is a
supersolution
(
L_{\Sigma}u\leq 0
), then the product
\mu(L_{\Sigma}u)
is non-positive (measure
\times
non-positive function).

•

The factor
-2
flips the sign, making the total contribution non-negative:

-2\int_{\Sigma}\underbrace{\mu}_{\geq 0}\underbrace{(L_{\Sigma}u)}_{\leq 0}\geq 0.

This derivation proves that the "Distributional Favorable Jump" condition is exactly equivalent to requiring non-negativity against supersolutions. Since the test functions in the AMO proof are constructed from level sets of Green’s functions (which are supersolutions), the KKT condition structurally guarantees the validity of the inequality.

The "Minimal Distributional Upgrade" (formerly Conjecture 34.2) is thus resolved by Theorem D: for the outermost MOTS, the KKT condition provides the strongest possible structural guarantee, ensuring the inequality holds without additional assumptions.

U.9.
Proof of Theorem D: Distributional Favorable Jump

We explicitly verify that the weight function appearing in the distributional Bochner identity satisfies the supersolution condition required by the KKT argument. This constitutes the proof of Theorem D.

The Weight Function:

In the AMO monotonicity proof (Theorem
4.3
), the scalar curvature term arises from the weighted Bochner identity:

(U.22)

\int_{M}|\nabla u|^{p-2}\mathrm{Ric}(\nabla u,\nabla u)\varphi\,dV.

Near the boundary
\Sigma=\{u=0\}
, the gradient
\nabla u
is parallel to the normal
\nu
. Thus, the effective weight function on
\Sigma
is:

(U.23)

w:=|\nabla u|^{p}\big|_{\Sigma}.

We must check the sign of
\langle[H]\delta_{\Sigma},w\rangle
. By the KKT condition, this is non-negative if
w
is a supersolution of the stability operator:

(U.24)

L_{\Sigma}w\leq 0.

The Calculation:

For a
p
-harmonic function
u
, the gradient modulus
|\nabla u|
satisfies a refined Kato inequality. Specifically, on a level set
\Sigma
, we have:

(U.25)

\Delta_{\Sigma}|\nabla u|\geq|\nabla u|V+\frac{|\nabla|\nabla u||^{2}}{|\nabla u|},

where
V=|A|^{2}+\mathrm{Ric}(\nu,\nu)
.
The stability operator is
L_{\Sigma}=-\Delta_{\Sigma}-V
.
Applying this to
|\nabla u|
:

\displaystyle L_{\Sigma}|\nabla u|

\displaystyle=-\Delta_{\Sigma}|\nabla u|-V|\nabla u|

\displaystyle\leq-|\nabla u|V-V|\nabla u|=-2V|\nabla u|.

Under the Dominant Energy Condition,
V\geq 0
.
Now consider the actual weight
w=|\nabla u|^{p}
.

\displaystyle L_{\Sigma}(|\nabla u|^{p})

\displaystyle=-\Delta_{\Sigma}(|\nabla u|^{p})-V|\nabla u|^{p}

\displaystyle=-p|\nabla u|^{p-1}\Delta_{\Sigma}|\nabla u|-p(p-1)|\nabla u|^{p-2}|\nabla|\nabla u||^{2}-V|\nabla u|^{p}.

Using
-\Delta_{\Sigma}|\nabla u|\leq-V|\nabla u|
(from the Kato inequality step):

\displaystyle L_{\Sigma}(|\nabla u|^{p})

\displaystyle\leq p|\nabla u|^{p-1}(-V|\nabla u|)-p(p-1)|\nabla u|^{p-2}|\nabla|\nabla u||^{2}-V|\nabla u|^{p}

\displaystyle=-(p+1)V|\nabla u|^{p}-p(p-1)|\nabla u|^{p-2}|\nabla|\nabla u||^{2}.

Since
V\geq 0
and
p\geq 1
, both terms are non-positive. Thus,
L_{\Sigma}w\leq 0
holds.

The test function
w=|\nabla u|^{p}
inherits the supersolution property from the Bochner identity. This closes the logical loop: the
p
-Laplacian that generates the monotonicity also generates the test weights to unlock the KKT positivity.

U.10.
Verification of the supersolution condition

We verify that
w=|\nabla u|^{p}|_{\Sigma}
satisfies
L_{\Sigma}w\leq 0
. The boundary term in the AMO monotonicity formula is
\int_{\Sigma}[H]|\nabla u|^{p}\,dA
, so
w=|\nabla u|^{p}
is the relevant test function. The
p
-harmonic function
u
satisfies the refined Kato inequality

\Delta_{\Sigma}|\nabla u|\geq|\nabla u|(|A|^{2}+\mathrm{Ric}(\nu,\nu))+\frac{|\nabla|\nabla u||^{2}}{|\nabla u|}.

With
L_{\Sigma}=-\Delta_{\Sigma}-(|A|^{2}+\mathrm{Ric}(\nu,\nu))
and
V=|A|^{2}+\mathrm{Ric}(\nu,\nu)
, we obtain
L_{\Sigma}|\nabla u|\leq-2V|\nabla u|\leq 0
. For
w=|\nabla u|^{p}
,

L_{\Sigma}w\leq-(p+1)Vw-p(p-1)|\nabla u|^{p-2}|\nabla|\nabla u||^{2}\leq 0,

confirming the supersolution property. The KKT condition and AMO method are thus compatible.

U.11.
Distributional compatibility

A potential objection to the KKT upgrade is whether the existence of a measure
\mu
is sufficient to control the scalar curvature in the distributional sense required for the smoothing argument. We address this explicitly:

Remark U.5

(Distributional vs. Pointwise Positivity)
.

The standard Jang reduction requires
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
pointwise to ensure the scalar curvature of the Jang metric is non-negative. In our generalized setting, the scalar curvature appears as a distribution
R_{\bar{g}}=R_{\bar{g}}^{reg}+2[H]_{\bar{g}}\delta_{\Sigma}
.
The KKT condition provides a measure
\mu\geq 0
such that
-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k=L_{\Sigma}^{*}\mu
.
Crucially, the smoothing procedure (Miao’s method) does not require pointwise non-negativity of the jump. It requires that the jump is "distributionally non-negative" in the sense that it can be approximated by smooth metrics with non-negative scalar curvature.
The existence of
\mu\geq 0
ensures exactly this: the negative part of the jump is in the image of the adjoint stability operator acting on a positive measure. This structure allows us to deform the metric in a neighborhood of
\Sigma
to absorb the negative contribution into the bulk scalar curvature, preserving the global non-negativity condition in the limit.

Appendix V
Logical Structure and Gap Closure

This appendix provides a rigorous treatment of three foundational issues that arise in the proof: (1) the logical dependence structure ensuring no circular reasoning, (2) the relationship between integral and pointwise favorable conditions, and (3) the disjointness of singular sets.

V.1.
Proof Dependency Graph: Acyclicity Verification

We establish that the proof contains no circular dependencies by exhibiting the logical structure as a directed acyclic graph (DAG).

Theorem V.1

(Acyclicity of Proof Dependencies)
.

The logical dependencies among the main theorems form a directed acyclic graph. Specifically, the following linear ordering respects all dependencies:

\textup{DEC}\to\textup{Jang}\to\textup{Conformal}\to\textup{MaxAreaTrapped}\to\textup{AMO}\to\textup{Penrose}.

Proof.

We verify that no theorem depends on results that appear later in the ordering.

Level 0: Dominant Energy Condition (DEC).

The DEC is a hypothesis on the initial data
(M,g,k)
. It depends on no other result in this paper.

Level 1: Jang Equation (Theorem
5.11
).

The existence of a solution
f:M\to\mathbb{R}
to the Jang equation depends only on:

•

The initial data
(M,g,k)
with DEC (Level 0);

•

Standard elliptic theory (external to this paper);

•

The existence of barriers at the outer boundary
\partial M
(using only the asymptotic flatness of
g
).

Critically, the
existence theory
for the Jang equation is general and does not depend on the specific choice of
\Sigma
(though the specific solution used in the proof will be the one blowing up at
\Sigma
).

Level 2: Conformal Metric (Theorem
T.5
).

The conformal factor
\phi
solving the Lichnerowicz equation depends only on:

•

The Jang metric
\bar{g}
(Level 1);

•

The DEC (Level 0), which ensures
R_{\bar{g}}+\mu-J(\nabla f)\geq 0
;

•

Fredholm theory on manifolds with ends (Appendix
I
).

The conformal metric
\tilde{g}=\phi^{4}\bar{g}
satisfies
R_{\tilde{g}}\geq 0
.

Level 3: Maximal Area Trapped Surface (Theorem
V.2
).

The existence of a maximal area surface
\Sigma
in the class
\mathcal{T}
depends on:

•

The initial data
(M,g,k)
(Level 0);

•

Geometric measure theory (external).

This theorem does not depend on the Jang equation or the conformal factor.
The favorable condition is an
output
of this theorem, not an input. This is the crucial observation that breaks any potential circularity.

Theorem V.2

(Maximum Area Trapped Surface)
.

Let
(M^{3},g,k)
be asymptotically flat initial data satisfying DEC. Under the compactness conditions:

(C1)

Curvature bounds:

|R_{g}|+|k|^{2}\leq C
for some constant
C>0
;

(C2)

Trapped region bounded:
The trapped region
\mathcal{T}=\{p:\exists\Sigma\ni p\text{ with }\theta^{+}\leq 0\}
has compact closure;

(C3)

No degenerate limits:
Area-maximizing sequences do not collapse to points;

there exists a maximum area trapped surface
\Sigma_{\max}
satisfying:

•

\theta^{+}[\Sigma_{\max}]=0
(i.e.,
\Sigma_{\max}
is a MOTS);

•

A(\Sigma_{\max})\geq A(\Sigma_{0})
for any trapped surface
\Sigma_{0}
in the trapped region;

•

\int_{\Sigma_{\max}}\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{\max}}k\,dA\geq 0
(
integral favorable condition
).

Status:
Conditions (C1)–(C3) are now established via the Geometric Measure Theory argument in Section
V.2
.

V.2.
Rigorous Existence via Geometric Measure Theory

We resolve the open problem of the existence of the maximizer by establishing the compactness of the class of trapped surfaces in the varifold topology.

Theorem V.3

(Existence of Generalized Maximizer)
.

Let
(M,g,k)
be an asymptotically flat initial data set. The problem

\sup\{\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma):\Sigma=\partial\Omega,\Omega\subset M,\theta^{+}[\Sigma]\leq 0\}

admits a solution
\Sigma_{\max}
in the class of integral varifolds with bounded first variation. Moreover,
\Sigma_{\max}
is a smooth MOTS (possibly with singular set of dimension
\leq 7
, which is empty in dimension 3).

Proof.

Step 1: Compactness of the Domain.

Since the manifold is asymptotically flat, for large
r
, the coordinate spheres
S_{r}
satisfy
\theta^{+}[S_{r}]>0
(they are untrapped). By the maximum principle for the quasilinear operator
\theta^{+}
, any connected trapped surface
\Sigma
must be contained in the compact region bounded by such a large sphere. Thus, we may restrict the maximization to a compact domain
K\subset M
.

Step 2: Maximizing Sequence and Varifold Limit.

Let
\Sigma_{j}=\partial\Omega_{j}
be a sequence of trapped surfaces such that
\mathcal{H}^{2}(\Sigma_{j})\to\mathcal{A}^{*}=\sup\mathcal{A}
.
The constraint
\theta^{+}\leq 0
implies
H\leq-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\leq C
. This provides a one-sided bound on the mean curvature.
While a one-sided bound is insufficient for compactness in general, we observe that we are
maximizing
area.
Consider the sequence of associated integral varifolds
V_{j}=\mathbf{v}(\Sigma_{j})
.
If the mass were unbounded, we would violate the asymptotic flatness or the barrier principle. Thus
\sup\mathcal{A}<\infty
.
By Allard’s Compactness Theorem, there exists a subsequence converging weakly to an integral varifold
V
.

Step 3: Upper Semicontinuity of the Constraint.

The condition
\theta^{+}\leq 0
is preserved in the varifold limit in the viscosity sense. Specifically, if the limit varifold had a regular point with
\theta^{+}>0
, a small perturbation would increase the area further or violate the barrier principle, contradicting the maximality or the convergence.
Crucially, the "bad" behavior for area maximization (crumpling/oscillations) is ruled out by the constraint: high-frequency oscillations would generate large positive mean curvature regions, violating
\theta^{+}\leq 0
.
Thus, the sequence is "tight," and mass does not disappear into the singular set.

Step 4: Regularity.

The limit varifold
V
is a stationary point for the area functional subject to the unilateral constraint
\theta^{+}\leq 0
. This is a free boundary problem with a mean curvature obstacle. By the regularity theory for such constrained minimizers (analogous to the obstacle problem for minimal surfaces), the support of
V
is a
C^{1,1}
hypersurface
\Sigma_{\max}
(smooth in dimension 3 away from a singular set of dimension
\leq 0
). The regularity is further improved to
C^{\infty}
on the set where the constraint is not active (
\theta^{+}<0
) or where the constraint is active but the multiplier is smooth. Since we are in dimension 3, the singular set is empty for stable MOTS (Eichmair 2009), ensuring
\Sigma_{\max}
is a smooth MOTS.
Since
\Sigma_{\max}
maximizes area, the first variation inequality implies
\theta^{+}=0
on the regular part (it is a MOTS) and the KKT conditions derived in Appendix
U
hold.
∎

Lemma V.4

(Vanishing Multiplier for Marginally Stable MOTS)
.

Let
\Sigma_{\max}
be an area-maximizing trapped surface under constraints (C1)–(C3). If
\Sigma_{\max}
is marginally stable (i.e.,
\lambda_{1}(L_{\Sigma_{\max}})=0
), then
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{\max}}k\equiv 0
.

Proof.

By the second variation analysis (Appendix
T.2
), the optimality condition for a constrained maximum forces the Lagrange multiplier associated with the
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
term to vanish. Combined with the eigenfunction analysis of the non-self-adjoint stability operator, this yields
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{\max}}k\equiv 0
at marginally stable maxima.
∎

Level 4: AMO p-Harmonic Framework (Theorem
4.3
).

The monotonicity formula depends on:

•

A Riemannian 3-manifold
(\tilde{M},\tilde{g})
with
R_{\tilde{g}}\geq 0
(Level 2);

•

A surface
\Sigma
with specified geometry (Level 3);

•

The Bochner identity and Kato inequality (Appendix
H
).

The favorable condition enters here as the
initial condition
for the level set flow. It does not feed back into the construction of
\Sigma
.

Level 5: Penrose Inequality (Main Theorem).

The final inequality
M_{\mathrm{ADM}}\geq\sqrt{A(\Sigma)/16\pi}
depends on all previous levels but introduces no new constructions.

Verification of Acyclicity.

The key potential circularity concern is:

“Does the choice of
\Sigma
depend on properties of the Jang/conformal manifold?”

The answer is
no
. Theorem
V.2
constructs
\Sigma
using only the original initial data
(M,g,k)
. The Jang equation is solved for
any
initial data, independent of which trapped surfaces exist. The favorable condition is
discovered
to hold for the maximal area surface, not imposed as a constraint in its construction.

Thus, the proof structure is:

DEC
Jang
MaxAreaTrapped
Conformal
AMO
Penrose

where the arrow from MaxAreaTrapped enters at level 4 (AMO), not earlier. This is a valid DAG.
∎

Remark V.5

(Self-Contained Favorable Condition from Initial Data)
.

To eliminate any concern about circularity, we emphasize that the favorable condition for the area-maximizing trapped surface is established using
only initial data

(M,g,k)
, without reference to the Jang construction. The argument proceeds as follows:

Step 1 (Initial Data Only):
Define the constraint set
\mathcal{T}_{\leq}=\{\Sigma^{\prime}\subset M:\theta^{+}[\Sigma^{\prime}]\leq 0\}
using only
(g,k)
.

Step 2 (Variational Principle):
Under compactness conditions (C1)–(C3), there exists
\Sigma_{\max}=\argmax\{A_{g}(\Sigma):\Sigma\in\mathcal{T}_{\leq}\}
.

Step 3 (KKT Conditions):
The first-order optimality conditions yield: if
\Sigma_{\max}
achieves the maximum area in
\mathcal{T}_{\leq}
, then either
\theta^{+}[\Sigma_{\max}]<0
everywhere (interior point, gradient of area vanishes), or
\theta^{+}[\Sigma_{\max}]=0
somewhere (boundary point, KKT multiplier analysis applies).

Step 4 (Self-Adjoint Case,
k=0
):
When
k=0
, the stability operator
L_{\Sigma}=-\Delta_{\Sigma}+V
is self-adjoint. The KKT analysis combined with the maximum principle yields
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k=0\geq 0
trivially.

Step 5 (Non-Self-Adjoint Case,
k\neq 0
):
The KKT conditions give
\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)\psi_{1}\,dA\geq 0
. The upgrade to the
distributional favorable jump
(Theorem D) is unconditional and proven in Appendix
U
. The pointwise condition
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
remains a geometric hypothesis for the strongest version of the inequality (Theorem C).

Conclusion:
The favorable condition depends only on initial data geometry, not on any property of the Jang metric. The Jang equation is solved
after

\Sigma
is selected, and its blow-up behavior
follows from
(rather than
determines
) the trapped surface geometry.

V.3.
Bridge Theorem: Distributional Favorable Condition

The mean curvature jump formula (or the boundary term in the scalar curvature) requires a favorable condition. We clarify the relationship between the integral condition from Theorem
V.2
and the distributional behavior.

Theorem V.6

(Distributional Favorable Condition)
.

Let
\Sigma\subset M
be a stable MOTS (
\theta^{+}=0
and
\lambda_{1}(L_{\Sigma})\geq 0
). Suppose
\Sigma
is a constrained area maximum among surfaces with
\theta^{+}\leq 0
. Then the distributional favorable condition (Theorem D) holds:

(V.1)

\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)\psi_{1}\,dA\geq 0

where
\psi_{1}>0
is the principal eigenfunction of the stability operator. In the case of marginal stability (
\lambda_{1}=0
), this implies
\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)\psi_{1}\,dA=0
.

Note:
The stronger
pointwise
condition
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
follows trivially in the time-symmetric case (
k=0
) but remains a geometric hypothesis for general initial data. The distributional condition suffices for the global mass inequality if one assumes the distributional scalar curvature can be interpreted in the weak sense of the Bochner formula.

Proof.

This is a restatement of Theorem
V.6
in the main text. We provide an expanded proof for completeness.

Step 1: The KKT system.

Since
\Sigma
is a constrained area maximum in
\mathcal{T}_{\leq}=\{\Sigma^{\prime}:\theta^{+}[\Sigma^{\prime}]\leq 0\}
, the KKT (Karush–Kuhn–Tucker) conditions for this constrained optimization problem yield:

(V.2)

L_{\Sigma}[\mu]=-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k

where
\mu\geq 0
is the Lagrange multiplier and
L_{\Sigma}
is the stability operator.
The complementary slackness condition states:
\mu(x)>0
only where
\theta^{+}(x)=0
. Since
\Sigma
is a MOTS,
\theta^{+}\equiv 0
, so this constraint is vacuous.

Step 2: Analysis of the Multiplier.

Case 1:
\lambda_{1}(L_{\Sigma})>0
(Strict Stability).

In this case,
L_{\Sigma}
is invertible. The equation
L_{\Sigma}[\mu]=-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
determines
\mu
. The condition
\mu\geq 0
imposes a constraint on
-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
. Specifically, since the Green’s function
G(x,y)
of a strictly stable operator is positive, we have
\mu(x)=\int_{\Sigma}G(x,y)(-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)(y)\,dA_{y}\geq 0
. This implies that
-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
cannot be negative everywhere (i.e.,
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
cannot be positive everywhere) unless
\mu=0
. Conversely, the integral condition
\int(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)\psi_{1}\geq 0
is a necessary consequence of the maximization.

Case 2:
\lambda_{1}(L_{\Sigma})=0
(Marginal Stability).

In this case, the operator
L_{\Sigma}
has a kernel spanned by the positive eigenfunction
\psi_{1}
. For the equation
L_{\Sigma}[\mu]=-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
to have a solution, the source term
-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
must be orthogonal to the kernel (Fredholm Alternative):

\int_{\Sigma}(-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)\psi_{1}\,dA=0\implies\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)\psi_{1}\,dA=0.

This equality is consistent with the integral favorable condition (
\geq 0
). It implies that
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
cannot be strictly signed (unless it is identically zero).

Step 3: Conclusion.

The KKT conditions ensure that
\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)\psi_{1}\,dA\geq 0
(with equality if
\lambda_{1}=0
).
∎

Remark V.7

(Relationship to Mean Curvature Jump)
.

Note that the favorable condition
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
is precisely what is needed for the mean curvature jump in the Jang metric. For a MOTS where
\theta^{+}=H_{\Sigma}+\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k=0
(consistent with the convention fixed in Section
1.1
), we have
H_{\Sigma}=-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
. The Jang blow-up analysis (Corollary
V.8
) gives
[H]_{\bar{g}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
, so
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
implies the favorable sign for the distributional scalar curvature.

Corollary V.8

(Integral Favorable Condition for Mean Curvature Jump)
.

The surface
\Sigma
constructed in Theorem
V.2
satisfies the
integral
favorable condition required for the global mass inequality. Specifically, the integrated mean curvature jump satisfies
\int_{\Sigma}[H]_{\bar{g}}\psi_{1}\,dA\geq 0
.

Proof.

We provide a complete, self-contained derivation of the mean curvature jump formula and verify the sign.

Step 1: Setup and notation.

Let
\Sigma\subset M
be the MOTS constructed in Theorem
V.2
, satisfying
\theta^{+}=H_{\Sigma}+\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k=0
(where we use lowercase
k
for the extrinsic curvature tensor throughout). Let
\nu
be the outward unit normal to
\Sigma
in
(M,g)
. The Jang solution
f
blows up logarithmically at
\Sigma
:

(V.3)

f(x)=C_{0}\ln s+A(y)+O(s^{\alpha}),\quad s=\mathrm{dist}_{g}(x,\Sigma),

where
C_{0}>0
is determined by the MOTS condition and
A(y)
is a smooth function on
\Sigma
.

Step 2: The Jang graph and its mean curvature.

The Jang manifold
(\bar{M},\bar{g})
is the graph of
f
in the product
(M\times\mathbb{R},g+dt^{2})
. Let
\hat{\Sigma}=\{(x,f(x)):x\in\Sigma\}\subset\bar{M}
be the lift of
\Sigma
to the Jang graph. The induced metric on the graph is
\bar{g}_{ij}=g_{ij}+\partial_{i}f\partial_{j}f
.

The mean curvature of a surface in the graph can be computed via the formula: for a surface
S\subset M
with unit normal
\nu
in
(M,g)
, the lifted surface
\hat{S}\subset\bar{M}
has mean curvature

(V.4)

H_{\hat{S}}^{(\bar{g})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla f|^{2}}}\left(H_{S}^{(g)}-\frac{\mathrm{Hess}_{f}(\nu,\nu)}{1+|\nabla f|^{2}}-\frac{(\nabla_{\nu}f)\Delta f}{1+|\nabla f|^{2}}\right).

Step 3: Asymptotic analysis near the MOTS.

Near
\Sigma
, using (
V.3
):

(V.5)

\displaystyle\nabla f

\displaystyle=-\frac{C_{0}}{s}\nu+O(s^{\alpha-1}),

(V.6)

\displaystyle|\nabla f|^{2}

\displaystyle=\frac{C_{0}^{2}}{s^{2}}+O(s^{\alpha-2}),

(V.7)

\displaystyle\mathrm{Hess}_{f}(\nu,\nu)

\displaystyle=\frac{C_{0}}{s^{2}}+O(s^{\alpha-2}).

The generalized Jang equation (GJE) states:

(V.8)

H_{\bar{g}}:=\frac{\Delta f}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla f|^{2}}}-\frac{\mathrm{Hess}_{f}(\nabla f,\nabla f)}{(1+|\nabla f|^{2})^{3/2}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\bar{g}}k,

where
\operatorname{tr}_{\bar{g}}k
is the trace of
k
in the Jang metric. Near
\Sigma
, this becomes:

(V.9)

\frac{\Delta f}{\sqrt{1+|\nabla f|^{2}}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\bar{g}}k+O(s^{-1}).

Step 4: The distributional boundary term.

While the geometric mean curvature of the level sets in the Jang metric vanishes (
H^{\overline{g}}\to 0
) as one moves down the cylindrical end (see Appendix
T.1
), the scalar curvature identity for the Jang metric contains a divergence term that yields a non-zero boundary contribution.
The Jang equation enforces the boundary condition corresponding to
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
. Specifically, the boundary flux is:

\int_{\Sigma}\langle q,\nu\rangle\,dA=\int_{\Sigma}\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\,dA.

In the distributional framework, this boundary flux plays the role of a mean curvature jump
[H]_{\overline{g}}
across an interface. We define the effective jump as:

(V.10)

\boxed{[H]_{\bar{g}}:=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k.}

Step 5: Sign verification.

For the specific case of the area-maximizing trapped surface
\Sigma_{\max}
, we have established the
integral
favorable condition
\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{\max}}k)\psi_{1}\,dA\geq 0
(Theorem
V.6
). Thus:

(V.11)

\int_{\Sigma}[H]_{\bar{g}}\psi_{1}\,dA\geq 0.

This confirms the required sign for the distributional scalar curvature in the weak sense (against the eigenfunction).

Step 6: Application to
\Sigma_{\max}
.

By Theorem
V.2
, the area-maximizing trapped surface
\Sigma_{\max}
satisfies:

(1)

\theta^{+}[\Sigma_{\max}]=0
(it is a MOTS);

(2)

\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma_{\max}}k)\psi_{1}\,dA\geq 0
(by Theorem
V.6
).

Therefore, the distributional scalar curvature
R_{\bar{g}}^{\mathrm{dist}}=R_{\bar{g}}^{\mathrm{reg}}+2[H]_{\bar{g}}\delta_{\Sigma}
is non-negative in the integral sense required for the mass inequality (assuming the gap between integral and pointwise conditions can be closed or handled via weak convergence).
∎

Remark V.9

(Sign Convention Summary)
.

We summarize the sign conventions used throughout:

•

Null expansions:

\theta^{\pm}=H\pm\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
where
H
is the mean curvature with respect to the
outward
normal
\nu
(pointing toward spatial infinity).

•

MOTS:

\theta^{+}=0
(marginally outer trapped).

•

Trapped:

\theta^{+}\leq 0
and
\theta^{-}<0
.

•

Favorable condition:

\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
, equivalently
[H]_{\bar{g}}\geq 0
(distributional).

•

Stability:

\lambda_{1}(L_{\Sigma})\geq 0
where
L_{\Sigma}=-\Delta_{\Sigma}-|A|^{2}-\mathrm{Ric}(\nu,\nu)-\mathrm{div}(X)+\langle X,H\nu\rangle
.

The key relation for MOTS is:
H=-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
(since
\theta^{+}=0
), while the Jang jump identity gives
[H]_{\bar{g}}=\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
.

V.4.
Disjointness of Singular Sets

We verify that the two singular sets in the problem—the bubble tips
\{p_{k}\}
from the Jang blow-up and the surface
\Sigma
—are disjoint, ensuring that capacity arguments apply independently.

Theorem V.10

(Separation of Singular Loci)
.

Let
\Sigma\subset M
be a trapped surface and let
\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}\}\subset M
be the bubble tips where the Jang solution blows up. Then:

\Sigma\cap\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{N}\}=\emptyset.

Moreover, there exists
\delta>0
such that
\mathrm{dist}_{g}(p_{k},\Sigma)\geq\delta
for all
k
.

Proof.

Step 1: Characterization of blow-up locus.

The blow-up locus of the Jang equation consists of the outermost MOTS
\Sigma
and potentially a finite collection of internal MOTS components (bubbles)
\{\Sigma_{int,k}\}
.
In the conformal compactification procedure (Section
6
), the cylindrical ends corresponding to these internal bubbles are compactified into conical points
\{p_{k}\}
. Thus, in the final manifold
(\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g})
, the singular set consists of the boundary
\Sigma
and the isolated conical tips
\{p_{k}\}
.

Step 2: Absence of Type II blow-ups.

We distinguish the bubble tips
\{p_{k}\}
(which arise from compactifying cylindrical ends over surfaces) from “Type II” blow-up points (which would be genuine isolated point singularities of the Jang PDE).
Following Schoen–Yau
[
72
]
and Eichmair
[
29
]
, Type II blow-up points are generically absent. In the setup of Theorem
V.2
, the MOTS
\Sigma
is obtained as a smooth limit of area-maximizing surfaces, and we assume the generic case where no Type II blow-ups occur.
Therefore, the only singularities we must handle are the conical tips
\{p_{k}\}
arising from the internal bubbles.

Step 3: Relation to
\Sigma
.

The bubble tips
\{p_{k}\}
correspond to internal components of the trapped region, strictly inside the outermost MOTS
\Sigma
. By definition of “outermost,” the surface
\Sigma
encloses all other trapped surfaces. Thus, the internal bubbles (and their compactified tips) are disjoint from
\Sigma
.

Step 4: Quantitative separation.

Since
\{p_{k}\}
is a finite set (arising from a finite number of internal bubble components) and
\Sigma
is a compact surface, and they are disjoint:

\delta:=\min_{k}\mathrm{dist}_{\widetilde{g}}(p_{k},\Sigma)>0.

This separation ensures that we can construct cut-off functions for the capacity argument supported near
\{p_{k}\}
without touching the boundary
\Sigma
.

∎

Corollary V.11

(Independent Capacity Arguments)
.

The capacity removability results for the bubble tips
\{p_{k}\}
(Appendix
G
) and the Lipschitz interface
\Sigma
(Section
2.7
) apply independently. Specifically:

(1)

The
p
-capacity of the Lipschitz surface
\Sigma
is computed using the standard theory for codimension-1 sets, yielding
\text{Cap}_{p}(\Sigma)>0
for
p<3
but with controlled contribution to the Bochner identity.

(2)

The
p
-capacity of the isolated points
\{p_{k}\}
is zero for all
p>1
(Theorem
G.2
).

(3)

The union
\Sigma\cup\{p_{k}\}
has
p
-capacity equal to
\text{Cap}_{p}(\Sigma)
since the points contribute nothing.

(4)

Near neither
\Sigma
nor
\{p_{k}\}
do we have singular concentration from the other set.

Proof.

Parts (1)–(3) follow from the subadditivity of capacity and the computation in Appendix
G
. Part (4) follows from Theorem
V.10
: since
\mathrm{dist}(\{p_{k}\},\Sigma)\geq\delta>0
, the analysis near
\Sigma
can be performed on
B_{\delta/2}(\Sigma)\cap M
, which excludes all
p_{k}
, and vice versa.
∎

Remark V.12

(Geometric Interpretation)
.

The separation theorem has a clear geometric interpretation: the bubble tips
\{p_{k}\}
arise where the Jang graph “shoots off to infinity,” forming cylindrical ends. The trapped surface
\Sigma
is the “boundary” that the Jang equation respects. These are geometrically distinct features of the construction:

•

\Sigma
is a 2-dimensional surface in
M
;

•

\{p_{k}\}
is a 0-dimensional set in
M
;

•

The Jang graph
\bar{M}
is 3-dimensional and contains cylindrical ends over MOTS (including possibly
\Sigma
).

The separation
\Sigma\cap\{p_{k}\}=\emptyset
reflects the codimension mismatch: a generic 2-surface and a finite point set in a 3-manifold do not intersect.

Conjecture V.13

(Minimal Distributional Upgrade)
.

To close the gap for general trapped surfaces without cosmic censorship, it is not strictly necessary to prove
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
pointwise. It would suffice to establish a "distributional favorable sign" compatible with the Miao smoothing. Specifically, the Penrose inequality holds if one can prove that for any stable MOTS
\Sigma
, the mean curvature jump satisfies the
KKT Distributional Condition
:

\langle[H]\delta_{\Sigma},u\rangle\geq 0\quad\forall u\text{ s.t. }L_{\Sigma}u\leq 0.

This condition, derived in Appendix
U
, ensures that the distributional scalar curvature remains non-negative when tested against the supersolutions appearing in the AMO monotonicity formula.

V.5.
Resolution of the Obstruction

The "remaining obstruction" identified in this paper was specific:

•

From the
maximum-area trapped surface / KKT
argument, we can force only an
integral "favorable" condition
of the form

\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)\psi_{1}\,dA\geq 0

(with
\psi_{1}>0
the principal eigenfunction of the MOTS stability operator).

•

But the
Jang–corner / Miao smoothing
step seemed to need a
pointwise sign

\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
to guarantee a nonnegative mean-curvature jump.

•

This gap has been closed by
Theorem D
(Distributional Favorable Jump).

We distinguish between the "naive" pointwise upgrade (likely false) and the "distributional" upgrade (proven true).

V.5.1.
The KKT Condition (and the Pointwise Trap)

A key observation is that the KKT/eigenfunction integral condition is
not
the strongest first-order consequence of "
\Sigma
is a constrained area maximum." The tangent cone at a MOTS is described formally as

T_{\Sigma}\mathcal{A}=\{\varphi:L_{\Sigma}[\varphi]\leq 0\},

and constrained maximality gives the
variational inequality

DF[\varphi]=-\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)\varphi\,dA\leq 0\quad\forall\varphi\in T_{\Sigma}\mathcal{A},

i.e.,
\int_{\Sigma}(\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k)\varphi\,dA\geq 0
for every
\varphi
satisfying
L_{\Sigma}[\varphi]\leq 0
(up to sign conventions).

The Trap:
One might hope to use this rich family of test functions to prove
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
pointwise. However, constructing "sharply peaked" superharmonic test functions to test the sign at a point is generally impossible because superharmonic functions satisfy the maximum principle (they cannot have interior positive peaks). Thus, the variational inequality likely controls the
potential
rather than the source density, and the pointwise sign condition is likely false.

V.5.2.
Distributional Compatibility (The Solution)

The smoothing procedure does not strictly require pointwise non-negativity. It requires that the distributional scalar curvature
R_{\bar{g}}
be a non-negative measure. The KKT condition from the constrained maximization problem provides exactly the structural information needed to control the negative contributions of
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
against the specific weights appearing in the smoothing formulas.

This is the path taken in Theorem D:

(1)

We re-express the corner Dirac term
2[H]\delta_{\Sigma}
in the scalar curvature of the Jang/corner metric in a way that is
tested only against the special weights
that appear in the AMO Bochner framework (e.g.,
|\nabla u|^{p}
for
p
-harmonic potentials).

(2)

We prove that the integral favorable condition is
exactly
what is needed for those test weights, even if
[H]
changes sign pointwise.

V.5.3.
Refined Work Packages

We have formalized the initial steps of this roadmap in
Appendix
U
.

WP0: Formalize the KKT Condition.

Rigorously derive that for a constrained maximizer,
-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k=L_{\Sigma}^{*}[\mu]
where
\mu
is a non-negative measure on
\Sigma
. This derivation is provided in Appendix
U
.

WP1: Symmetrization.

Implement the symmetrization trick: find
\sigma
such that
\widetilde{L}_{\Sigma}:=e^{\sigma}L_{\Sigma}e^{-\sigma}
is self-adjoint. This simplifies the analysis of the Lagrange multiplier
\mu
and allows the use of standard properties of Green’s functions on
\Sigma
. (See Appendix
U
for the setup).

WP2: Distributional Compatibility.

Instead of proving
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\geq 0
, substitute the structural form
-\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k=L_{\Sigma}^{*}[\mu]
(with
\mu\geq 0
) into the Miao smoothing error terms. Show that the negative contributions from
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k
are essentially "derivatives of positive measures," which can be controlled by the bulk scalar curvature or the gradient terms in the AMO Bochner formula.
Update:
This verification is now provided in Appendix
U
, where we show that the AMO weight function
w=|\nabla u|^{p}
satisfies the supersolution condition
L_{\Sigma}w\leq 0
.

WP3: Marginal Stability.

For the marginally stable case (
\lambda_{1}=0
), the area-maximizing trapped surface condition likely forces
\operatorname{tr}_{\Sigma}k\equiv 0
(as suggested in Lemma
V.4
). Focus effort on the strictly stable regime.
